AN old bachelor wants to know if you ever sat down to tea, where skimmed milk was on the table, without being asked, "Do you take cream?" "SAM," said a master to a sleepy-headed appren- tice, "have you ever seen a snail ? ' Yes, sir." "Then you must have met it, for you could never have overtaken it." AMY, speaking of the responsibilities of matri- mony :—" Would you be afraid to marry on a thousand a year, Tom !" Torn—" Not a bit, if I could only find a girl with an income ot that amount."

A STUMP orator wanted the wings of a bird to fly to every village and hamlet in the broad land ; but he collapsed when a man in the crowd sang out— " You'd get shot for a goose before you flew a mile." _

LITERARY man laughingly :—" Yes, I took to literature naturally. I was vaccinated from a quill." Friend, grimly :—" Ah, the world would have been the gainer if you had been vaccinated from a pick or a shovel.' DAN M—,a genuine son of Erin, while dig- ging in the ground, was accosted thus :—" Dan, what are you digging; a hole in the ground ? " " Arrah, no," was the answer; "I'm diggin' the dirt away and lavin' the hole." A BEGGAR in Dublin had been a long time besieg- ing an old gouty, testy, limping gentleman, who refused his mite with much irritability; on which the mendicant said, " Ah, plase your honour's honour, I wish your heart were as tender as your toes." _

"WHO is that man applauding so vociferously near the front ?" asked a friend of a theatrical manager on the first production of a play in a pro- vincial theatre. "That long-haired man with a light-oclored coat?" "Yes." "He—he's the author et the play." A BAD-TEMPERED old bachelor declares that an ex-team is singularly symbolic of courtship and marriage, for it begins with a bow, continues with a ring and yoke, progresses with a tongue, and ends by presenting to the world the picture of a goaded pair. "I DECLARE, Charley," exclaimed Clara, "you take the words right out of my mouth 1" "Oh, mamma," piped in the little pitcher, "now I know what Clara and Charley were doing out in the hall when she let him in 1"

A GOOD story is told of Butler's sarcastic retort noon a Judge, whom he was teasing for a ruling -favourable to a cause he was defending in Court. The Judge got out of patience at last, and some- what testily exclaimed :—"Mr. Butler, what do you think I sit here for ?" The counsel quietly shrugged his shoulders, and replied—" The Court has got me now."

A story is being told in the Law Courts which, if not true, is ben trovato. A judge, it would seem, wrote to a dispenser of legal patronage to protest against his appointments. The dispenser replied, " My dear , who is your man, and what does he want ? "

Mr. Labouchere has a bitter and telling gibe in answer to Lord Salisbury's appeal to the blood and treasure lavished by England on the banks of the Nile. "This means," he says, " that by killing Egyptians at a considerable cost to the British tax- payer, we have acquired a right to rule over Egypt till doomsday.

Lady Meux is one of the latest to be attracted by Theosophy. She has been paying several visits to the " Spookeries " in Avenue-road, and her interest in the movement has manifested itself in the pre- sentation of a cheque for £2O towards the "Clare " creche which is in process of formation in connec- tion with the Theosophical Society.

Mr. J. F. Hogan's article in the new "West- minster" on "The Outlook in Ireland," will repay perusal. It is written mainly from the Irish- Australian standpoint, and it makes a convincing case for Home Rule based on colonial precedents and parallels. His contention that Ulster has no- thing to fear from a re-established Dublin Parlia- ment is strikingly and forcibly put.

The ring given to the now Lord Mayor, agreeably to the bequest of Mr. Alderman Wilson, of Castle Baynand, has a magnificent diamond of the' value of three hundred guineas. It is the first ring given since the trust was established in 1831. After care- ful consideration the design of Mr. J. W. Benson, of Ludgate-hill and - Old Bond-st., was selected. Mr. Benson is to be congratulated on the production of such a fine specimen of the goldsmith's art.

It is reported in New York that the late Mr. Dennison, whose suicide is still fresh in every- body's mind, was engaged to be married to Miss Hudspeth, the actress. The day poor Dennison cut his throat Miss Hudspeth was busy rehearsing " A Parisian Romance" at the Lyceum Theatre. Just as she was about to go on the stage in the !ast act, someone ignorant of the fact that she knew Denni- son,remarked, "Awful sad that Dennison should kill himself !" Miss Hudspeth fainted, and was uncon- scious for some time.

Earl Grey's illness is regarded with much anxiety in his native county of Northumberland. He will enter his ninetieth year in seven weeks' time, and his prostration at the beginning of winter is seri- ously viewed by his friends. Earl Gray was sitting in Parliament for Winchelsea some years before Lord Salisbury was born. At one time he seemed destined for high office, but soon after his father's, the Premier's death, he developed a cross-bench mind, and has since then been increasingly dismal in his forebodings of natural decay.

It may surprise some people to learn that the Mrs. Fitzgerald, of Heavitree, near Exeter, whose death was recently announced, was a daughter-in- law of the famous Irish patriot, Lord Edward Fitz- gerald, who died nearly a hundred years ago. Yet such is the fact. The deceased married the only son of Lord Edward, who was, as all know, captured after a hard struggle in 1798, and died of his in- juries in Newgate Prison,Dublin, after a few weeks' agony, leaving a wife and three children. His son became a British officer. and died in 1863, and the lady just deceased was his wife.

Princess Christian has gone in for the present fashion of having her head ornamented with sable tails. On Saturday at the Memorial Hall her Royal Highness wore a bonnet, thus trimmed and a long boa and regular " Grannie " muff to match. Princess Victoria of Schleswig-Holstein (lid not look as radi- ant as one might expect, if all tales about an ap- proaching royal betrothal be true. Truth to tell,this young lady appeared both pale and worn, and was not by any means becomingly dressed. The narrow pointed hat did not suit her long features as well as the wide-brimmed headgear which she usually dons.

Lord Dufferin's appointment as Lord WaTden of the Cinque Ports, foreshadows his settlement in England when he retires from the Diplomatic Ser- vice next spring. Lord Dufferin has kept strictly to himself his views on home politics, and, if he is still a Liberal, he would make an excellent Lord- Lieutenant of Ireland when Mr. Gladstone returns to office after the general election. Lord Dufferin was a member of Mr. Gladstone's first administra- tion, when beheld the Chancellorship of the Ducky of Lancaster for more than three years, resigning that office on his appointment to. be Governor- General of Canada.

Mrs. Parnell is still so unwell as to be unable to attend to business, and the probate cause of Parma (formerly O'Shea) y. Wood has been again postponed. An application was made in Chambers on Wednesday morning before Mr. Justice Jenne, and oil an affi- davit from her medical man, It was ordered, with the consent of the defendants, that the suit should stand over until after Christmas. As it is No. 3 in the special jury list, it Would probably have come on about the 26th, but since the death of Mr. Parnell the case has lost all the sensational interest it once possessed, and it will no longer be necOssary to go into certain details which might have been pertinent to current politics.

It has been reserved for Mr. Henry Matthews to discover the most awful consequence which will follow on the return of a Liberal Government. This is that it will " postpone the careful discussion of all those questions in which the working-men take e deepest and most vital interest for instance, the eight hours question." This shows, indeed,- how little the people know their true friends. Of all the reactionaries on the Treasury Bench, to think that Mr. Henry Matthews should be the one who dreads to se the eight hours ques- tion shelved ! Matthews who out of the whole gang is the man most responsible for the Govern- ment betrayal of its pledges to the people—the people of Europe, as well as the people of Great Britain—on the question of child labor!

A capital story comes from Tyneside, where a great deal of pride is taken in dogs and ratting, and where a clever fox-terrier is able to make a reputa- tion which would not be possible in some districts. A Tynesider's cellar being overrun with rats, he procured the services of a small-sized fox-terrier dog, famed for its ratting proclivities, and putting it in his cellar, retired and left it there for the night. Next morning he hied him to his cellar to survey the result of the night's slaughter. The champion ratter was nowhere to be seen. At last he &spied Mr. Doggie, lying fast asleep inside a large rat trap that had been baited with a lump of fried ham, with which he had made himself comfortable before settling down to his nap. What a lark those rats must have had when they found their enemy in "the pit that was digg'd for Vother !"

With characteristic persistency, Mr. Chamberlain sticks to his old-age Pension scheme. He expresses himself as as confident in its success as he was in the ultimate adoption of his earlier "unauthorised pro- gramme." His latest step has been to draw up the sMeme with the modifications, and to submit it to a skilled actuary, who will be responsible for, the figures adopted. Then the scheme is to be sub- mitted to the heads of the various friendly societies for their criticism or. approval. - Later experience has convinced Mr. Chamberlain that it will greatly assist the scheme if he obtains the co-operation of the friendly societies, and a leading feature to be introduced to it will be a plan to enable State aid to be given to those who obtain old-age pensions through friendly societies or other agencies, with- out in any way subjecting- them to Government in- terference. Facilities will also be granted by which workmen may insure for their families in case of death as well as old age.

Apropos of the trouble which is said to have at- tacked Sir William Harcourt's eyes, it is interesting to note how many Chancellors of the Exchequer have suffered from affections of the eyes. Mr. Robert Lowe, now Lord Sherm coke the famous Chancellor of the proposed matchbox tax, is quite blind, and to those who remember nim in the vig- our of his earlier days, when he was one of the most combative members of the House of Commons, it is pathetic to see him, on the rare occasions that he attends the debates, brought into the Upper House , and led step by step to his seat, and as carefully and as slowly led out again. Sir Michael Hicks- Beach, who has held the Chancellorship for a short time, had to retire from the Cabinet on account of failindrght. Mr. Goschen is one of the Most ghort- sighted men in the House, and reads his papers within two or three inches of his eyes, moving his head as he scans each line. For some time past Sir

William Harcourt has sported a tortoiseshell-framed eye-glass, through which in the periods of his speech he has professed to look down on his notes lying flat on the despatch box, but it is used more for action than for sight. The one brilliant excep- tion in what a peculiar combinaticn of circum- stances seems to have made a rule is Mr. Gladstone, who in his 82nd year wears no artificial aids.
THE STORY OF AN INNOCENT CONVICT,
BY ALFRED R. CALHOUN
CHAPTER XXIV. AN UNEXPECTED SUMMONS. Although it was near ten o'clock when he left Reybold's gambling den—for such the place was—
the- doctor Went at -once to the tenement quarters
occupied by Florence and her mother. He had been attending Mrs. Lee, wlio was voi7 feeble, but his business, and it may be added, his doubts as to Allen's innocence, kept him away that
day. He found Florence brave, calm and patient under this blow, that would have prostrated an ordinary woman. _ _ _
" I dare not give up; I dare not lose hope," she said to the doctor; "for if I did, I must die. It is only the sense of duty and the belief and reliance in God that make this life endurable."

" Ah, Florence," he said, with undisguised admiration, "it is faith like yours that shames our unlvelief ;. it is- courage like yours that makes us feel that there is much that is admirable left in our race."
Mrs. Lee had not been told of the trouble that had come to her son and to all of them, and she
was so weak that his absence did not attract her notice.
After the doctor had seen his patient, he came back and sat with Florence in the little sitting- room.

It was not in her nature to be secretive, and when the doctor asked her to explain all she knew about the case, and particularly about the man Mingo, she did so without a particle of hesitation. "I begin to see why this man Reybold should want your brother out of the way," said the doctor, when Florence had concluded. "And yet," he added, "I cannot imagine how any man, granting that he had the demon-like skill to weave this web about your brother, could have the demon- like inclination to do so. Such revenge is mon- strous." _ _
"But the man Is not influenced by revenge," said Florence, with that calmness of manner that carrisd
conviction.
"y what, then ? "
"By- the desire to save himself."
"To- save himself from whom ? "
"From the law. It was he who got my brother Into trouble at first by selling him a paper that was forged by one of his tools." "And have you any idea who the forger is?" "We are sure of him."
" May I ask who he is? Mark you, Tam not in- fluenced in ray question by idle curiosity, but rather by my desire to. do justice to all."
"lam sure of that, Doctor."
Florence hesitated and stroked her brow, as if debating the propriety of going on. At length, convinced that it was right he should know all, she added:
"The forger is a young man named Frank Lef, ferts."
"Frank Lefferts!" exclaimed the doctor "Yes, Frank Lefferts."
" Irene Leffertli's brother?"
"The same, it gr eves me to say."

"Why,. this grows worse and worse," groaned the perplexed doctor. "Miss Lefferts is determined to hunt the criminals down, and I am eager to help her; but will it not be awful if the search leads her to trace the crime to her own brother?"
"Yes, truly awful,. Doctor: but can you imagine anything more awful than the sufferings these criminals have brought to- my brother, and to those who are dear to him ?." .

"That is true ;: that is true," the doctor hastened to :,ay. "The wonder tame is that you have borne up under it so bravely."' They sat talking till midnight, the doctor blam- ing himself more-and more every minute for permit- ting his faith in Florence's brother to be shaken. Early the next morning Dr. Putnam was at the Tombs, and in Allen's cell. "It is all hard to bear, Doctor," said Allen, when his friend had pledged his help, and assured him of his confidence;: "but your coming gives me confi- dence."

The doctor told of his conversation with Florence, the night before, and then said : "I am here to help you; but that I may be able to do so to the best advantage, there must be no secrets between us; tell me all,, as you would tell it to Florence, if she were not already aware of the facts." "You already know everythino— 'hut to remind you of the incidents in my life that have 10 to my ruin, I will go over them all again." And so, with his head bowed and his hands olasped before him, Allen Lee once more told the cruel story of his persecution ; and as he spoke, the tears rose to :the doctor's honest eyes. At lenth. as it unable longer to control himseltr he threw his arms about the prisoner's neck, and cried out: "I believe you, Allen Lee,, r believe you! Say no more, for the torture you have suffered pains my heart, as if I had shared it. Now I shall leave you, 1 but let the thought comfort you that Florence is praying for you at home, and.that Irene Lefferts and I are sleepless in our, efforts to bring the conspira- tors to justice." The doctor left the prison, and went at once to the office of a bright young lawyer;. who had been his friend and classmate in oollege. "I want to see you ,alone,. Fred," said the doctor, when he had. shaken hands- with his• friend, Mr. Crosley. "Why, Doc, you look as, if you, might have law business on band. You. are the last man in the world I should expect a.oase from But come into my consultation room, and let us talk it over." When Mr. Crosley and the doctor were seatell in the private office, the latter, with his customary earnestness proceeded at once to. tell Allen Lee's story. "It is not a little curious," said: the lawyer, when his friend had finished, "that you, should want me to defend thi.E.,young man." "What is there curious about it?" asked the , doctor.

_ " It is this ::My father was the district attorney, the prosecuting officer, who convicted Allen Lee of forgery, and had him sent to prison. I was still at the law schcol, but I recall all the events as -lividly as if they occurred yesterday, for I was much in- terested in the case ; and, only a few days before father died, he told me that subsequent events con- vinced him that young Lee had been wrongly sen- tenced,"said Mr. Crosley. "Then, Fred, let it be your duty, your life work, to undo the unconscious wrong done by your father," said the doctor, earnestly. The young lawyer. must have felt this way, for, after taking a carefulmemorandum of all, the facts In the doctor's possession*,he pet on his. hat and overcoat, and hnstened, to the Tombs with the energy of R. man thoroughly in earnest. Satisfied with what hehad done, stillt impatient that he could not do more, the doctor started for the hospital of which he-had general charge. Not far from the lawyer'Seilice he passed a man in rough dress, with a heavy beard ana shaggy red hair. The doctor hali, stopped and looked into the fellow's face, wondering where he had seen him before, but never suspecting that he was gazing at the man for whom he had secured a watchman't positioa with,the plundered firm of Edgefield arsl Phi?ps, "We have rather- a remarkable ease here, Dr. Putnam. It was brought in late last night," raid one of the young house physicians to Dr. Putnam, when he enterea, the hospital about noon. "What is it 2" "A woman who appears to have had her neck "token, and still:lives." "How did it happen?" "No one knows. But it is supposed the woman was injared by leaping from, a rookery that was burned, last night in the lower- part of the city, fox she was picked, up near there, and brought herd in the Chambers-street ambulance," said the house physician. " Ls she conscious r "No.; and I fear she never will be. That I should' like you to see her at once," said the doctor is attendance, as he led the way to the cot on which Minnie—Mingo's wife—lay like one dead. It would seem that she simulated death after her cruel treatment by her husband, and when the fire broke out she managed to crawl from the building, but lost consciousness in the place where she was found, and had not regained it since. Dr. Putnam examined the woman, and shaking his head, he said, sadly: "She does not look as i she had had a happy time of it. Perhaps it will be better for her." "Then you think there is no chance?" said the house physician. "I will not say that; but if she should recover and tell the truth, we shall hear of an attempted murder. These discolourations about the throat were made by the fingers of a strong man." Dr. Putnam did all that was in his power for Minnie—there was nothing about her to indidate , who she was--and then, g .ve his, _attention_ tsl jtie

other patients, all a whom were there at the city' expense. After lecturing to a class of doctors In embryo, the doctor started for his own home late in the afternoon, and on the way he decided to step in and see Irene Lefferts_s,
As he ascended the broad stone steps he was shocked to see a bunch of crape fastened to the AI servant answered his summons, and said, in reply to his question about the crape:
Leffeits is gone. lie died, sir. about an hour and a half ago."
CHAPTER XXV.
rv. THE SHADOW OF DEATH.

) Dr. Putnam was shoeeed at the servant's report. He had only a slight acquaintance with Mr. Lefferts, but he had known of him for years as a merchant of large wealth, cultured manners, and unblemished reputation. When the doctor could recover from his pained surprise sufficiently to speak, he ashed the servant the cause of her employer's 'death. "He came home yesterday at noon, sir, feeling pretty bad," said the girl, "but he didn't go to bed till the usual hour last night. Just before he retired, him and Miss Irene had a long, stormy talk about something in the library, and I guess that up- set him."
, t` What ,does the doctors say was the cause of death ? "

"They say it was his heart, but that's a way them doctors has; when they're in the dark they always say it was the heart. But there was a lawyer here, and I heard he'd drawed up a new will, and Mr. Lefferts signed it before the witnesses, just before he dropped back dead, with, the pen still in his hand." ,
The doctor wrote a few words of condolence on the back of a card, and went into the parlourwhile the servant took it to Irene.

Great as was his grief at Mr. Lefferts's death, the doctor could not separate that event from Allen Lee's condition; both were linked together in his mind, and he could not but think, that one was the sequel of the other. ln• a short time Irene came down, and it needed ,no second glance at her dry eyes and haggard face to show the doctor that she had not recovered, even in a slight degree, from the awful -blow that had fallen upon her with the suddenness and force of lightning. ' have just heard of your terrible loss," said the doctor; .taking her cold hand and leading her to a chair. "I! felt I Inuit see You and express my, grief, andy at the same time, place my services at your disposal." Irene bowed her thanks; then, aftern pause, as if she were trying to recall words to' express her thoughts,,she said with a painful calmness: "1 feel,that I cannot think. I wantkyou to see Florences Tell her to come to me." "1 shall do so, and I will come with her, if I can be of the least use," said the doctor, seeing that Irene hesitated.

"I shall ,want to see you. But, Doctor, crushing as is my' grief, the sight of you reminds me that we owe a duty to the living." "I understand you,': be said, "and I assure you our friend's • interests shall not suffer for-My nk- lect." . .
He rose; pressed her hand again, and 'left the houSe of death,' •
At any time;. even if expected, such a doss as Irene's would: have been overwhelming, fdr she dearlyloved her father, and had been the idol.of his life. ' ,

But with the sense of her loss came the incident that led up to.it. Her father was firmly convinced of Allen Lee'-4..gulit, and he so expressed himself to Irene the night before his death. Strong in her faith, and loyal to the ptedge she had made to en. prispner at the Tombs, Irene com- bated her fathe• a statement*

Mr. Leffert - a F.:lf-,kilfed man, rarelythang- ing, as we h etn by his treatment of his un, fortunate SDE,• oneehe had made up his mind.. He stoppec Ireie hi the ;midst of her defence. and with a u.ashness of manner such as be had never used to her before; he accused her of; hiving an "ex-convict," and she —stung by the taunt— acknowledged that she did love Allen Lee. "Better he had let you sink in the waves from which he dragged you," said Mr. Lefferts, angrily. "He thinks you will be rich. but I shalt' guard against that,. L shall make a new will to.naorrow. and not one cent of my estate will go to you long as there is a chance of your becoming the wife of this lawless,, unprincipled wretch." Mr. Lefferts was as good as his word. He changed his will, and he had just signed his name to it when Death found him and called him away to answer for .this, and the other acts of his life. _

This misunderstanCting, immediately preceding her father's- taking off, added to the weight of Irene's burden. Though still believing that she had not erred in What-she-told him, she coulsli not rid her mind a the feeling that she Was in some way responsible forthis•lo4 It was heart-breaking to think that he had na.ssed away while in the act of showing. that his heart was not kindly to her. _

Dr. Putnawertat once to see Florence, and he found she had' just retumed from a visit ;to, her brother, having left her little friends, Brtha and Victor Blancirto care or her mother while she was away. The doctor;,lika-most men in his prolessicin, had, a great deal of tat f but in the face ofi Florence's present aMictions.ho was puzuled to know,- how he could tell,her. of Iten&l. less, and so add to the already crushing burden, which she had: to hear. In such circumstances, the better wary is to come directly to the point; • and then he knew that an added pain. is; never felt- so keenly by those who.are, being tortured to the Terge of endurance. He told Florence- at once that IVL-a. Lefferts was.; dead and that Irene mettle-A to see heil "Yours little, friends- wEI remain here till I cam

fetch a wornan,..,a trained nurse, to care for yout mother:. As this is. Something I thought about doing bPiare," said. the doctor, in oonolusion am suie you will let me lave my vvay.7 Florencewas in no humour to debate this polat. For the timelseing she lost sight of her own great troubles in tha•thought, of the .lo that had come to her friend...

Telling Victor, Binue and his sister Rertha—Rie former, it will, be- remembered, had been Allan's office boy—that she would return in about• an,-4our, and asking 'them to, remain with her mother till then, Florence hurried to the Lefferts's mansion. By the time, she, arrived there, the news„af-, Mr. Lefferts' death, had reached + many of his, and Irene's friends, and these, withr,tite undertaker -and his assistants, began to swarmshato the house. The story, of "-Irene Lefferts' a attachment, for an ex-convicb"”hail already become a topic of .fashion- able. gossip; anal, many of her old society friends resented her conduct by .remaining aloo2`from her. Some distant friends of her mother'sfaraily were among the first callers, and, they were- pouring out their consolatinns and tendering their:services when Florence arrived. Irene.took Florence to her own room::the.visitors 'thought, she, was a milliner coma to,. prepare a mourning dress.s, and so made no comment.. Florence offered no ward of sympathy, nor was it necessary te the expression of her ieelings. These two suffering women, understood:.. .eah other thoroughly. "Florence," began Irene, " you:know, about my brother: Much as he- has sinned, against Heaven and against the livinpand the dead,,yett I feel that,. he:should be here at this time." "You are right," was Florence's.repl", "Will you find nubrother far, mel." ".Yesi, if in my power." "Here is Mr. Reyhold's address, I do not won-, der that the mention of his name startles you. I am in no conditionto write tathis Mail, nor is there any one else I caret° trust With my message. Mr. Reybold knows where my brother is; see him,, and say !wished yoa.ta ask that. Frank Lafferts b sent here at once.' "I understand you," said. Florence, taking the card and rising. Without waiting to say. more, she kissed Irene, and at once started off on her mission. , Florence of all Irene's friends, knew all about Frank's eviit doings an this is why—in order to save him—that she did not ask some one else to undertakethis delicate: mission. "Yes, Miss, Mr. Reybold's in," said the nign who answered Florence's ring at the partner's lodgings. He was evidently surprised at seeing a young lady there, bathe had the tact to hide his feelings while he wont into the parlour—used for gambling at night—to announee the visitor's name. "Show her into the reception-room, James," said Reybohl to the servant; and when the man was out of hearing he turned to Jack Hyde and continued: "L'y Jove! this is Lee's sister. I wonder what she can want." "Ever see her before ? " asked Hyde, as be began to straighten out his waxed moustache, " Yes ; many times." "What is she like ? " `.!I ~hQ,N_Va§_riell Oae. would be a belle in any

society in the world. You &in take a peep. at her as she goes down. I guess she's here to get me to help her brother. You know I sent the fellow up. before." Without waiting to hear whether Hyde lineTelc stood this fact. or not, Reybold went into the liwd: reception-roorn off the parlour, and found.Flof-e;t.it Lee standing in the midilieofthe floor. . - "Ali! Miss L. I belleve,"-said 'Reytold. ;bow,,on the skill ,to liz;i!ce' which be Iprided him,• : sel. "I am Mr. Reybohl, and your Obtflie:-..t

vant." • . Without recognising his salutation, though she, looked Squarely into his dark eyes till he.. felt Un— easy, Florence said: s "I am here with a message from Miss :Lefferts." "Alt !—Miss Lefferts— yes." said Ilei,bokl, de.- lighted to think that Irene had sent for finn sooner than he expected.. . "Yes. She wanes to see her brother at once,. and she believes voll know where to find "Well, really, I am not Miss Lefferts's brother's.'.. keeper ; but granting that I am, and that I ever-find' him, wbxt then'!" "Miss Lefferts must see him at once."' . " UrgerA business, &al" Reybold pointed tr a- chair, and loolted •if he were ready to • sit down. when she set the example. Florence without heedlng the gesture, said "Yes, the 'basineSs is irgent. -Frank i LeffertßYW father is dead." • "Dead!" exclaimed lieybold. • "Yes—dead." '9Vhen did he die ?"- "'To-day." "And Miss Lefferts sent' you• to me' to tell me

this?" "No, sir; she sent me to'-rott to ask that her brother be sent to her. if you can do this I presume you will." Without another word, Florence walked out, and Mott Reybold was so dum'bibunded that he could not utter a syllable. div.head: STAMBOURNE MEETING-HOUSE
div.p: STAMBOURNE MEETING-HOUSE
BY THE RBV. C. H. SPURGEON.

With the title of "Memories of Stambourne," Messrs. Passmore and Alabaster have published a shilling volume of contributions by the Rev. C. 11. Spurgeon, and the Rev. B. Beddow, We take the following from Mr. Spurgeon's racy description of the Stambourne Meeting House, where his grand- father used to preach : It was a rare old chapel. I wish it could have remained for ever as I used to know it: let me see if I can sketch it with my pen. The pulpit was glorious as "the tower of the flock." Over it hung a huge sounding-board: I used to speculate as to what would become of grand- father if it ever dropped down upon him. I thought of my Jack-in-the-box, and hoped that my dear grandpapa would never be shut down and shut up in such a fashion. At the back of the pulpit was a peg to hold the minister's hat: inside there was room for two, for I have sat there with grandfather when quite a little boy; but I guess that two grown- , up people would have found it "quite too small ; enough," as my Dutch friend put it. Just below, and in front of the pulpit, was the table-pew, wherein sat the Riders of the congrega- tion, the men of gracious light and leading. There Uncle Haddon generally stood, and gave out the hymns and the notices; and from that semi-sacred region was raised the block of wood by which to the , singers upstairs the metre of the hymn was made known—Common, Long, or Short. There were big tomb-stones forming the bottom of this large pew, , which took its name from containing the table, on , which were spread the bread and wine on days when I they had the ordinance: 1 think that was the correct phrase when our good folks intended "the com- munion." I don't remember hearing them style infant baptism " the ordinance " ; but I suppose they thought it to be one. A few had qualms upon the question, and were baptized quietiy at some Bap- tist Chapel. The pews in the middle were mostly square in form, and roomy. Those on either side were aristo- cratic, and lined with green baize, for tile most part very faded. In some cases, brass rods carried up little curtains, which made the family pew quite private, and shut out all sights but that of the grave and reverend senior who dispensed to us the Word of Life. There were flaps inside the pew so as not to lose the space where the door opened, and flaps for the poor to sit upon in the aisle outside of these pews ; and when the time came to go home, there was such a lifting up and letting down of flaps,and flap-seats, within the pew, and without the pew, as one never does see in these degenerate days. A little boy on a hassock on the floor of one of these holy loose-boxes ought to have been good ; and no doubt was as good there as anywhere, especially if he had a pepperment to suek and nobody to play with. The aisles were paved with bricks, and were gen- erally sanded. Here and there a portion of a grave- stone indicated how the floor of the old building was honeycombed with vaults and graves. There was no need to go to the parish church to encounter ancient dust. Bacilhe and microbes were not dreaded in those days. There is no reason to be- lieve that in later years any body or bodies were buried in the meeting-house : it sufficed to lay the departed within the hallowed enclosure of the meeting-yard." It was not absolutely essential that those whose souls inherited eternal lire should leave their bodies beneath the feet ot their descendants for the spread of death on the Lord's-day. On the right-hand side from the pulpit, there were two large doors which admitted a wheeled cal-rico-Es into the chapel. There it stood with its shafts turned up out of the way, and the sick per- son comfortably housed. I dsn't remember another instance of a person driving into the house of God, and continuing to abide in her chariot throughout the service. The gallery went along the whole inside front of the meeting-house. and turned round a little way on each side. It was to me, as a child, an elevated, obscure, and unknown region. There were men with flutes who let the water run out at the ends of the tubes on the people below, and the clarionet man, for whom I had more esteem, because I could make some sort of noise when I blew through his instrument ; but the fifes (why not fives?) always baffled me. The bassoon man was there, and the serpent, and the double-bass, and a lot more of them. THEY COULD PLAY. There's no mistake about it. At least, it was almost as certain as that other undeniable fact, that our singers could sing. Well, it was hearty singing; and say what you like, it's the heart in the singing which is the life of the business. Besides those who could sing, we had about twice as many who could neither play nor sing ; but excelled in sharply criticizing what was done by others. I cannot forget the big clock which had a face outside the chapel as well as one inside. When his long body had been newly grained, he seemed a very suitable piece of furniture for a nice, clean, old-fashioned Puritan meeting house. if lam ; rightly informed, the veteran time-keeper, was bought by the miller, and is now upon one of his , sheds. To what strange uses we may come at last.
SOUTH LANCASHIRE NEEDLEWORK
GUILD. EXHIBITION AT NEWTON.

The annual eihibition of clothing made by the Association of the South Lancashire Needlework Guild, took place on Saturday afternoon in the Town Hall, Newton-le-Willows. The Guild, which was founded by Lady Wolverton in 1882, was ex- tended to South Lancashire in 1888, in connection with which a division was formed under the presi- dency of Mrs. Royse,of Newton. In 1890 the mem- bership of the division numbered 718, and the num- her. of Articles exhibited was 1,824, whilst this year the number on exhibition was 2,300, being an in- crease of about 30 per cent. The objects of the Guild have already been fully detailed,and it is not neces- sary to repeat them here. The exhibition on Satur- day was of a most encouraging description, and the tables,ranged the full length of the hall. were heavily laden with all manner of useful articles of clothing for men, women, and children. There has been .a falling_off in the contributions from some of the districts, but new districts have to a certain extent taken their places. The principal defaulters are St. Helens and Hindley, but Mrs. Royce hopes to induce the Vice-Presidents of those places to reconsider the matter, and afford their help to the good cause again. The oldest contributor of work was an old lady of over 90 years of age, and in order to show that articles can be made from the smallest frag- ments, a quilt was exhibited, which had been made from collected patterns of different kinds of stuffs. Dur- ing the afternoon, the exhibition was visited by the Rev. Canon and Mrs. Penrhyn and family, Rev. H. Monk, Dr. and Mrs. Watkins and family, Mrs_ Hayward (Haydock), Mrs. Jones and family, Mrs. Seton and family, Miss Dickenson, Mrs, Gaskell (Brynn), Mrs. Brown (Golborne), Mrs. Camrn, Mrs. Statham(Eccles), Miss Bowden (Patricroft), Mrs. and Miss Melville (Ashton),, Mrs. Siddal (Ashton), Miss Cooper (Widnes), &c. Amongst others the follevring institutions and places benefited by the contributions :—Ancoats Hospi- tal, Pendlebury Childrens 'Hospital, Little Sisters of the Poor, Blue Ribbon Army (Eccles), Si, Joseph's Home (Patricroft), Waifs and Strays Society, Mersey Mission ' to Seamen, H.M.S. Akhar and Clarence, St. Margaret's Home, Magdalen Home, Canon Postance, Canon Major' Lester, Mrs. Bin's Home, Father Nugent, Widnes Acci- dent Hospital, Widnes Infectious Diseases Hospital, Warrington Infirmary, Children's Ward, Accident Ward, Prevention of Cruelty to Children, Haydock Cottage Hospital, St. Anne's on Sea Children's Home, Wargrave: Bamfurlong, Burtonwood, Dewnall Green Earlestown, Golborne, Haydock, Lowton, Newton, St: Mary's R.C. St. Peters, Widnes and Penketh, &c. '

div.head: IS AMERICA AHEAD?
div.p: IS AMERICA AHEAD?
BY H. WHITHAM.

I think that in one of my previous letters, I make some reference to the general statement,that, "this city is not to be taken as a fair sample of what American cities are." I propose to make further statement as to • the fact, or otherwise, of there being more substantial progress on this side the Atlantic than there is in England, or in Europe. I grant that there is apparently a something, which mere sight-seers, or surface observers take for sub- stantial and beneficial progress. I submit .that this is not real, but that, as a matter of fact, America is attempting to rush on at such a rate, that her steam valves cannot, and will not, be kept in order much longer. I am not going to speak in bitterness of this country in which I have so far proved to be only a dead-beat. I have an ardent desire to make it my

home. I have a strong desire to see it get on the right track, and keep there, so that it may be a home for my children, when I pass over. Thou- sands are flocking here every year from Europe ;they will continue to do so in spite of all writers having the same mind bias as myself; the, is, they will continue to do so until it becomes clear as day, that the conditions of life in Europe are equal to those of the American continent. When this comes about, few men will be found who will leave home and all it means, to gratify the mere whim of a rov- ing temperament. I think I see signs that these equalizing conditions are close at hand. More than this, I am sure that the keen, active, competitive spirit which is not only in the people, but is in the air, is so moulding events, that it will need all the cool heads and well-balanced intellects to keep the ship of state away out from the breakers. Baring Gould in "Court Royal" says—" To look out for self is the law of life and of progress. This it is which makes the United States so great and pros- perous, that every man lives as a unit, CARES NOTHING FOIL HIS FELLOWS,

and beats his way through and over all who stands in his path." Baring Gould has, unconsciously, stated here what may be the cause of America's ruin, selfishness, and I propose to show that this same selfishness, does not, and cannot, in the long run, lead to her prosperity. I doubt if any sane man can be found, who will venture to compare Ameriean politicians with those of Europe. To Russia only, the most despotic of nations, could the American politician look for his compeer. Bribery, and corruption are rampant in Russia. Can any deny that they are not equally if not more rampant in this free country? I could not possibly give even a resume of what daily appears in ti.e press. No measure can possibly be sent up to either Senate, Congress, or State assembly, but it is surrounded by log-rollers, or boodlers. The worst of it is that these are no.: ignorant and uncultivated men, but are keen, cultivated men who, with the best education to be had in the States, seem to be turned out for no other purpose than that of prey- ing on their fellowmen. Ignatius Donnelly, author of" Caesar's Column," and the famous Shakespeare Cypher, is now leading the way as one of the most 'corrupt men of the time. The reading of the trial is simply•sickening work. A trial is just commenc- inc; of our own State of California Assembly men. Nearly every member of this State Parliament is quaking in his shoes for fear lest he will be ques- tioned by the efrand Jury as to his votes. One is now under arrest ; others will certainly follow him to the cells. These men See the right, and approve it too, Condemn the wrong, and yet the wrong pursue. We have just now quite a number of prominent politicans who have left the country, not for the country's good exactly, but through fear of the Grand Jury. It is stated in the press that one of these men, Boss Buckley, has been using for years both the labour and plant of the corporation for his own private purposes. Coming down to lesser and simpler folk, the evil gets no better certainly. It only gets into the courts when the thieves, of which the richer classes here are chiefly composed, fall out. Each and every boss in the various Cor- poration Departments is A POLITICAL BOSS. , Each official connected with the post is a political boss,and not a situation is given in any one of them imless the applicant is backed by "influence." All the railway and cable lines are owned by men who ' give situations only to men who can show that their votes have been given to seed men up to Con- gress or Assembly who will vote for or against cer- tain measures. These law-makers for the people not only have all the situations at their command, but they are able to squeeze out of all the Compan- ies immense sums of money,yearly. It is not neces- sary for me to go more into detail with this dirty subject, more than to point out that corruption above means corruption below, because all have in a sense to work hand in hand. Just now one of the largest importing firms in the city is engaged in entering upon what will be A SENSATIONAL TRIAL.

This firm receives quite a number of cases of dry goods from Europe each week. The goods have come invoiced as cotton. A marked case has each time been opened by the Custom House. olflcial. It has been taken as a sample of the rest, and all have been passed as cotton. By accident one case burst and another official saw it who wasn't in thesenret, and of course, had no pull. He made a statement that the case contained wool and velvet goods, and detectives were put on the job. The importing firm has been supplying other firms with "cheap bank- rupt goods"; and so the game has been going on, prominent protective politicians exalting the pro- cess of swindling the Government into a fine art. Does any one fanc3, that the result of this, and a thousand times more of the same sort that I could put forward, will result ih prosperity to the coun- try? Certainly not. Of course r am, referring es- pecially to California. Thesepoliticiarrs remind me of Ashmead-Bartlett and his set. We all remember the noise they made while 111. r. Gladstone was in power. When the change came about, the present Tory Government gave the noisy rot their sops ; quietness has 'leen the order since. What conduces more than all to make these wind-blown asses more conceited than nature intended therais the careless statements made by English travellers as to America and the Imerican people. These tourists on their arrival are immediately met, and if not inclined, or unable, perhaps, to do a bit of quiet speechifying, why, the reporter does it, for them. SIR RDWTIC ARtfOIID• has just landed in New York and tells a reporter the following, which is immediately telegraphed all over the country :—" You know, I think the Ameri- can people are the most intelligent, all over, I have ever known. They are so quick, so keen, so lively in their appreciation. r have bad' the honor of possessing an American wife for twenty-one years. I tell her enjoy hearing her better every day. You see I have a very warm' side for Americans. They have always been so warm' in their appreciation of my work that I could hardly help this." Such ruii- bish as this appears pretty well every day; it makes one sick, when one knows so much different. A week or two ago I attended a large and influential meeting of capitalists and ranch owners. I was very much interested in the reading question to, be put forward, which was Immigration. is scarcely possible to discuss any question without side issues slaking their appearance, and semetitaes they prove very troublesome. So it was in this case; they would crop up, and your humble servant would have liked to crop up, too, but he was only a limited capitalist. "California is a big State-, the finest orchard land in the world, and we want to tell the people back east, and in Europe too." So spoke one landowner. " Workmen get higher wages here than in any European country, and we want to tell the European this. so that he will come; we have plenty of work." So spoke a large capitalist employer, and to the same tune did all ths•speakers cry" Amen.' If Englishmen come here, they will have, as well-to-do farmers, to employ Chinese, or Italian labour. As English farm labourers..., they will have to compete with these at 3s. or 4s.per day. If the poor come into the city, they will Mad the say- ing still holds good, "The poor ye have,always with you." if they can bring, as poor men, about .E3al with them they can make a good home here. They must have no encrumbrances however; a wife may do, hut no children. Before goingto another phase of this subject, I may say, that California would simply die out. were it not for immigration. Work- men dare not marry, because there is no settledlife. Those who do marry will not have families, and these two evils are fast growing to be a menace. Respecting the latter evil, the advertising columns of the daily press give clear intimations as to the causes of death so cleverly shrouded in mystery at so many coroners' inquests. (To be continued.)

div.head: PEASANT AND TFER: KING.
div.p: THE PEASANT AND TFER: KING.

At,Szanad, in Hungary, lives a poor peasant far- mer named Pere Bati. The destruction of his crops and loss of cattle-had plunged hini-into difficulties. One sleepless night he conceived a novel idea and rose early the next rcorning and carried it out. This idea,took the form of the following_ epistle : "To the Most Honourable and Well-born Herr King ! My cow is dead—with great respect I submit this-- and my noble farnaproduce has been struck down with hailstones. The wicked 'men in possession' plagues me sorely, though he is my brother-in-laves godfather. There is no living soul in Szanad that can lend me a krelizer, because no in•Szanada has a kreuzer. If my lord would lend me a couple of gulden—for which i he has no mmediate need—l would pay him back with interest when my next year's kukuruznrop (maize) is sold. I trust that good health may wait upon my good King and his exalted house and also his dear family. Oh that I could kiss the pretty hands of our high-born Lady Queen! All happiness to your King's majesty.— Truly yours,PEnot BATT." This letter was duly des- patched, and a messenger was sent to ascertain the truth of Bati's statement. This proving correct, the two gulden (about 35.) which the Frnperot was 1" not in immediate need of" word placed at Pero Bad's disposal.

div.head: 3iORMONS ABANDON POLYGAMY.
div.p: THE 3iORMONS ABANDON POLYGAMY.

We',have now the authority of Mr. Zane,'Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of: Utah, for the fact that the Mormons have yielded to the pressure put upon them, and have formally abolished polygamy. President Woodruff; in a remarkable-passage qu,oted by Mr. Zane in "The Forum," advises the members of the Church to:obey the law prohibiting polygamy and unlawful cohabitation, and adda" I want to say to all Israel that the step which I have taken in issuing this manifesto has not,beeri taken without earnest prayer before the Lard." The manifesto referred to publicly declares that the President's . advice to the Latter-day Saints is to refrain from contracting any marriage forbidden by the law of - the land. Since then, Mr.. Zane states, he has . examined more than a hundred persons, who came -before him forisentence, or who were applicants for • Udionssion to citizenship, and3they have universally ;said that they would obey the law and woultl regard. as wrong to:violate the doctrines of their church. Some have i-aiel that they, regarded polygamy as: , legally wrong after the courts had declared the against it constitutional and: valid, but that they; did not believe it religiously or morally wrong' until the appearance of the manifesto. "By that: • action," says Mr. Zane, 'I ama convinced.that the.. Mormon Chureli abandoned polygamy. and that it . will never adopt it againdn. the United States." It. is estimated that there. are now about 150,00 a) Mormons in the Territory, but many are only nominally so. Amid th &contentions between them and the aientiles, manybave sided with the churcht in which are their parents, relatives, and friends,, without embracing its-faith. These, are described, generally 4 as an industrious and temperate people,. and Mr. Zane considers it would be. idle now, tea_ think obdisfranchising the Latter-day Saints.

div.head: THE...BISHOP:. AND TRU SWEEP:
div.p: THE...BISHOP:. AND TRU SWEEP:

' An old Scotch gardener, whoP comes once in a while to trim some of my choicest,trees and shrulra, told ma this story. He was at 'X ork on the estate of a Itorthumberland Bishop, when the prelaite ar- rived from a long tarry in London, and ehmtp;e day of the master's arrival home a, chimney svveever had been at work cleaning tbechimneys of the large mansion and its conneations, and had. just completed his work as the gentleman met him in the driveway. " Mercy on use cried the Bishop, as he came face to, face with the man,.for the fel- low had just come from the hist chimney,,aad was &literal mass of soot from bead to fost,;.` • vuho and what art thou?? "I, your Grace, am your most humble and devoted servant and helper—the cleaner sand amender of' your chimneys." "Oh, h ! you ;have been sweeping the chimneys r "1 have your lGrace, and you may now build your fires with solid »assurance of Reace and comfort." "•I am glad of, that." "And now, I supßose you would, like me to pay you?" "From yourself, my lord,. either the pay, or an order on your treasurer." pay you.. How much will it be ?""•Indeed„Sir„i3 is a prett,y.- job— take 'em, big and little, sir, there were six-and- twenty chimneys,and I, should surely have a shill- ing apiece; but we'll call it foair-and-twenry. " Four-and-twenty shillings?" cried; the Bishop. "And how long have you been at it, r' "Yesterday and to-day, your Grace." "Well, I de-• dare!. You manage to earn a great deal of inoneY in a very short space of time.* " Ah, your Grace! retorted the sweep with a comical shrug, az the same time giving a sweeping indication of his finger towards ths prelate's glossy habiliments of matchless broadcloth, "we that wear the black cloth most needs get good pay for our work." The Bishop laughed heartily at the humour of the re- tort, and paid the four-and-twenty shillings will- ingly.

WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. ELECTION OF MAYOR.

The annual meeting of this council was held at the Town Hall, on Monday at noon. for the purpose of selecting a Mayor for the ensuing year, appoint- ing committees, &c. There were present Alderman Francomb (retiring mayor), Aldermen Holmes, Har- rison, Greenell, Chandley, Wright, Burgess, Platt, Councillors R. T. Fairclough, Shaw Green, Cannel], Greening, Tinsley, F. W. Monks. Muir, Ashton, Hep- herd, Smethurst, Heaton, Hill, Bolton, J. Fairclough Garner, Dixon, Plumpton, F. A. Roberts, Beaman, Walker, Flood, Browne; Messis. Whittle (town clerk), Longdin (borough surveyor), Gornall (medi- cal officer), Chorley (borough treasurer), Madeley, (librarian), Fairhurst (collqctor), W. Pierpoint, J. White, J. Walker, W. Roberts, &c.

div.head: ELECTION OF MAYOR.
div.p: ELECTION OF MAYOR.

The MAYOR,. having announced the results of the recent elections, said the first business was the election , of a Mayor for the ensuing year. Alderman SUTTON said he had a gentleman to . propose as Mayor. They were aware that at the caucus meeting of the Council held on the Friday previous, a deputation consisting of the Mayor. Alderman Holmes, Councillor Blackhurst, and himself were appointed to wait upon two or three gentlemen to see if one of them would allow himself to be elected Mayor for the ensuing year. Each of these gentlemen refused to accept the honour, so that they were in a little difficulty. He remarked at the meeting on Friday that though they had undergone a hotly-contested election, he hoped that now that they were all met together again they should all be good friends and endeavour to conduct the business of the Corporation as amicably as possible. (Hear, hear.) With that object it was desirable they should select some gentle- manto fill the office of Mayor, who would beracceptable to both parties, and he was very pleased to say that since then Alderman Greenall had expressed his willing- ness to accept the office if elected. (Applause.) As he felt certain there would be no objection to Alderman Greenall, and that if elected, he would fill the office with credit to himself and the town, he begged to propose that he be elected Mayor for the ensuing year and until the ac- ceptance of office by his successor. (Applause.) Alderman BURGESS seconded the proposal, and assured the Council that he did it with a large amount of satis- factionand gratification. He felt no hesitation in say- ing that in Alderman Greenall they would find a Mayor that would not have been surpassed by his predecessors and one upon whom when his term of office expired, might be pronounced the verdict usually pronounced upon the retiring Mayor, s' Well done, good and faithful servant." (Hear, hear.) With reference to the deputa- tion that had been appointed to ask a gentleman who was not a member of the Council to become the Mayor he thought it was truly humiliating that the Corpora- tion of a town of upwards of 50,000 inhabitants, and composed of 36 of the foremost gentlemen ix the town, had not a Mayor in it. He hoped the thing would never occur again. Alderman HARRISON: It never has occurred.

Alderman BURGESS: The asking has occurred, and I hope it won't occur again. He was not saying that with reference to Mr. Monks or anybody, but he disliked the principle' for gentlemen who came into that room, and were elected by a constituency, came in with a right to be asked to take the Mayoral chair. (Hear, hear.) He should infinitely prefer the most humble member the Council had in it should take the chair, than that they should go outside to confer the distinction upon a gentleman who was taking no part whatever in the Government of the borough. (Hear, hear.). So far as Mr. Greenall was concerned they all knew he came of a right good stock ; they lived a good while and remained in harness up to the end or nearly so. (Bear. hoar.) He hoped Alderman Greenall would live long to serve the town in his capacity as an alderman of the borough, and that at the end of the year they would ask him to take the office for a second year and that he would place his services at the disposal of the Council. (Applause.)

Alderman Surrox explained that Alderman Greenall wee one of the first gentlemen asked to take the office,but it was only at the lak moment he expressed his willing- ness to do so. Alderman HOIXES said that after the Committee had waited upon the three gentlemen named on Friday night and they had refused, they were open to any other can- didate, and he had spoken to Mr. Percy Davies—(a laugh)—and he said he would be very glad to accept the office if he was elected. He (Alderman Holmes) told him there and then that he would propose him, and he would now carry out his promise by proposing Mr. This proposal was not e secondd. _ _ __ _

Alderman HARRISON said he should be very much dis- appointed if Alderman Greenall did not make an excellent Mayor. He could assure' the Council that Alderman Greenall was connected with every good movement in the neighbourhood of Grappenhall, being closely asso- ciated with the Sunday school and the church and every other institution the object of which was to ameliorate the suffering of the poor. He also congratulated Alder- man Greenall upon the possestsion of a helpmate who would, he was sure, make her influetice felt with good effect amongst the poor people of Warrington and neigh- bourhood. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The proposal that Alderman Greenall be elected mayor VIM then put to the meeting and carried with acclama- tiog. _ _ _

Alderman Greenall then retired with the Mayor, Deputy Mayor, and Town Clerk and returned wea ring the robe and Chain of office. He was welcomed to the Mayoral seat with applause. The MAYOR thanked the Council very heartily for the honour they had conferred upon him by placing him in that chair, an honour which he must confess he should have been inclined to shrink from if he had consulted his own feelings only. He was aware that he was de- ficient in many of the qualifications that had distin- guished the long list of able men who had preceded him in the Mayoralty, and he must-appeal to them,and he did so with confidence, for their indulgence in respect of his shortcomings which, he feared, would be many and great. But, however much he might fall behind his predecessors in many respects, there were two things in which he declined to yield to them. In the first place he claimed to have the welfare of the borough as much at heart as any present or Past members of the Corporation. —(hear, hear )—and secondly, his wish and desire would be to deal fairly with all members of the COrporation without the least regard to party politics. (Hear, hear.) He again thanked them for having bestowed upon him so great and undeserved an honour. He had only now to add that he appointed the ex-Mayoras his deputy,the Rector of Warrington as his chaplain, and to intimate that, in accordance with ancient custom he should pro- ceed to the Parish Church on Sunday next,and he should f9el highly gratified if as many members of the Corpora- tion as conveniently could would accompany him. (Ap- plause.) •
The MAYOR then took the oath of office. THE WATCH COMMITTEE.—CoUNCILLOR BOLTON
LEFT OFF.-LIVtLY DISCUSSION.

Alderman BURGESS moved that the Watch Committee consist of Aldermen Chandlev, Francomb, Harrison, Platt, Sutton, and Councillors Cannel!, Fleming, Heaton, Tinsley, and the Mayor, by virtue of his office. Councillor FLEMING seconded.

Councillor HILT. moved that the name of Councillor Bolton be added in place of Councillor Tinsley. He did not know, he said, why Councillor Bolton, who was an old member of the Committee, should be left off. The only reason that had been assigned was that Councillor Bolton was interested in the liquor trade, but then their Mayor was also interested in the liquor trade, and yet would act as Chairman of the Watch Committee. Thq Mayor was personally interested in the liquor trade, and yet was fit to be Chairman of the Committee,_ and he (Councillor Hill) maintained that Councillor Bolton, as a brewer, was fit to be on the Committee as well. If any man who kept a public-house, or any teetotaller, was proposed for the Committee, he should oppose him. Councillor H. ROBERTS: Thank you. Councillor CANNELL seconded Councillor Hill's amend- ment

Councillor GREENING supported the original motion. He thought the amendment was in very bad taste after the decisive vote they had at the caucus meeting of the Council on Friday night. There were then 32 members present out Of 36, and they had a decided vote that Councillor Bolton was not entitled to a seat on the Watch Committee. He (Councillor'Greening) romarked at the meeting on Friday night that Councillor Bolton was a brewer and a publican, but Mr. Bolton denied being a publican, and he believed Mr. Bolton spoke the truth; and he had no reason to believe that Mr. Bolton spoke other than the truth that day 12 months when he declared his principal desire to go on the Committee was in the interests of his businoss. (Hear, hear.) He contended it as not fair to that Council Or just to the police to allow a brewer or a publican to have a controlling voice in the management of their constabulary. (Hear, hear.) He wished it to be understood that his opposition to Coun- cillor Bolton was not a teetotal opposition, and it was not out of any personal disrespect to Councillor Bolton ; it was simply because he had been sent there as a repre- sentative of a part of Warrington to do the best he could for the interests of the borough, and by having publicans off that Committee he. believed they were serving the best interests of the borough. He hoped the Council would give such a vote as to show the people of War- rington that it was prepared to recognise that which was best for the borough. (Applause.) Councillor FLOOD opposed the amendment, and said be'could not be accused of raising opposition from a teetotal point of view ; he had raised it from pure motives and from a desire to steer clear of what was known as jobbery. The desire he had was, that the police force should be free from any undue influence,not subject to coercion in any form. That could not be con- strued into any political dodge, as they had just sunk all political differences and bias in the election of the Mayor, and if they were capable of doing that, he would ask them on that occasion, to lift themselves up to the level of morality, and remove the stigma of having a man upon the Watch/Committee who was an owner of property that required watching on behalf of the police. Councillor Bolton was subject to personal interest, and,
if on the Watch Committee, rust occasionally sit upon Committees, when those questions came under consid- eration.
Councillor BOLTON: We nevei do.

Councillor FLOOD: Your association with the trade itself would influence you to watch these matters on be- half of the trade. (Hear, hear.) Alderman SuTTorr said he very much disliked those words of Councillor Flood about "jobbery." He had as much objection as any member of that Council to either a publican or a teetotaller sitting on the Watch Com- mittee, but inasmuch as Mr. Bolton was paced on the Committee by the Council last year, and it was not al- ways a very pleasaat thing to throw a man off a Com- mittee when ince put on he should support-Councillor Bolton on that occasion, believing at the same time that, if he was elected he would on 'a very early occasion re- tire from the position. In future he (Alderman Sutton) should always object to any one who was a publican, or even a brewer, or a teetotaller being placed on that Committee again. Councillor Dixox here excitedly protested against Alderman Sutton's reference to teetotallers: He was a teetotaller' and had been 35 years in Warrington, and he challenged anyone to say anything against his character, or his qualifications to sit on a Committee, although he was not a member of any Committee. It was a shame , that he should be used in the way he had been. Councillor H. ROBERTS said they had heard a few words from Alderman Sutton as to the disqualificatims of brewers and publicans on the one hand, and teetotallers on the other, to sit on the Watch Committee. He was one who had rather a high opinion of his own opinion, but he was quite prepared to accept the situation as it stood and recognise that, in the minds of some people who did not take strong views, both the teetotaller and the publican might be equally undesirable on* the Watch Committee. He was quite prepared to accept I that situation,but he asked the Council to be logical. But the Council should remember that a teetotaller on the Watch Committee could do nothing but what the law re- quired, and they only wanted the law as it existed affec- ing licensing carried out fairly and properly. They did not want those publicans in Warrington who were con- ducting a respectable business—and they might believe him .when he said there were publicans in Warrington who were conducting a respectable bus,iness, and trying,in spite of many and great difficul- ties to make an honest and a fair living within the limits the law permitted—to be harrassed in a trade which was, unfortunately a harassing trade to carry on legitimately. What they did wish,and what they intended to have soon , or later, was that the law should be carried out fairly and tquarely in regard to those houses which were a nuisance and a pest to the neighbourhood in which they were. They told him that he was not fit to go on the Watch Committee. He accepted that position, but he asked in what earthly respect Councillor Bolton was fit to go on the Watch Committee if he was not. (Hear, hear and laughter.) They were told that Councillor Bolton was put on the Committee 12 months ago, but if the Council made a mistake 12 months ago that was no reason why it should repeatit that day. What right had the Council of 12 months ago to dictate to the Council of that day what it should do? The constitution of the Council had considerably changed since then, and they had no right to say what their successors of 12 months hence should do. (Hear, hear.) He therefore objected to the argument of Alderman Sutton that because a man had once been a member of that Com- mittee, he had a right to sit on it. The whole ques- tihn came up de novo, and the Council had to decide whether in its opinion Councillor Bolton was a fit and proper person to be put upon the Watch Committee. He contended that a man who was the owner of any licensed premises was not a fit and proper person to put upon a committee which had the administration,through the police, of the licensing laws, and be was surprised that Councillor Bolton himself could not see the inde- cency of the position which he was attempting to force upon that Council. (Hear, hear.) He knew for a fact that the bulk of the members of the Conservative party were in agreement with them. The thing was indecent, and if it were not for certain—perhaps, personal regard, for the person in question—each member would vote against him on the issue that morning. Councillor Bol- ton had told them he was not a publican. That was a question open to very grave consideration ; but what they did know was that if Councillor Bolton had not got licenses in his own name, he was the owner of a number of licensed premises, amounting, he believed, to some- thing like 17, in this town. He put it to them, as busi- ness men ,could they have from a Watch Committee that fair administration, or, at any; rate, the feeling that the actions of the Watch Committee were above suspi- cion, when one of the most active and prominent mem- bers of it was himself the owner of 17 licensed premises within the borough in which the Watch Committee acted. The thing was inconsistent; it was indecent, it was one of the greatest anomalies, and he hoped and be- lieved the Cpuncil was going to redeem itself that day. (Applause.) They teetotallers were prepared to stand in the background until public opinion was sufficiently ripe to justify them in going upon the Watch Committee. What they wanted was a committee which was above suspicion ; they asked for nothing more, and would be content with nothing less. (Applause.) Councillor BOLTON said there was hardly a speaker who had not thrown out some insinuation but all that they could say against him was that he was a Conserva- tive. (" No no " and "Oh oh.") It began and ended there, for he defied Councillor Fleming and Aid. Platt, who were members of the Watch Committee to say that there was a single instance or case during the past twelve months that they could point to in which he had attempted or could have attempted to use his 'position for the benefit of the trade. The matters referred to never came before the Watch Committee as the police got their instructions either from the Watch Committee or the Chief Constable, and all they had to do with the police was to deal in the way of punishment when anything went wrong. Councillor Flood said that his houses wanted watching, but if Coun- cillor Flood would tell him what it was that needed watching he would see that it was entirely done away with. He was under the impression that if he could Councillor H. Roberts would set the police on to watch those public houses which were occupied by those who were not' politically his own friends. (Laughter.) Let them look at the mud that was flung last Monday, and the only man they could talk about in the Liberal Club was himself. (Laughter.) They said that because be was a brewer he.would not be honest, and he could not be anything, yet if they could bring anything against him while he had been in that Town Council he hoped they would bring it forward. He did not care about being on the Watch Committee, and if he was elected that day he would leave it for the simple reason that it would take the sting out of the taunts. Councillor ROBERTS: Resign now. • _ _

- Councillor BOLTON said wlien he was returned to the Town Council he promised that he would suffer himself to be placed on the Watch Committee and that promise he intended to keep. There was a principle involved. He contended that if a man was elected to the Town Council he came there fit to be put upon any Committee and to do any work ; if he was not fit for that he had no right to be sent as a member of the Council. If a man was not qualified to do certain work the law ought to step in and debar him. (Hear, hear.) He had one of those pamphlets or handbills, which were sent round at that election for electioneering purposes, containing questions, and the first question asked of the candidates was whether if.. elected they would vote against any person connected with the liquor trade having a seat on the Watch Com- mittee, and went on to say the first thing those people who never did anything wrong—he was al- luding to the teetotallers or the professed te;totallera— did was to elect to be Chairman of the Watch Committee a gentleman who was connected with the liquor trade. He could not see where their consistency was.

Councillor H. ROBERTS: We 'cannot displace the 'Mayor. Councillor BOLTON said they could have voted against his being made Mayor. That was purely a personal affair. Councillor H. Fairciough, Flood, Heat- on, Hutchinson, Muir, and Smethurst. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 14, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 14, 1891.

Alderman PLATT seconded the proposal, and said he believed Whitecross Ward particularly needed the attep7, tion of the Paving and Sewerage Committee. Councillor BOLTON supported the appointment of Mr. Smethurst.

_ Councillor SHAW GREEN supported the amendment, and said he had been approached by residents in White- cross Ward who said they were very anxious that Councillor Plumpton should be placed on the Committee. - -

CouncillOr HUTCHINSON and Aldermen HARRISON both supported the original motion. Councillor PLUDIPTON said that he and the opposing candidate in Whitecross Ward were both specially pledged to look after the paving of the streets and back passages in Whitecross Ward.He was particularly anxious to be on that Cemmittee .because there were some in- direct interests affected. Streets belonging to a gentle- man on the Paving and Sewerage Committee were noth- ing better than a midden, and they had been in that state five or six years. He had been told only that morn- ing that water lay in the streets and when children went add stirred up the midden the stench was so strong that people could not bear it in their houses. They said they had got up two petitions signed by the occupiers but to neither of them had they received a reply. He had no interest to serve on that Committee except the interests of the electors of the ward. (ffttar, hear.) ROBERTS said he believed Councillor Smethurst would just as soon be placed upon some other Committee as upon that one, and he should certainly like to see one of the representatives of White,cross Ward on the Committee.

He maintained Whitecross had been for some little time receiving as much attention as any other ward in the town. Councillor PLUMPTON What about Keen-street?
