The following gentlemen were appointed ths return- ing officers :—Town Hall Ward, Alderman Green& II; Whitecross, Alderman Platt ; Bewsey, Alderman Holmes; Orford, Alderman Harrison ; St. John's, Alderman Sut- ton ; Fairfield, Alderman Wright; Howley, Alderman Francomb ; St. Austin's, Alderman Burgess; acd Latch- ford, Alderman Chandley.
ANOTHER ATTEMPTED SUICIDE IN THE MERSEY.

At the Borough Magistrates' Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. E. J. Guest, Ruth Jones, wife of John John Jones, Ship Canal worker, of no settled home, was charged, on remand, with attempting to com- mit suicide, by drowning,in the Mersey, on the pre- vious Friday night.—Chief Constable Hunt said she had been found in the water up to her knees, or deeper in it, on the Cheshire side of the Warrington Bridge, near to Mr. Fairclough's corn warehouse. She cried out, and a young man went and pulled her out. She said her husband had been drinking for some time, and they had had a quarrel, and she, in a fit of passsion, committed the act. She was brought before Alderman Burgess, pn Saturday, and remanded for further information, and, if possible, to have her husband present.—The husband corro- borated Mr. Hunt's statement. He said he was walking down Mersey-st. about ten minutes past eleven, on the night in question, with his father, and heard a scream from the direction of the river. He ran there, and found the prisoner in the water, and pulled her o.ut.—She was dismissed with a cau- tion, but ordered to pay costs.
The tomb of the morganatic wife of King Victor Emanuel has been entered, and the coffin in wnich the deceased was enclosed set fire to.

Dr. Hensley, of Newton Abbott, was called in to attend a little son of the Rev. T. Hudson. The doctor was accidentally bitten by the child, who was suffering from diphtheria. After the child's death Dr. Hensley :also was seized with diphtheria, and died on Monday.

div.head: UNIONIST MEETING AT THEL WALL.
div.p: UNIONIST MEETING AT THEL WALL.

A Unionist demonstration was held in the Tem- perance Hall, ThelWall, on Saturday night, which was largely attended. Mr. R. A. Naylor presided, and was supported on the platform by Mr. T. W. Russell, M.P., for South Tyrone. Mr. Coningsby Disraeli, Unionist catididate for the Altrincham Division, Rear Admiral Parry, Major and Mrs. Pickmere, Mr. and Mrs. W. IL Bleckly, Dr. and Mrs. Lister Kaye, Mr. and Mrs. L. W. Reynolds, Mr. and Mrs. Callender, and Dr. and Mrs. Sherratt. The CIIAIILISAN said he had received a telegram from Hon. Alan de Tatton Egerton that he was prevented by a severe cold from being present; and read letters of ' apology from Mr. Stubs, Mr. J. C. Parr, and the' Mayor of Warrington, for absence. The Chairman pro- ceeded to say that it seemed to him that when there was an important question before the country it was necessary for every true patriot, whether he cared for politics or not, to come forth and show,oh which side he was. They owed this as a duty to those who had gone before them, as well as to those who would have to follow them. This great nation had been built up by the sacrifices of their high-minded forefathers. They had no right to tamper with the integrity of the empire or to undo the good work which their noble minded ancestors had done for them.

Rear-Admiral PARRY moved a resolution congratulat- ing the Unionist Government on their home and foreign policy, and expressing a hope that in the next election the patriotic vote would return them to power. Major Pickmere seconded. '

Mr. T. W. RUSSELL, M.P., then addressed the meeting in support of the resolution. He said he was very glad to be able, on his way to the Unionist meetings in Man- chester next week, to come to Thelwall and address those who, he hoped and believed, would be Mr. Con- ningsby Disraeli's constituents before 12 months had passed. (Applause.) The resolution was a. vindication orthe Government in its home and foreign policy. How did the case stand with regard to home policy? That had been the main feature of the Government policy during the last five years. The Government came into power upon that, and he hoped they would remain in upon it. (Applause.) What was the state of Ireland in 1886 when the Government took office? In 1885 Ireland was in a state of confusion and chaos and disorder. Murder was rife, agrarian crime was steadily rising, evictions for non- payment of rent were numerous, contracts everywhere repudiated; the plan of campaign, an organised system of robbery, was episcopally blessed, and boycotting al- most universal. What was the state of Ireland now? Murder was much more rare in that country than in Scotland or England. Agrarian crime had diminished by 60 per cent., evictions had diminished by 50 per cent. the " plan of campaign" was either dead or dying, con- tracts were respected, boycotting had all but ceased, and everywhere the constabulary were employed not in protecting Mr. Balfour, or the landlords, or the tenants, but in protecting the sacred persons Of Mr. T. Healy and Mr. W. O'Brien—(laughter)—from the tender mercies of the people of Ireland. • Ireland had entered upon a time of prosperity, such as she had not known for the last 35 years. The Coercion Act, was not in existence in Ireland at present, except in the county of Clare, at Blarney in Tipperary, and at Blarney in Galway. It had not been repealed, but simply laid on the shelf; and if Mr. Gladstone's friends commenced in any neighbourhood coercing and intimidating people It could be taken down and applied to them. The speaker, dealing with foreign affairs, claimed that there had not been a shilling of war expenditure during the five years. .We had been at peace with, and had the respect of all the world. If they looked at the contrast between 1880 and 1885, when Mr. Gladstone was in power, they would be horrified. We would find the forts of Alexandria battered down, and the wastes of the Soudan strewn with thousands of Arab corpses—corpses of men who Mr. Gladstone said, were struggling to be free, and yet whom he killed. They would find Gordon sent to Khartoum and left there. Dealing with the Home Rule question, Mr. Russell said that Mr. Glad- stone's Newcastle programme meant that it was to be put into the front, if he were returned to power, and that social reforms should take a back seat. If they were men they would insist that Ireland should take a back seat. (Hear hear.) Irelaad had got more than justice, and it was time other people had something. (Applause.) He challenged Mr. Gladstone's statement that Ireland was oppressed. She had 30 per cent. more representation per head of the population than England had. The Imperial Parliament hail done nothing, for the last twenty years but redress Irish wrongs. She had a Land Court such as no other nation possessed. The position of the Irish farmer was enough to make the mouths of English farmers water. They hoped to give Ireland next year local government and free education, both bills being ready,and this being done the Irish book must be closed and the consideration of measures of reform for England and Scotland be en- tered upon.—The resolution was put and carried with one dissentient. (Applause.) Mr. CONINGSBY DISRAELI proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Russell. He said the Unionist cause was one that , brought together Liberal and Conservative,that brought ' on the same platform Lord Salisbury and Lord Harting- I ten, Mr. Chamberlain and Mr. Balfour, and kept fresh the commands of John Bright from his grave, that they should always resist any attempt at destroying the integ- rity of this Empire. (Applause.) He considered It was a great triumph for the Unionists that the late Chief Secretary for Ireland, Mr. Balfour should have become leader of the House of Commons. The two sections of the Unionist party would now be bound clOser and closer together,and now the Opposition could have no hope that there would be a split or difference between them. If. he said, in the next election the Gladstonian party obtained power the Irish question would be brought up again and kept to the front by wrangling and by jangling until the people of England rose in a body and drove the new Government from power. But if the Unionist power obtained the majority then the Irish question would be done with, and they could proceed to social legislation for England and Scot- land. (Applause.)
Mr. Mealy seconled the motion, and the vote of thanks was carried and acknowledged by Mr. Russell. Another was accorded to the Chairman and the meeting concluded.

div.head: MINISTERIAL CHANGES.
div.p: THE MINISTERIAL CHANGES.

It is officially stated that the Queen has been pleased to approve the appointment of the Right Hon. W. L. Jackson, M.P., to be Chief Secretary to theLord-Lieu- tenant of Ireland, in room of the, Right Hon. A. J. Balfour.

Her Majesty has also been pleased to approve the appointment of the Right Hon. Sir John Eldon Gorst, Q.C., M.P., to be Financial Secretary to the Treasury, in room of the Right Hon. W. L. Jackson, M.P. • The North Leeds Liberal Association has decided to offer no opposition to the re-election of Mr. W. L: Jack- son, but to contest the seat vigorously at the general election.

div.head: MEETING OF THB CABINET.
div.p: MEETING OF THB CABINET.

The first Cabinet Council since the prorogation of Par- liament in August was held at half-past twelve on Tues- day at the Foreign Office. 'Mr. Jackson, who was the last to arrive, was escorted to the Cabinet Chamber by Mr. Akers-Douglas. Both Mr. Balfour and Mr. Jackson received hearty congratulations from their colleagues upon their new appointments.
For newspapers, books, and patterns for places abroad it is contemplated to ,make shortly very substantial re- ductions of postage.

div.head: GAS AND WATER.
div.p: GAS AND WATER.

The Gas and Water Committee reported that Messrs. Johnson, Clapman, and Morris, had claimed £lO for damage alleged to have been sustained at their works in consequence of the bursting of a water miin, belonging to the Board, and the Clerk was instructed to reply, denying liability. The gas had been tested on the 7th, 23rd, and 29th October, and the tests read, illuminating power 17.49, 1930,. and 17.30 candles, free from sulphur- etted hydrogen.—The engineer reported that a water meter had been fixed up 4rt Waterloo-road district, but the whole of the district had not yet been connected up. Of the 243 houses at present under check, the total consumption per head was 17.08 gallons, of which 1308 gallons, were waste, leaving the actual quantity used, per head per day 3.26 gallons. The mean rainfall of the month has btea 309 inches, and the water in stock was 8,535,737, gallons. It was decided that Messrs. Ellison and Sons be engaged as architects to prepare plans, and superintend the erection of the proposed additional buildings. The wages required for the Gas and Water Works for the first four weeks, amounted to 1115 per week. The tender of Mr. Hanor Locker, and of the concrete -engine had at Netherley was accepted: The minutes were approved, on the proposal of Mr. D. Wright.
HIGHWAY MATTERS.

The Highway Committee reported that the wages estimated for the next four weeks were V2B 12s. per week. It was recommended that application be made to the County Council fir Norlands-lane from Rainhill to be declared a main road, in addition to the road already proposed. It was recommended that notices be served upon several owners calling upon them to sewer and pave the back passages of their property.—The Surveyor was authorised to enter any place of public resort to see that the provisions of the Public Health Act were carried into effect.—Mr. Taylor moved the adoption of the minutes. —Mr. Neil seconded.—Carried.
HIALTH COMMITTNE.-THE SULPHUR NUISANCE.

The Health Committee recommended that John McNaughten O'Keeffe,L.R.C.P.and L.R.C.S.,Edinburgh, be appointed M.O.H. for this district under the Public Health Act, 1875, for a period of one year, at the salary of £llO per annum. That Walter L3we be appointed Nuisance Inspector for this district under the Public Health Act, 1875, for a period of one year, at the salary (if £ll4 per annum. That Dr. O'Keeffs be appointed Superintendent of the Infectious Diseases and Accident Hospitals of the Local Authority concurrently with his appointment as M.0.H., at a salary of £lO per annum ; and that his duties be to superintend the management of and regularly visit tne hospital, regulate the ad- mission of patients thereto, and report at each monthly meeting of the committee upon the state and condition -of the hospitals. The Clerrsubmitted correspondence whch had taken place between himself and The United Alkali Co.:and Dr. Affleck, with reference to the complaints made of the escape of sulphuretted hydrogen in this district. He also reported that Dr. Affieck had called and discussed the matter with him, and that it was Dr. Affieck's , opinion that the nuisance did not emanate from the Chance Claus process but from the waste heaps, to which he in- tended to give special attention with a view to remedy- ing, as far as possible, the evil complained of. Recom- mended that the Clerk write to the manufacturers and depositors of waste requesting them to keep the waste from the Chance Claus process separate from the ordin- ary waste; and that manufacturers be requested when forwarding consignments for the purpose of deposit to label and keep them in two distinct divisions. At the suggestion of Superintendent Noblett, the In- spector and from Sergeants of police were appointed inspectors of common lodging houses. The Medical Officer reported that during October there were 114 births and 52 deaths being at the respective rates of 44.12 and 2012 per 1,000. Resolved unanimously that this Committee being satisfied with the manner in which Miss Milburn has discharged her duties as matron recommended unanimously that her salary be advanced to £4O per annum. Mr. D. Wright moved the adoption of the minutes.—. Mr. Timmis seconded.—The minutes were passed.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

The Finance Committee reported that the Rey. W. Thornley and Mr. David Wright attended as a deputa- tion of the Trustees of the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Simrn's Cross, and asked the Committee to remit the charges for street expenses (£4B 16s. 11d.) apportioned upon the Trustees in respect of the land belonging to them in Frederick-st., on the ground that such land bad been acquired solely for the purpose of the erection of a chapel thereon. Resolved that provided the Trustees enter into a formal undertaking, to be prepared by the Clerk, that in the event of the land being at any time used for any other purpose than the erection of a chapel they will pay the amount of such charges, the Board be recommended not to press for payment thereof at present.—The minutes were approved on the motion of Mr. Midwood.
TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION COMMITTEE

This Committee, reported that the sub-Committee appointed to make arrangemonts for establishing extra classes, reported that classes had been formed for teach- ing the French language, mathematics, and shorthand; and that they had engaged Mr. William Harrison, 8.A., head master of the Farnworth Grammar School, and Mr. B. Meunier, of Liverpool. as teachers. Circular letter read, dated 29th October, from the Clerk of the Peace. stating that the Technical Instruction Committee would recommend to the County Council the payment to the Local Board of the sum of £4BO for the purposes of technical instruction. Resolved that application be made to the department of Science and Art for a grant towards the purchase of apparatus, as shown on the lists prepared by the teachers, amounting to £154 17s. The sub-committee were requested to take into consid- eration the advisability of forming classes for the teach- ing of dressmaking..—The minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Wright. Dr. O'Keeffe and Yr. E. Carey were unanimously appointed 'nembers of the Committee.
THE VACANCIES.

The Board went -into -C-Wricrnit-tee to consider the vacancies on the Board caused by the resignation of Dr. O'Keefe, and by the absence of Messrs. E. Carey and F. C. Liddell. It was resolved on the motion of Mr. Cook, seconded by Mr. Hayes, that the Clerk apply to the Local Government Board for an extension of time for filling up the vacancies.

Immediately after the funeral of the late Mr. Bond, on Monday, the East Dorset Tories selected the Hon. Humphrey Start as their candidate. The increase in the value of American agricultural products this year over that of the preceding year is estimated at not less than 100 million dollars.

Mr. John Hockaday, inspector of the Postal telegraph Engineering Department in Sheffield, on Monday, com- mitted suicide by taking a quantity of nitric acid. M. Lafargue, the Socialist, having been elected to the French Chamber of Deputies while in gaol, the House votel in favour of the suspension of his imprisonment. Clara Hall, a young Nottingham woman, lay down before the fire after a hard day's washing. She fell asleep, dropping cinders set her clothes on fire, and she was so badly burned that she has since died. A young Paris man, on Monday night, attempted to assassinate his mistress, who is two years older than himself. Seeing the blood flow, his reason returned to him, and he was very much distressed and gave himself up to the police.
THE SHIP CANAL.
THE ST. MAWE'S CASTLE

It is- stated that the St. Mawe's Castle,- which __is now running front Eastham to Northwich via the Ship Canal and Weaver Navigation, is the largest steamer—at any rate, the largest passenger steamer—which has visited that inland town. She is a screw steamer, 25 tons but:- den, capable of accommodating 259 passengers.

div.head: FATAL ACCIDENT TO A WARRINGTON MAN.
div.p: FATAL ACCIDENT TO A WARRINGTON MAN.

A man named Joseph Tinsley, living off Hall-st., was found'dead in the canal cutting near Morris Brook at eleven o'clock on Monday morning. Deceased left work at eight o'clock on Saturday night for the purpose of going to his supper, and took a short cut instead of going along the high-road. The cutting at this point is 50 ,)r 60 feet deep. When found he had a large fracture in his skull. The body now lies at the Latchford Hospital.

div.head: FIRST ARRIVAL FROM AMERICA.
div.p: FIRST ARRIVAL FROM AMERICA.

The first arrival from America in the Manchester Ship Canal took place nn Monday night. The Norwe- gian bark, Deodata, from America, with a cargo of tim- ber, arrived in the Manchester Ship Canal in charge of the company's pilot, Captain Sinnett, and in to* of the company's steamers. The height of the tide was 12ft. 3in., and the draught of the barque was from 18 to 17ft. This clearly proves that ships of large tonnage will be abls to pass into the Ship Canal without risk when the canal entrance is deepened at the Eastham Locks, which is in progress. It must be an encouragement to the company to be able to take in a ship of large draught with heap tides.

div.head: BANKS AT EASTHAM.
div.p: THE BANKS AT EASTHAM.

The banks of the Canal on the Eastham section are not yet complete. Whea in a complete state they will be terraced, and will be of no greater height than those of the Ince section. Along the whole of the terrace it is the intention ef the Canal Company to run a line of rail- way for the benefit of the users of the Canal, manufac- turers who may locate themselves on its banks, and to form easy connection with the lines of the great railway companies. The banks of the Eastham section have in many places slipped, thus showing that the reduction in their height will be an advantageous gain' as it will inerease their strength by reducing the weight above. In the meantime woven osiers are being staked and laid ia any part showing a weakness. Once weeds grow among these the solidity of the banks will be very great. In spots where the banks pass through the rock, fissures and crevices are being bricked up and made into one solid flat perpendicular wall, the strength of which will be able to withstand the wash of all steamers. The opening of the Ince section is the last of the piecemeal opening of the great waterway. No further portion will now be opened until the whole is complete and opened for traffic from end to end. Even if it were wished this could not be avoided, as it is the centre portion of the Canal which is incomplete. Both ends are practically finished. This was unavoidable, as the Canal could not be proceeded with in the Runcorn district until accom- modation had been provided for the Weaver traffic. Work hereabouts on all the backward portions will now be pressed on with all speed. PROGRESS OF THE WORK. (FROM "THE SHIP CANAL NEWS.")

On the north bank of the Canal, between the locks and Pool Hall Bay, the work of pitching above water level still continues. The pitching appears to be of bet- ter quality than much of the earlier work which is now hidden by the water of the canal. Possibly this improve- ment is due to the fact that there have occurred many slips of the lighter kind of pitching. On the south or land side of the canal we notice that a commencement has been made of taking off to a little above water level the clay and other spoil which by its slipping has caused se much extra work. At Ellesmere Port the whole of the new wharf, the wall of which is 900 feet long for the Shropshire Union Railway and Canal Co., is safely above tide level, and will not again suffer from the inrush of the river water. Active steps are being taken to rebuild the whole of this Company's river will, from a much lower foundation, in accordance with the increased depth of water,and dams are now being constructed for this work. With the opening of the 11 miles of the canal, com- mences the passage of the Salt Union boats from North- wich to the Mersey, along the canal, instead of through the Weston Point lock, and already a commencement has been made of piling a gantry to allow the canal bank to be more rapidly tipped round Weston Point. Great energy is to be concentrated, in the immediate future, upon that portion of the canal which lies between the Weaver sluices and Norton sluices,and already great difficulty is being experienced in housing the workmen. Workmen's huts are rapidly rising at Bigfield. It is rumoured that many more huts are to be erected on Frodsham Marsh, and that a workmen's mail train is to be run from these huts to Weston Point and Runcorn.

The walls of the Bridgwater Lock aie above tide level, and the coffer dams at each end of this lock nearly com- pleted ; the rest of the work to the walls and excavation of the body of the lock will be pushed forward as rapidly as possible. The same also may be said of the-other lock at Old Quay, and the concrete wall from Old Quay lock to Runcorn Bridge is nearly all of it above water level, and work can be prosecuted at any state of the tide. At Old Quay swing bridge work has been commenced, as also has the erection near of the hydraulic house. From here eastward to Norton occurs the highest lane, and therefore the deepest cutting for the canal. At one point it already looks deep enough for its purpose, but 22 feet more has to be taken out, and this spoil is being used to raise the land between the the river and canal. In consequence of the great depth of the cutting here, it has been decided to widen it considerably at the top, so that the banks, not being so steep, shall not have the same liability to slip. At Norton Dock work has again been resumed after a long interval of quietness, and being excavated in stone the shot firing is here very frequent. At Moore Lane Swing bridge Armstrong's men are now busily engaged in putting in the hydraulic machin- ery for opening and closing the bridge, but the work ap- pears to progress but slowly. The Morley Common cutting, which passes Lower Walton, has been almost entirely in rock, and very ted- ious, but the work is approacking near to the Acton Grange huts, and fresh changes may be expected. At Wilderspool a commencement has been made of the pier excavation for the swing bridge which is to cross the canal at this point, and at Latchford the Knutsford road bridge pier is completed, and ready for the roller path. . _ •
- Altogether besides the canal high level bridges, there are four swing bridges to be constructed by Messrs. Arrol. of Glasgow—Moore lane, Stagg Inn, Old Quay, and Knutsford-road.

Messrs. Handyside and Co., beside the Barton Aque- duct and road bridge, have the erection of the two can- tilever bridges at Latchford and Warburton, and the large swing bridge at Trafford-road is being constructed by a Leeds firm. At lrlam, the railway arch to cross the new Liverpool road is completed, and a commencement has been made of a road under the London and North-Western line, which must be completed before the old way can be stopped. Of course, the new road, passing under, in- stead of over, the line, will be much lower, and it has been found necessary to put steps to a few houses about here, and to strengthen the foundations by underpinn- ing. The Barton Swing Aqueduct makes a good show, and has been specially visited by engineers from various parts of the kingdom. The sheets of iron to form the tank for the canal water are being placed in position, , and some portions of the floor are already down. Here, also, the hydraulic house is rapidly rising, and appears as if it would be a larger structure t:ian others. At that portion of the Salford Dock where the wall , has to be built across the river, workmen have gone as close as they could to the water,but it appears to us that more than this cannot be done until the water has been allowed to enter the new channel of the canal. Tha excavation for all the Pomona Decks is ccitnpleted, we noticed a few days since, the railway lines being removed from the long arm which comes close to the Bridgewater Canal at Cornbrook. Workmen are also busy excavating the soil between the river and the timber wall, near the old site of Bennett's timber yard.

div.head: CORK ELECTION.
div.p: THE CORK ELECTION.
NATIONALIST VICTORY.
The High Sheriff of Cork (Mr. Roche) nn Saturday declared the restlt of the election to fill the vacancy in the representation of the city caused by the death of Mr. Parnell, as follows :

Flavin (Nationalist) Redmond (Parnellite) 2,147 Sarsfield (Unionist) Followed by large crowds and escorted by the military and police, Mr. Flavin and Mr. Redmond, with their supporters, proceeded to their respective hotels, where they addressed meetings of their supporters. After some remarks from Mr. Flavin and Mr. Davitt, Mr. William O'Brien, M.P., who was enthusiastically received, said he was proud to say that the Sheriff had announced figures which completely passed his expectations. Those figures prociamed like the trumpet of the archangel that faction was crushed, that dissension was dead, and that Ireland smoko once more in the voice of a united Irish nation. He had no personal joy of any sort in thrashing men who were once his old friends and 'old comrades. He hoped and prayed that their opponents would accept that as the final verdict of Ireland, and that the ccuntry might be saved from a continuance of the present most terrible and unnatural strife.

SAVAGE ATTACK ON A. SALFORD POLICE
CONSTABLE.

At the borough police court, on Wednesday, before Aldermen Holmes (chairman) and Chandley and Mr. John Fairclough. John Southall, engine driver for the Ship Canal Co., lodging at 48 Mersey- at., was charged under a warrant, with there assaulting John Costigan, police officer, of Salford, on the night of the 10th inst. Mr. P. Davies, defended. The complainant said he was with the prisoner at his lodgings, lying on the sofa, fast asleep,when without provocation,Southall assaulted him, and throwing him on to the floor, kicked him. He was perfectly sober. Witness whose face was a mass of bruises, said the defendant had caused them all. The landlady of the house, Mrs. Baxter, was witness's wife's sister.—By Mr. Davies : He did not accuse the prisoner of wronging his wife's sister, call him a liar, or strike him. He did not get the black eye through fighting the night before. —Alice Costigan, the complainant's wife, corroborated, and said she struck Southall in the eye. There was a bit of bother about the prisoner's relations with her sister. The complainant had some whisky, and she firmly be- lieved that something was put. into it that made him senseless. She, and not her husband, made the accusa- tion against the prisoner. He was not sober. He came in and said hp had had fifteen glasses of brandy. (Laugh- ter by the prisouer.)—Ann Melia deposed to seeing the complainant bleeding on the floor,and the prisoner kick- ing him. Costigan had had some drink, but she could net say whether he was drunk. Sullivan was sober.— P.C. 35 deposed to apprehending the prisoner, who said he did not hit the, complainant until hit by him. He was sober. He saw Costigan, who was also sober.— Thomas Rushton, another lodger with Mrs. Baxter, deposed that he saw Costigan fighting on the night of the 9th, and that his face was marked the next morning be- fore the quarrel with Southall. Witness was sleeping in a chair at the time of the row with Southall, and was awoke by the complainant's head being shoved against him; and the prisoner called attention to his mouth, which was bleeding, and asked him if he would stand this. When witness went out of the room he believed Mrs. Costigan was in the room. Both Costigan and Southall were sober.—P.S. Cheney voluntarily came into the box and said he had made inquiries, arid found that Costigan was not to blame 5,t el.—Mr. Davies told the officer that it was very unwarrantable for -him to come forward in that manner.—The defendant was c,n- victed and bound ,over in the sum .of £5 to keep the pace for six months, and mulcted in the costs, 17s. 6d.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY. NOVEMBER 14. 1891.

THE Unionists have been demon- The Unionists Again. strating at Manchester, and nevrer home—at T.helwall, they have been holding a meeting by way of letting it be seeit,that there is still such a party, in existence. These Unionist gatherings are as; a matter of fact Tory gatherings ; but the fiction. will be kept up,w.e sup- pose, until after the General Election. The Thel- wall meeting was held cn. Saturday evening,. and, ;with Mr. T. W. Russell, M.P., as the principal _speaker, the percentage of mistatements, was un- gusually high. The principal resolution was in sup- port of the Government.. It was proposed. by Roar :Admiral Parry, who ought to have been a rear speaker, for he had really nothing to, say; and seconded by Major Pickreere, who made it known that his heart on that occasion was " aiiittle full." Why this was so was not made clear.. Perhaps he wished it to be understood that it was sad to re,- fleet how soonthe Unionists would have to surren7 der the sweets of office. He next proceeded th make the extraordinary statement that" the muni- cipal elections which had just taken place were, in favour of the Otwernment throughout the =ni- fty." Really,,but, is this so? What does the Major read itkhisretirement at T,Lhelwall ? Or does , he spend hia time in dreaming rather than in wad- ing ? The very first returns of the Municipal Elections that were issued indicated that the gain was on the Liberal side; and the final returna show that the Liberals gained 128 seats and the Tories 71, showing a net Liberal gain of 57. If, this is Major PiciumnE's idea of favouring the, Govern- ment, we can only say that we shall ,be delighted to see them favoured in a. similar way when they appeal to the country. Mr. T. W. RUSSELL in supporting the resolution, seems to have taken his cue from the. MAJOR, fox the best known facts were turned topsy-turvy,an.d his whole deliverancewas a travesty of recent his- tory. What could be in greater contrast to tin truth than his statement that in 1886, when the Government came into office— "Ireland was in a state of confusion, chaos, and disorder. Murder was," he says," rife, agarian crime was steadily rising, evictions for non-payment of , rent were numerous; contracts were everywhere repudiated, the Plan of Campaign, an organised , system of robbery,was episcopally blessed ; boycott- ing was almost universal from one end of the coun- try to the other." It is notorious that, so far from this being the state of the case, the condition of Ire- land had so improved under Mr. GLAD- STONE'S r administration that the Tories, when they came into office, actually allowed the

then existing Crimes Act to expire. The reasort they gave was that, in the improved state of the country, its renewal was unnecessary. It comes to this, that either the Government, which Mr. Rus- SELL now praises, were guilty,at the time, of delibe- rate lying—for they must have known how things stood—or Mr. RussiLL is now guilty of the most glaring misrepresentation of the facts. Ile can say, if he likes, that the Government of all the virtues perjured themselves; or he can admit that Mr. T. W. Russ= is entirely in the wrong. He is quite welcome to either horn of the dilemma.
Ireland, he tells us, is peaceful and contented now,
and "Coercion is gone." Then it would seem . there has been such a thing as" Coercion" on the part of the Governtnent, notwithstanding bare-
'aced donials in view of a hundred instances of it.
The fact is, Coercion as a weapon has broken in Mr. BALFOUR'S hands, and he has almost ceased
to use it, having an eye to his reputation and to the approaching appeal to the electors.- There is, it is true, a more contented feeling in Ireland, but
that is because Irishmen are convinced that the time is at hand when Mr. BALFOUR and all his works will be driven out oi the country, avid when

a Government will be placed in power which will grant Home Rule. Mr. Russell complains that there is not a man in England who knows what the Home Rulaßill is going to be; but he knows what the principles. of

_ the measure will be, and he knows, too, that it is not for the Opposition but for the party in power to lay bills before the country. Since he is thirst- ing for information, why does he not demand of the present Government the details of the Irish Local Government Bill which was promised as soon as they came into office? At the Unionist demonstra- tion at Manchester, on Tuesday, it was deemed necessary to remind the Government by resolution of the need for local self-government for Ireland. The Unionists are on their death-bed; and they have reached the hour of repentance.. As Mr. Coningsby Disraeli innocently admitted "the General Election is fraught with the greatest, anxiety to all of them." They see the handwriting, on the wall; it is written in large characters at - Cork. The Nationalist candidate has polled: more votes than the Tories,, the Liberal. Unionists, and the Parnellites combined!. Where is that sign of " gratitude " which, it is foolishly said, Ireland entertains for Mr. Bal- four's "successful policy." Succewfull. Why, the Unionists of Cork have actually lost ground. In 1885 they brought 1,400 voters to the poll; yesterday week they polled 1,161 only. Lord HARTINGTON is "knocked over" by,. the result,. and he may well be. "He regretted," he said on Tuesday, "that the recent election in Cork made it appear that the apathy, indifference, and want of courage of the Irish minority was not yet re- moved." Unionists, and yet capable of "apathy, indifference and want of courage !" Why doesn't Mr. R. A. NAYLOR, who talks about " marching through fields of fire and blood," go over to Ire- land, with Mr. T. W. RUSSELL, and show these 'chicken-hearted defenders of the, faith what 'valiant men can do? Is it that to preach is eo much easier than to practise ? Or is, it that .the Unionists know that it. is all up with them—that they have played a poor game and lost? The Generat Election may ,well be "fraught with the greatest anxiety ; " fcr, the end of. the present , .Parliament will be the end of the political career of the majority of the Liberal Unionists, who have long since lost all traces of their Liberalism.

But sufficient for. the day is the good thereof, and it is good that a brewer, in the person of Councillor Bolton, has been removed from the Watch Committee.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

Accorling to the new regulation of the new Postmaster-General old soldiers, with a good re- cord, are to have a preference in appointments as letter-carriers. This is not much to look forward to ; but it is something. It is better at any rate - than the workhouse, after fighting at Balaclava.

The Mormons are finally beaten in their -.struggle with the United States Government; they have formally decided to abandon polygamy. By taking this course, the leaders of the sect, practically confess that their "revelations "are all humbug—unless they are prepared to show that they aro acting under a new "revelation."

The new Liberal paper for Birmingham, " The Daily Argus," made its appearance on Monday. It is well edited,takes a firm stand in favour of Home Rule, and is likely to make a good organ of the party. The weak point—and it is usually a weak point with a first number—is in the printing; but there should be no difficulty in remedying its de- fects in this respect.

The London correspondent of the "Dublin Express" states that "it is rumoured in the clubs that Lord Randolph Churchill will absolutely abandon his political career in England. It is not improbable that overtures have been made to him to take the supreme command of British interests in Central Africa." How would it be if Joseph were to join Randolph? They might succeed in -forming a "National Party" of blacks ; the whites willhave none of it.

We have received, too late for our use, a letter from Messrs. Edward Bolton and Sons, comment- ing on, and poking fun at, a summons before the Sanitary Committee "for allowing offensive smoke." They decline, "fine or no fine," to ap- pear before the Sanitary Committee, and suggest that action is being taken against them because of their complaints against the Intercepting De- pot. We quite approve of Messrs. Bolton object- ing to the summons of the Sanitary Committee. That body is acting illegally in levying fines, and it is quite time that this irregular Court was abolished.

What Burns calls "chill November's surly blast" has this week made "fields and forests bare." To quote another poet—Alfred Austin—we are now— In that sad season of the bygone year, When woolly mists the chillierglandscape wrap, And beggared Autumn, with a silver tear, Empties her gold leaves into Winter's lap. The gold leaves are blown who knows whither? and with winter approaching, and trade declining, the prospect is not by any means cheerful.

It certainly seems as if we were at the turn of the tide in the matter of foreign trade. There is a falling off in exports, and the specialists predict that there will be a further decline. What have shallow Tories to say about this—those who have been loudest in .declaring the improvement in trade was owing to the Tories being in office? Perhaps they will explain. How would it be to say the change is due to the fact that the Liberals are ex- pected to triwnph at the General Election? Per- haps the Fair Trader will offer his solution of the problem?

This is what Lord Salisbury had to say in his Mansion House speech about Protection :—" The fact that the articles in respect to which we should have to exercise protection are mainly articles of consumption bearing upon the necessities of the whole body of the population is an absolute guaran- tee that we shall never return to the ways of pro- tection." How do the Fair Traders feel after this? If Mr. John White still classes himself as one, per- haps he.will tell us.

The Rector of Warrington has been quoted by the supporters of the liquor trade as a moderate- minded man; whose ideas are worth listening to. Let them listen, then ; for this is what he had to say, on Monday evening, at a temperance meeting in the National School :—" He was in favour of general Sunday closing. He did not think that those interested in the drink traffic should sit upon the Bench to grant licenses, lie was in favour of the entire suppression of tied houses. He was glad to hear that this year the number of licences had been reduced by about 250."

It is true that Mr. Willis expressed himself as favouring the principal of compensation ; but that is raising an issue which is somewhat out of date. The public have twice had the question of com- pensation before them, and have twice declared against it. More than that, the matter has been before the highest clurts, and they, too, have decided against compensation. That horse is dead: it is no use flogging it.

A Warrington Correspondent writes :—" I beg to state that I have in my possession three bills of the Confederate States of America, one for 100 dollars, and another for 10 dollars ; these two are genuine hills, and the other is a fac-simile of alO dollar bill. .Would you kindly tell me through the medium of your paper, if you think they are of any value and where I might dispose of thein."—The bills are of no value whatever except to collectors of such curiosities. When Richmond was taken, the Confederate States collapsed, and their bonds and bills became so much waste paper.

The Warrington Liberal Club, like Osman Digna, has been killed a great many times by people whose wish was father to the thought. But here it is again—alive and flourishing. From the Balance Sheet read at the annual meeting, on Tuesday evening, it appears that the club has not only paid its way during the past year, but made a handsome profit. Mr. T. Pemberton, the hon. secretary, has worked hard, along with the Committee,to achieve this result; and it is a pleasure to the members to contribute to the fund for the presentation which is about to be made to him.

Now that it is definitely settled that Sir Gilbert Greenall will not risk defeat at the next election, "Brother Bloomfield" has let it be known that— just as one suspected—the member for Warrington has given secret pledges to the Orangemen of War- rington. "Brother Bloomfield," speaking at an Orange celebration on Monday evening said :—" At the last general election five . questions were sub- mitted to Sir Uilbert, all of which he answered to the satisfaction of Orangemen, and they expected similar answers to be given by the next Conserva- two candidate. It was not necessary for him to state what the answers were, but Sir Gilbert's re- fusal to serve again was very much regretted by the Orangemen throughout the borough."

Just so ; but is it quite fair to the electors that a candidate should enter into a secret alliance of this kind? What do the Catholic priests think of the way in which they have been stabbed—so to speak —in the back And what have laymen, like Mr. Voisey, to stly on the subject? It is no use, maybe, crying over spilled milk; but, as the new Tory candidate is to be called upon to toe the same mark, it will be as well to ascertain what that mark really is. Perhaps the new candidate will be an Orangeman. We shall see.

It seems that even the poor worm of a reporter will turn at times. After a three years' fruitless agitation to obtain better accommodation in the Burnley Town Council Chamber, all the repre- sentatives of the local and district papers sent to the Council on Monday morning a request that the grievance should be attended to before the next meeting. They received no reply, and consequently left the building. At Warrington there is a lack of suitable accommodation for the Press both at the Police Court and the County Court. How would it be if the local reporters were to strike— something or somebody?
SUDDEN DPATH AT RUNCORN
Ellen Birch, 66 years of age, of 23, Church-street, died suddenly on Saturday afternoon after complaining of pains in the head. The Coroner did not deem an inquest necessary.
HYMNS ANCIENT AND MODERN.
The Rev. G. A. Leßeet, vicar of St. Ambrose Church, Widnes, on Sunday evening preached a sermon on the above subject which proved itighly interesting to the large congregation.
A WIDNES PUBLICAN FINED.
Frederick Simcock,of the Black Horse Inn,Farnworth, was fined 10s. and costs, at Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, for being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and trap. The defendant did not appear.
TIER ORMAND FAMILY AT RUNCORN.

This talented family gave performances in Runcorn Public Hall on Friday and Saturday evenings last week. The demonstration of hypnotism by Dr. Ormand was a wonderful exhibition of power, and mystified the audience.

GREENWAY-ROAD BOARD SCHOOLS, RUNCORN. The children attending these schools were given a magic lantern entertainment on Friday evening last week, and were kept interested and amused by a large variety of pictures. Mr. Rosser, assistant master, mani- pulated the lantern.and Miss Kilburn, the head mistress, described the views. DEATH FROM SCALDS AT RUNCORN.

An infant named Thomas Griffiths, aged 1 year and 6 !months, son of Edward Griffiths, of Surrey-st., pulled a cup of tea upon him on the 20th ult., and he died from the effects of the sca!ds on Sunday. An inquest was held on Tuesday by Mr. J. E. Worsley, and a verdict of accidental death was returned.

The Rev. John Yonge has found it necessary to issue a placard in order to give an unqualified contradiction to the statement which the Tories have circulated to the effect that he drew up the circular containing the questions which were put to the candidates by the Warrington Temperance Felderation. He approves, however, of the questions as the Rev. J. J. Langham does ; and he recognises that they have done good work. It is just because they have done good work—that is resulted in Councillor Bolton being left off the Watch Com- mittee—that the Tories are "striking wild."

" A member of the Temperance Federation" giyes particulars in our correspondence column of the circumstances under which the circular was issued. It will be seen that the fuss which is being made about the Rev. J.. J. Langham not having authorised his name being used is a red herring drawn across the scent. The usual course was taken, Mr. Langham being furnished, as hereto- fore, with an account of what was done at the meeting in his absence, along with a copy of the cir- cular which was being issued. Ho made no objec- tion to the use of his name as one of the two hon. secs.,but wrote back to say the questions were very proper ones to put. And so they were, and they have done their work—properly.
