div.head: Fine AT RUNCORN.
div.p: Fine AT RUNCORN.

On Sunday night, a shed and about 60 tons of hay, be- longing to Mr. Thomas Clough, butcher, Church-street, were destroyed by fire. The shed was on the banks of the Bridgewater Canal, at Halton, adjoining Mr. Abel's boatbuilding yard. The damage, which is stated at about £3OO, was covered by insurance in the Sun Office.
ALL THROUGH TIIH DRINK.

At Widnes Police Court, on Tuesday, Wm. Newman Carlisle, was charged with stealing a clock, valued 75., the property of Ann Jennings, of 24 Church-st., On the previous afternoon Mrs. Jennings left her house for a few minutes, when she returned the clock had disappeared, The prisoner afterwards sold it for 23. to Robert Frod- sham, a labourer, of 47, Church-st.--The prisoner said he was drunk at the time, otherwise he would not have stolen the clock.—He was remanded for a week. ROBBERIES AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Police Court on Thursday, John Atkins, a navvy,was brought up on remand charged with stealing two shirts, the property of Peter Noon, draper, Church- street, and he was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour.— George Walker was convicted of stealing a coat, value 12s. 6d., the property of W. Craddock, pawnbroker, Church-street, and he was also sentenced to 14 days hard labour.—A similar sentence was passed upon George Carrington for stealing a coat, value 133. 6d., the pro- perty of Carl Paikin, clothier, Waterloo-road.
A CONGREGATIONAL AT HOME AT RUNCORN.

The second At Home in connection with Bethesda Con- gregational Church took place on Wednesday evening, in the schoolroom, which had been decorated in charm- ing style by Mr. Steele and his assistants. The walls were draped and the windows curtained, and the plat- form was transformed into a beautiful recess. The com- pany present numbered about 150, and for their amuse- ment and edification the Mowing programme of music • was gone through :—Quartette, " On the banks of Allen Water ;" selection on pianoforte, Miss Forrester ; song, "Only once more," Mr. E. Worrall ; song, "The mission of a rose," Miss N. Handley; duet, " A.8.C.," Miss Ains- worth and Mr. C. Weedall ; pianoforte solo, Mr. C. Le Couteur ; song, " The singing lesson," Mr.F. Scott ; song, "I couldn't, could I," Miss Heatherington ; song," They all love Jack," Mr. J. Weedall ; pianoforte duet, " The fairies' waltz,"Miss Forrester and Miss D.Cameron ; song, " Ali, ha," Mr. George Lacey ; song," Ada's serenade," Mr. F. Scott; quartette," Good night beloved," Misses Ainsworth and Handley', and Messrs. Worrall and Ains- worth. The accompanists were Miss Handley, and Mr. C. Le Couteur. Light refreshments were provided, and at intervals the good things were dispensed by Mrs. Ryder, Mrs. Forrester, Mrs. Cameron, Miss Richardson, Miss Lydiate, and Miss Handley. The proceedings was brought to a conclusion at ten p.m. by the usual votes of thanks, passed on the proposition of Mr. Chadwick, seconded by Mr. Slade, all having spent a most en- joyable evening. The Rev. John Simpson, the pastor, conducted the proceedings.

BMIGRA.TION.—Intending emigrants to New York. Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canada, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Zealand, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the" Examiner" Office, by Cunard, Onion. American. Aus- tralian, Oriental, and other lines.—John Walker, agent. "Examiner' Office. Bewsev-st.. Warrinzten.—Advt. AN ALLEGED DANGEROUS DOG AT RUNCORN.

Mr. Harry Wright, ot Greenway-road, was summoned before Mr. C. Reynolds and Major Hazlehurst at Run- corn Petty Sessions on Monday to answer a charge of having a dangerous dog which was not kept under proper control.—Catherine Monks, a licensed hawker. from Prodsham, said on Tuesday afternoon the third inst. she went up the passage leading to the back of Mr. Wright's house, and when about a yard from the gate defendant's dog flew at her and caught her by the nose. When she felt the gush of blood she did not know whether she had a nose or not. Dr. McDougall dressed the wound. She did net go into the yard at all. By defendant: She was not drunk,—The defendant said he had no evidence to show whether the woman was bitten by his dog or not, and his parents and sisters who were in the house did not know anything of the occurrence until informed by P,C. Crowder.—The dog was a collie about 3 years old and he had had it since it was a pup, and it had never displayed any dangerous proclivities. It was a docile dog, and the children played with it in the street. The dog was on his premises at the time stated by the woman, and he could not do any more than that. Miss Wright said the yard doer was shut, at the time.— P.C. Crowder deposed that there were marks of blood on the yard steps. He had known the dog for 3 years. and it was a very quiet one —Complainant said she wished the dog destroyed,but Mr. Reynolds said the Bench would not order that, and if she wanted compensation she should have taken the case to the County Court.—The Bench made ln order that the dog should be kept under proper control, and ordered the defendant to pay the costs, us. 6d.—The defendant said he thought it was an injustice to burden him with the costs.—Mr. Reynolds : You will have to pay the costs. it is not shown that the woman was not bitten by your dog, and being a licensed hawker she had a perfect right to be where she was.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 14, 1891
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 14, 1891
BRUNSWICK IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, RUNCORN._
At the weekly meeting on Wednesday, Mr. James Povah read a paper on " Hobbies " Mr. T. Simister presided.
MILTON LITERARY SOCIETY, WIDNES

On Wednesday night Mr. W. Brown read a paper on " A comparison between English and German Customs and Manners." Mr. W. Harrison, 8.A., presided. SIMMS CROSS PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, WIDNES. During the past week a series of very successful evangelist services have been held in this chapel. the principal speakers have been Rev. W. Thornley, and Messrs. T. Rollason, W. Witter and J. Wharton. BAPTIST CHAPEL, DEACON-ROAD, WIDNES.

Special services were held in this chapel, on Sunday. when Mr. J. W. Schofield, J.P., of Bootle, delivered two eloquent sermons. The choir rendered several anthems in an admirable manner. A large congregation assembled at each service.
A LANCASHIRE STEEPLE JACK KILLED.

On Saturday afternoon, a man named Pilkington, of Accrington, was killed by falling from the stone chimney at Holden Vale Hill, Haslingden, which is being repaired. He was being drawn to the top of the Chimney, when the rope broke as he was nearly at the top. He fell on the weaving shed, and re- bounded into the road below. Death was instan- taneous. The chimney is 180 feet in height.

shops amongst them. He knew one shop in the city of Mandalay, which was under Government patronage, support, and sanction, and it turned out 500 gallons of distilled liquor every day. In Upper Burmah according to latest Government statistics there were 139 licensed liquor shops although the people had begged that not one should be established. He hoped that the conscience of England would be touched before it was too late, and that something would be done to stop the torrent of evil that was coming up in consequence of our rule in that country. (Applause.) Mr. Winston described his difficulties in starting the mission in Burmah, and the routines of his daily life, and the success that had at- tended his labours. In conclusion he made an appeal for help for the Foreign Missionary Sociaty.—Mr. Simp- son moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Winston for his speech, to the collectors for their labours ; and to tne Chairman for presiding.—Mr. J. R. Frith seconded the moticn, which was carrien by acclamation. Mr. Wilkes announced that the collection that night had amounted to £5O 4s. 6d., making the grand total raised £163 16s. 2d., being an increase of £1 16s. 6d. over last year. The proceedings then concluded.

div.head: EVININGS POD TH3 PEOPLE AT WIDNES.
div.p: EVININGS POD TH3 PEOPLE AT WIDNES.

The third of a series of evenings for the people took place in the Widnes National School, on Thursday night, when the Rev. Wycliffe Vaughan M.A., delivered a lec- ture entitled " Reminiscences of Paris and Switzerland." The lecture was illustrated by limelight views.
LECTU'RET AT RUNCORN ON JERUSALEM.

The Rev. Dr. Preston, M.A., on Wednesday evening delivered an interesting and instructive lecture on the " Leading lights in Jerusalem," the subject being illus- trated by means of a lime light lantern manipulated by Mr. W. E. Lea. Mr. P. Speakman, C.C., presided. ST. MICHAEL'S CHURCH, RUNCORN.

In aid of the school funds special services were held on Sunday. The preacher in the morning and afternoon was the Rev. T. W. Sturgess,B.A , vicar of Marston ; and in the evening the Rev. Canon Maitland Wood, M.A., occupied the pulpit. There was a good congregation at each service.
ALBERT-ROAD WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WIDNES.

In connection with the Wesleyan Foreign Missions, the Rev. J.D.Sutcliffe,missionary from the Gold Coast,Africa, delivered two sermons on Sunday in this chapel. There were large congregations. The annual missionary meet- ing was held on Monday, when the missionary delivered an address on mission work in Africa. DEACON ROAD BAPTIST CHAPEL, WIDNES.

The annual tea party took place on Thursday evening, when a good company sat down to tea. Afterwards a miscellaneous concert was held under the presidency of Mr. W. Clarke of Hough Green, and addresses were delivered by Rev. J. Cottam, Messrs. J. Taylor, E. Maunsey, and J. Cripps J.P. (Waterloo.)
Aw HABITUAL WIFE BEATER AT RENCORN.

At the Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, Peter Knight was sentenced to a month's hard labour, for as- saulting his wife. The prisoner had been convicted of similar offences on several previous occasions, and had been sent to gaol. A separation order had also been granted to his wife. On Monday the prisoner beat his wife with his fists, and kicked her, bruising her severely.
WIDNES TRADES COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting was held on Monday evening, when a deputation was appointed to wait upon those societies who had not already joined the Council, to explain the objects of the same. The delegates were desired to lay before the members of their respective societies the desirability of holding the trades demons- tration on the arrival of the charter of incorporation. The following officers were appointed for the ensuing twelve months :—President John Clarke (Railway Ser- vants) ' • vice-president, Michael Dugan, (Bricklayers Society) ; treasurer, James Pritchard (Plumbers) ; secretary, Alexander G. Lowry (Coopers).
A DROWNING MYSTERY AT WESTON POINT.

On Tuesday afternoon, Mr. J. E. Worsley, the corcner, hold an inquiry into the circumstances of the death of Thomas Hargreaves Wilson, a wood turner, employed on the Ship Canal. Wilson, who was 42 years of age, arrived at his lodgings on Saturday night to some extent under the influence of drink. About midnight he went into the yard, which abuts on the Weaver canal, and as he did not return after some minutes, the landlady went to bed, leaving the door unfastened and the gas burning. He had only one shoe on at the time. Next morning it was found that he had not returned, and the:canal being dragged his body was found. There was no evidence to show whether he had committed suicide or had acciden- tally fallen into the canal, and an open verdict was returned. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W.PUTTON. Sankey-st. , Warrington.—Advt. A REVENGEFUL LODGER AT RUNCORN.

Before Mr. Brundrit and Mr. Henry Reynolds, at Run- corn Police Court, on Thursday, George Gilbert was brought up under a warrant charged with wilfully damaging the windows of the lodging-house kept by Tom Scott in Frver-st. For some time last year the prisoner had lodged. with Scott, and in September, 1890, he was sent to gaol for a month for assaulting Mrs. Scott. He did not make his appearance again until the 29th ult., when he smashed a pane of glass, doing damage to the extent of £5. A warrant was issued, but he could not be found, and on Wednesday he again turned up, and smashed another pane, the damage being £5 on this occasion.—He was fined £1 and costs in each case and ordered to pay the damage, making a total of £l2 18s. 10d., or in default two months' _imprisonment.
UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. BUTTON, Saukey-st., Warrington.—Advt.
RUNCORN SONS OF TEMPBRANCH.

At the usual fortnightly meeting of the above order an essay was given by Mr. Thomas J. Holt on the Quin- quennial valuation of Friendly Societies. The paper was of considerable length, and dealt exhaustively with the whole question. He gave valuable statistics about the various Friendly Societies and urged the importance of periodical valuations so as to put the order on a firm financial basis. He pointed out the danger :of Temper- ance Benefit Societies losing sight of the financial aspect of the question in their anxiety for the reclaimation of the drunkard, in introdncing lives which were not healthy. The subject was well handled, and provoked a discussion, in which the following members took part : Messrs. Thomas Heesom, Edward Key, John Withington, Samuel M. Temperley, and Daniel Bisbrown. A vote of thanks was accorded Mr. Holt for his paper. Mr. Wesley Cooke occupied the chair. THA ACTION OF ALCOHOL ON THE BODY.

During the present week, Mr. W. C. Wilson, the scien- fic temperance lecturer, has been engaged in delivering lectures at the day school of the town on the "Action of alcohol on the body" and he has dealt with his subject in such a way that the young people have been highly interested, and have derived much instruction. On Thursday night Mr. Wilson delivered a lecture under a similar title to a good audience in Bethesda Lecture Hall. He sought to prove that alcohol was not necessary to a person in a healthy condition, and was on the other hand, injurious to the system. He was prepared to admit that alcohol lad many valuable properties, but they were medicinal M their character, and ought only to be used in that way. The lecture was illustrated by limelight views,shown by Mr. T. Bowyer. The Rev. Canon Wood, M.A., presided. It should be stated that Mr. %Nilson has acted under the auspices of the Runcorn Women's Tem- perance Society.

ILLNFSB OF Mn. THOMAS RIGBY. We regret to learn that Mr. Thomas Rigby, one of the best known agriculturists in England, for many years secretary of the Manchester and Liverpool Agricultural Society, is laid up with severe illness at his residence, Preston Brook, Cheshire. UMI3RELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Aevt.

ANOTHER ACCIDENT IN THE HUNTING FIELD. On Saturday, Colonel Jocelyn, while out, with the North Cheshire Hounds, fell, together with the first huntsman, at a fence, and sustained severe injuries to the head. He was picked up in an insensible condition and conveyed to his residence at Dacen- ham Cottage. It is many years since the opening of the Cheshire season was characterised by acci- dents su:th as have befallen Colonel Jocelyn and Captain Mesham. PETROLEUM Ora.—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger, Bridge-at., Warnngton.—Advt. . BURTONWOOD SCHOOL BOARD.

A special meeting of the members of the Burton- wood School Board was held at Burtonwood School on Tuesday afternoon, Mr. James Warburton pre- siding. The business consisted of the appoinment of a new clerk in succession to the late Rev. W. Wilson, and Mr. William Webster, solicitor, St. Helens, was unanimously selected. A vote of con- dolence with the relatives of the late clerk was passed, and ordered to be forwarded to Mrs. Wilson. GAS FITTINGS.—J. S. Garland, Gas Fitter, Dridge-at., Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: DINNER AT DARESBURY.
div.p: DINNER AT DARESBURY.

On Friday evening,--he— Members of the Dares- bury Wanderers' Club held their third annual din- ner at the Ring o' Bells, Daresbury. About 30 sat down to an excellent dinner provided by Mr. C. W. Phillips, the landlord, and ample justice was done to it. After dinner the usual loyal toasts were given and well received. Songs were given by Messrs. C. W. Phillips, James Wilde, and Isaac Ellison. Mr. Edgar L. Smirk was at the piano. The party broke up at 10 p.m. after having spent a very enjoyable evening. KITCHEN R ANGERS.-4arland Builders Ironmonger, War- rington.— Advt.

div.head: STAGNATION IN THE SALT TRADE.
div.p: STAGNATION IN THE SALT TRADE.

Owing to continued depression. the Salt Union havd issued further orders for the stoppage of a number of pans at Northwich and Winsford. In the latter town there is a considerable amount of distress. At least 150 men have been thrown out of employment, and there is every prospect of more being stopped. Very little salt is being exported, and on the river Weaver, traffic is almost at a stand still. It is feared that more of the watermen, 70 of whom have already been discharged, will toe thrown out of work. Many people have been compelled to leave Winsford, and signs of a terrible winter are manifested. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. Durna, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: ENGINE AND BOILER MEN'S ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ENGINE AND BOILER MEN'S ASSOCIATION.

A meeting of delegates from the various Engine- men's and Boilermen's Societies in the surrounding Lancashire towns was held on Saturday, at the George Hotel, George-st., Sr.. Helens, to consider the advisability of forming an association of the various societies. The towns represented were St. Helens, Bolton, Widnes, Farnworth, Ramsbottom, West Leigh, Bury,and Ratcliffe. After a discussion a resolution was come to that an association should be formed, and that the name should be the Lanca- shire and Cheshire Amalgamated Association of Enginemen and Boilermen. Several other resolutions were passed in respect to the proposed rules that were laid before the meeting by the St. Helens representatives.
UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Adv. M. HENRY IRVING AND THE ST. HELENS MINISTERIAL "CRANK."

In the last issue of a St. Helens newspaper ap- peared a report of a ,ermon on "The Theatre and the Drama," by the Rev. J. T. Wardle 'Stafford. a local Wesleyan minister. In the course of his address Mr. Stafford strongly denounced the theatre and its frequenters, and said that as an institution its existence depended upon its immorality. , A copy of the paper was forwarded to Mr. Henry Irving, who has written to Mr. Wallace Revill, the proprietor of the new Theatre Royal, St. lielenp, expressing his regret that any notice should have been taken of such a sermon, as with all sensible persons it would tend to lower respect for the Church. It was a mistake to report the "silliness" of Mr. Stafford, who seemed to be a well-inten- tioned "crank," as they were termed in America, and eaten up with his own vanity, Mr. Irving added that it was evident Mr. Stafford had not taken the trouble to learn the facts of the matter upon which he spoke. Mr. Wilson Barrett and other leading actors have also written denying the allegations of the preacher. The incident has ex- cited considerable feeling in the town, and on every hand it is admitted that, as applied to the local theatre, the remarks of Mr. Stafford were uncalled for and exaggerated.
UMBRELLAS RECOVERED._-J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS,
div.p: WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONS,
RUNCORN BRANCH.

The annual services in aid of the Wesleyan For- eign Missions were held in St. Paul's Chapel, Run- corn,on Sunday,and were carried out with the usual success. The pulpit was occupied in the morning by the Rev. W. Arroi,vsmith, and in the evening by the Rev. Thomas Wilkes, representative to the "Ecumenical Conference in America. The choir sang several anthems in admirable style under the leadership of Mr. R. Morris, and hymns were also sung by the scl.olars frum Brunswick school. The collections amounted to .ElO 10s. 10d.

On Tuesday evening the annual missionary meet- ing was held in the chapel, and theta was a large audience. Mr. P. Speakman, C.C., presided and there were on the platform the Revs. W. Ripley Winston, missionary from Ceylon and Burmah ; iThos. Wilkes (superintendent), W. Arrowsmith, and J. Hanley; Messrs. John Simpson, J. R. Frith, R. Norman, E. Taylor, B. Kniveton, Robert Rawlinson. and others. There were also three little girls attired in the picturesque costume of the Burmese. DUN ing the evening the choir and scholars sang several hymns in good style, after the usual devotions, The Rev. NV. Arrowsmith read the general report. He said whatever had been the varied experience of the Wesleyan Missionary Society it had never lacked the divine encouragement which comes from spiritual pros- perity. The year 1830 might ba thankfully compared with those that had gone. From the Mission districts there came the sound of the joy of the harvest, although it was overpowered by the louder call for reapers. As they looked there was everywhere something to hearten both toilers and reapers. On the continent of India there was much straitne=s because available resources were not equal to the demand arising from success. From the Burmah district tidings had reached them that several Buddhists and Hindoos had been baptised. Good Sam- aritan work was attempted there, and M. Winston had been constrained to open a " Home for lepers." The record from China was that the missionaries, the lay mission agents, " Joyful News," Evangelists, and native preachers were all working in harmony,striving together for the salvation of the people, and with abounding en- couragement—a statement which had a terrible coun- terpart in the distressing details of the terrible revolt there and the murder of Mr. Argent—the first missionary martyr of the Methodist Church in China. The Wesleyan Methodist Missionary Society had under its immediate direction 363 circuits 1.572 chapels, 338 missionaries, 34,722 church members, 5,250 on trial, and 65,803 scholars in schools. The total income of the society from all sources was £122,072 6s. 3d. ;of this amount £18,311 18s. 9d. was raised by the children of Methodism, or about £1 in every £6 10s. The receipts from the Liverpool district of which Runcorn formed a part, were £6,598 12s. 2d., a decrease of £166 10s. 9d. Runcorn circuit oontributed last year £255 16s. 7d. It was distressing to know that the expenditure exceeded the income by £10,813 12s. 3d., whics added to the pre- vious deficit of £8,563 13s. 3d., made a total deficiency ,of £19,377 ss. 6d. It was only right to state that the present year's deficit was chiefly attributed to a dimin- ished income from extraordinary sources as annuities, &c., and to increased amounts in extraordinary expen- diture. Still it could not •be ignored that there was a decrease in the gifts of living Methodists of £1,844 during the year. The income from the Home Church was £12,400 less than was reported in 1879. when the thanksgiving movement was in full force. Since then the number of members of the Society had increased 12 percent., and the number of adherents still more. Pro- portionately, therefore, the contributions placed at the diseosal of the General Committee were £25,000 less. Mr. Edward Taylor read the local report, which showed that Mr. Soulby had collected £8 18s. ; Miss Speakman and Mrs. A. R. Norman, £5 195.; Miss Simister. £9 7s. ; Miss Crosby, £5 6s. ; Miss Norman, £lO Bs. 6d. ' • collected in Brunswick Sunday Scheol, £63 Es. 4d. ; Sunday collections in St. Paul's, £lO 10s. 10d. ; total, £ll3 us. Bd. ; a decrease of £3 6s. 6d., on the previous year. The Chairman said the missionary spirit to his mind was a grand one, and it could only be understood and appre- ciated to the fullest extent where they had the presence of one who had been taking a part in that work abroad like Mr. Urmston. He did not wish to advertise himself in the least on the question of having been where mis- sionaries exist, but it was his pleasure this year to be with missionaries in Palestine, and when he saw them in the midst of people who knew not God, and remembered how they had learned the language so that they might instil into the minds of those people the good tidings,it was indeed a pleasure to him because from his earliest days he had been connected with missionary work. It was his privilege when a little boy to have a missionary box and card, and he remembered very well the pictures that used to be given to him detailing the atrocities perpetrated upon their missionaries,which lie was glad to a great ex- tent had been swept away by the gospel of our Lord Jesus. Anyone who said anything against the missionaries had not the missionary spirit within them, and having wit- nessed the good work that was being done by the mis- slenaries he was pleased to notice the fruits and the rejoicing amongst the people consequent upon their labours. The missionary, who was one of the finest Christian men that it had been his pleasure to meet, took him throughout his district in Jerusalem. They visited all sorts and conditions of men,women, and children, and In administering succour for the body they also gave succour for the soul. That was testimony which ought to be realised and understood, and in stating it he wanted to encourage them in their foreign missionary work. The deficiency in the funds of £19,320 was a most serious thing, but they could all do something to wipe it out if they would allow their spirit of sympathy with the great work now beinglaccomplished to have fair play. (Ap- plause.) The Rev. Thomas Wilkes referred to his visit to the "Ecumenical Conference. He said the importance of that conference lay in the fact that it represented the unity of Methodism; that it modified all the many branches of that faith, and indicated that the Methodist Churches were growing nearer together. In the near future there would not only be unity of the Methodist Churches but of all Nonconformist Churches the world over. Doctrinally there was now very little to divide them, and as there was a confederation of States in America, he hoped in the near future to see a confedera- tion of Nonconformist Churches all the world over. (Applause.)Mr. Wilkes then described in detail the pro- ceedings of the Conference. 'The, Rev. W. Ripley Winston, the deputation then delivered a speech dealing with missionary labours in Burmah. Upper Burmah, he said, had increased in prosperity year by year since it was annexed by the English five and a half years ago, and the revenne was collected without any appreciable difficulty on the part of the people. Our Government had displayed admin- istrative capacity of the highest order' but he should like to see the Englishmen in Burmah lead cleaner lives and to see England ceasing all complicity and connection with all liquor and opium in Upper Burmah. (Applause) It was practically the law of the land that the people should not drink anything that intoxicated, and what did they find now ? They found people on their knees begging that the English would not establish any liquor

div.head: EDUCATION AT WIDNEi.
div.p: EDUCATION AT WIDNEi.
PUBLIC MEETING.

Under the auspices of the newly-formed Widnes Educationalist Association a public meeting was held in Lacey-st. Schoolroom, on Thursday night. Mr. James Hargreaves presided, and amongst those present were the Rev. J. Hurst Hollo well, of Roch- dale (formerly chairman of Nottingham School Board), Rev. R. G. Hughes, Rev. D. Davies, Messrs. S. Owens, G. Davies, G. Rae, T. Cosier, J. W. Coxon, R. Roberts, D. Lewis, J. Robinson, W. Hodgkinson, G. H. Danby, T. S. Swale, R. Booth, F. J. Poole, and T. J. Peters.

In opening the proceeding, the Chairman said there was only a small attendance, but that meeting did not represent the amount of interest felt in the question of education in Widnes, but everybody shirked the work in the hope that somebody else would do the work. The object of this Association was to rouse that interest, but up to the present the Association had done no work and the people could scarcely know that they existed. The educational question happened to be overshadowed bylthe political, and objections had been made to raising the educational question now because it was alleged that it might have some influence adverse to Use interest of some political wirepullers at the approaching election, but he should not allow his politics to influence his views of education. In an educated population there was very little danger politically, but in his opinion the constitu- tion was in continual danger so long as the citizens were ignorant and illiterate. It was very much to be regretted that sects had anything to do with the matter. How did the various sections of the religious world regard the educational question? Confining themselves to Widnes alone, the Nonconformist party had invariably been the advocates of liberal and extensive education for all chil- dren of the town. (Applause.) He wished he could say the same thing of those that belonged to the English Church. They had very little complaint to make of the laymen, but as to the clerical part of the church it had so far been rather injurious to the progress of edu- cation. They did not need to mention any better names, any better advocates, any more liberal thinkers on edu- cational questions than Timmis, Deacon, and Wareing. (Applause.) If at the next School Board election the Nonconformists could not find sufficient candidates of their own, he was sure they would distribute their votes to these three persons quite as freely as they would to the Nonconformists themselves. (Hear, hear.) There was a third section of the religious creeds which interfered in the educational question, and certainly not in favour of education. They must bear this fact in mind that they were the servants of.a foreign ecclesiasti- cal power,of a power which had no sympathy with Eng- land or England's progress. (Hear, hear.) They were the servants of a power which had anathematised Eng- land fca. centuries. They claimed full control of the minds of their devotees, and they assert that they alone have the right to educate the youth of any country. And it was this corporate body—he did not know whether he ought to call it a church or not—that burned Bruno at the stake for asserting that which almost every schoolboy knew nowadays—that threatened Galiieo with Bruno's fate for simply putting down a few mathematical facts, and he did suffer imprisonment. Had it been in their power, Isaac Newton would have been equally silenced, and when his works appeared on the Continent, they were rigidly suppressed by this power. One of its dignitaries had declare d geometry a diabolical art, th tt ought to bs banished from all Christendom. Possibly Father Finegan had this gentleman in mind when he raised fees for teaching, , geometry in the Board schools of Widnes. (Laughter ' and applause.) The Catholic Church did not now do the things he had described, because they dare'nt. (Hear hear.) As far as the Nonconformists were con- cerned, they were not afraid of the truth, no matter where it came from. (Applause.) Like the ancient philosopher, they had only one fear—to IsSieve a lie. (Hear hear.) They knew what the action of those men were in Widnes. For instance, one of these men went to a child who was in a Board School. If lie knew that he belonged to his denomination, he frightened the parents with the terrors of eternity if they did not take the child away from that school, and send it to the one over which he had control. The struggle at present , was between priest and schoolmaster. He thought , the Educational Association of Widnes might bn depended upon in future, to show itself the schoolmaster's frien.l. (Applause.) The school- masters could not very well speak for themselves, as the persons who had authority over them had determined that they should be kept in their subordinate position,and he thought that merely for the schoolmaster's sake,on purpose to secure him his proper and legitim tte status, and if for nothing else, Widnes Educational Asso- ciation was completely justified. (Applause.)—The Rev. J. Hurst Hollowell then delivered an address in which he said the question was whether Education should be carried on by the people for the good of the people or by denominations for denominations. That: education should be carried on at the cost of the nation both the School Board party and the Denominational party were perfectly unanimous, and their denominational friends were inure enthusiastic than themselves that nearly the present cost , should come out of the pockets of those who had no con- trol over most of it. The denominationalist managed schools but they took good care not to pay for them. The last important return dealing with school fees and volun- tary subscriptions fur the ye tr ending August, 1819, showed that there were three voluntary schools in Widnes—the National School, which drew in fees from parents in that year £431 9s. 24. ; St. Mary's, £459 ss. 51. ; and St. Patrick's, £348 16s. 4d. ; total, £1,239 103. 11d. If they would average that sum over the 1,683 who were in average attendance that year they would discover that the fees charged in Widnes were about 4s. above the average of England and Wales. Then there were the grants which the people paid just as much as the fees,and the total for that year was £1,647 12s. 6d. ; making the total receipts from public sources— parents and taxpayers-22,887. That was a magnificent sum for three schools to take, and they must remember that attendance at these schools was compulsory, because the School Board had not found accommodation for the whole of the children. They , would suppose that the denominations in question fur- nished a very large contribution toward the cost of the teaching staff, and the school maintenance generally. Well ,the denominations contributed the magnificent sum of £67 ss. sd—(laughter)—of which St. Patrick's contri- buted not one brass farthing. St. Mary's managers con- tributed exactly £lO, and the National School managers £57 ss. sd. They could save money on the Sunday school by keeping a day school in the same building, and he asserted that the day schools in Widnes connected with the Roman Catholic and National churches were carried on at a practical profit to those denominations, and did not cost those denominations so much as a penny. (Applause.) The Bishop of Salford was very fond of saying we built these schools and we claim them, but that did not apply to Widnes. When the National School was built the Government found £285 of the cost ; £332 ss. of the cost of St. Mary's, and when St. Patrick's was erected, the amount paid out of the Trea- sury was £6BO 15s. (Applause.) Nonconformists did not get Sunday schools built on this principle. (Hear, hear.) They were sometimes taunted that they did not erect school buildings, but the fact was that Nonconformists had school accommo- dation in their Sunday schools for a million more children than the Church of England—(applause)—but they did net use national education for the purposes of proselytism. (Hear, hear and applause.) The Non- conformists objected to education being deminted. by any one sect, and in the interest of any denomination, and as they had had to be reckoned with for three centuries they would have to be reckoned with on. this question. (Applause.):The fact was that denominational education had been not educating the children but strengthening the ecclesiastical interests and privileges more than ecclesiastical necessities. (Applause.; The speaker then referred to the objects of the National Society, to the tyranny exercised by the clergy in rural districts,and urged that there ought to be a School Board formed by Act of Parliament in eeery district in Eng- land. He advocated children staying longer at school and having a fuller education, and pointed out that in the specific subjects the denominational sc.hools, were far behind the Board Schools in the education given. In conclusion he pointed out that of the seven millions and three quarters spent on education seven millions were found by the people, and only the people ought to been- trusted "with the management of elementary. education. (Applause.)—On the proposition of Mr. Lewis, seconded by Mr. Hodgkinson, a vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Hollowell.—Mr. S. Owen moved this resolution—" That this meeting views with satisfaction the formation of the Widnes Educational Association, and considers the As- sociation worthy of the confidence and support of the ratepayers of the district."—Mr. George Davies seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously.
A marriage has been arranged, and will shortly take place, between his Honour Judge Shand and Isabel Eleanor, eldest daughter of the Rev. John Richardson, vicar of Knowsley, Lancashire.

Br AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

The Wesleyans throw much enthusiasm into their missionary meetings, and the one in St. Paul's, on Tuesday, was no exception to the rule. The collec- tion at the meeting was over £5 in excess of last year, the worthy Chairman's contribution being £25,

The case decided on Monday with respect to Mr. Wright's dog is causing dog owners to inquire what is the use of having a (log if you cannot allow him to roam about the yard to protect the premises. A licensed hawker, like other people, must knock, in order to gain the ear of the inhabitants of a dwell- ng, andnot do as the woman in this case did, and as most of her class do, walk into the yard. Then there would be no danger of being bitten by the animal inside.

The charter of incorporation for Widnes is a long while in coming. Mr. Oppenheim, the clerk, has just been in communication with his London agents, who state that from past experience they know that the officials take a considerable length of time to move in regard to the granting of charters. From inquiries they found that the Local Government Board had suggested some amendments arising out of the scheme and that these were now under the consideration of the Privy Council, and they hoped soon to hear de- finitely from that body. It is to he hoped that they will. It is now twelve months since the application for a charter was made, and seven months since the Government inquiry was held as to the scheme, and it is surely time the ratepayers were put out of their suspense.

There are now three vacancies on Widnes Local Board. Dr. O'Keeffe has resigned, and Mr. E. Carey and Mr. F. C. Liddell, have allowed their seats to become vacant, through failing to attend six meetings. As there will of necessity be an election within the next four months, the Local Board have asked the Local Government Board to extend the time for filling up the vacancies.

Mr. H. Wade Deacon. J.P., met with an accident en Tuesday, which might have had more serious results. A horse he was riding shied, and became almost unmanageable, and in its movements it forced Mr. Deacon's leg against a telegraph pole, bruising the limb from the knee downwards. div.head: WIDNES LIBE It.A.L CLUB.
div.p: WIDNES LIBE It.A.L CLUB.
ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meeting of the Widnes Liberal Club was held in the club room, on Tuesday evening. under the presidency of Major Wareing. Mr. J. Morrison read the fourth annual report of the com- mittee, which stated that :they finished the year with a balance in hand of £2O 58. 9d. The furniture and property of the club now amounted to the value of £3OO, and it was all paid for and covered by in- surance. The membership of the club now num- bered about 150, and the subscription is paid at the low sum of 28. 6d.; and as they had not asked for a single penny beyond members' subscriptions during the year, it was clear that a club of this kind could be made self-supporting with careful arrangement. Regret was expressed that Mr. Browne had been compelled to resign the hon. secretaryship through ill health, and his past services were eulogised. The re- port was adopted,and the following committee appointed for the present year :—Messrs. J. Morrison, H. B. Shores, 11. R. Colquett, J. Sadler, J. Johnson, A. Parkinson, E. Develin, J. Whilan, J. McElroy, H. Fairclough, R. Lea, T. J. Peters, F. J. Poole, C. Browne, T. Brady, and A. 13. Pickering.—Mr. H. Wade Deacon, J.P., the candid- ate,then delivered an address or description of his recent visit to Ireland. He said it was sad to see the poverty- stricken appearance of many of the villages and to see field after field covered with thistles and weeds and the general deadly look of the land. The evicted tenants were as a body a far better class of men than he had expected to find ; they were most intelligert, and many expressed themselves anxious to return to the land, and would agree to any reasonable offer in order to gtt back to it. He (Mr. Deacon) had no reason to doubt their statements, and a life of idleness was good for no man. (Hear, hear.) This strife might have been avoided by the exercise of jndgme.nt and tact and a little humanity, and he believed that even now a settlement might be obtained if the affairs of the country were properly managed. He (Mr. Deacon) could not help thinking that if a Liberal majority was returned at the next election, a satisfactory settlement would be brought about. The speaker then proceeded to state how a certain landlord ordered his agent to have the goods of one of his tenants sold for arrears of rent. The agent proceeded to the farm, accompanied by a number of men armed with firearms. On arriving at the farm they were , met by the farmer and a number of his workmen at the farmyard gate. The tenant demanded to see a copy of the warrant, and then went into the house. One of the agent's men, named Kinsella, attempted to climb on the gate, when a man struck the gate with a fork, but did not strike Kinsella. Immediately afterwards two shots were fired, an 1 Kinsella fell dead. The emergency men were then told to fire, which they did, but, fortunately, no one was injured. As he had seen the place where this occerred, he could hardly believe that no one else was injured. The attack of these emerg- ency men was utterly unjustified, and at the police inquiry no man was found amenable for the murder of the man Kinsella. Such was the outline of what occurred in Ireland in the year 1888, under Eaglish rule, or, rather, under Mr. Balfour's coercion. Is it any wonder that the people are dissatisfied with such laws? The saddest result of the misgovernment of this country, was the absolute want of faith amongst the people in the just administration of the law. Until the country was properly governed, and the people had voice in making the laws,peace could not be expected. If the people of Ireland were allowed to make their own laws, and to have them administered by those whom they elected, there 'would be peace. Coercion might produce sudden sequence, but it was not lasting. He (Mr. Deacon) was more convinced than ever that the only thing which would satisfy Ireland would be the carrying cut of the policy advocated by Mr. Gladston. in 1886. (Applause.) Ninety years had passed since, the Act of Union had been obtained, and the work of the Government could be summed up in one word, "Failure." He did not expect that Home Rule would cause a sudden reformation, for wrongs which had been suffered by the people for years, could not be remedied in a single day ; but they, the people of England, were responsible for this state of affairs, and he hoped that those present would take the oppertunity which would very soon be given them of abolishing the present system of coercion for ever. (Loud applause.) On the motion of Dr. O'Keeffe, seconded by Mr. D Wright, a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Derron, and a similar compliment was paid to the Chairman on the motion of Mr. Deacon, seconded by Mr. F. J. Poole. A proceramale of music was gone through in capital style by Miss Dwyer, Mr. M. Cambridge, Mr. J. Morrigen, and Mr. A. G. Davies.
--•,-... THE FRODSHAM WATER SCHEUE.

A special meeting. of Frodsham Parochial Committee wa,s held on Tuesday night, under the presidency of Mr. A. Thomas,J. P., and Mr. Ashton, the: Clerk, explained that the meetine had been called for the purpose of con- sidering an application from the West%Cheshire Com- pany, wbe desired the townships of Frodsham and Fred- sham Lordship to join with them in a scheme for obtaining water from the Vyrnwy mains at Kingsley. The Clerk also reported that he had had an interview with Mr. Maples, of the firm of Messrs Gill, Archer, Maples, and he had given a scale according to which houses on the line of the mains might be supplied. The annual cost on this scale would be, in his opinion, as regards this scheme, about £475 4s. 10d.. and the an- nual cost according to Mr. Timmins' scheme would be k:433 6s.—ln reply to Mr. Edwards,the Clerk stated that no persons would be .rated except those who took the water. Further, if they had a good supply of water on their premises, they need not be rated.—The Clerk Any house without sufficient water isbound to be rated. Mr. Edwards had been in correspondence with the Local Government Board on this point, and had been given to understand that every house would be rated.— Dr. Robinson considered that Mr. Timmins scheme was by far the best, as the cost of the same would be paid off in 30 years.—Mr. Edwards could not agree with Dr. Robinson.—Mr. Tiley inquired if the company would have power to include the townships in their bill.—Mr. Heywood replied that the Frodsham Gas and Water Company have power to exclude any company from supplying water within the townships for four years.— Mr. Edwards thought this w.:.s " A dog in the manger " policy on the part of the Gas Company.—Mr. Edwards moved that a deputation, consisting of the Chairman, Mr. Heywood, and the Clerk, go to Liverpool, and as- certain on what terms Frodsliain and Frodsham Lord- ship could be supplied,—Mr. Heywood having seconded the motion, it was carried.

The death is announced of the Marchioness of West- minster, mother of till Duke of Westminster, in her ninety-fourth year. About one o'clock on Thursday morning a train on the Chicago, Milwaukee, and St. Paul Railway was robbed Within twenty-tree miles of Milwaukee by robbers who are supposed to have boarded the train at a station The amount of their booty is believed to amount t 100,000dols. or more.

The usual weekly meeting of the members of the above association was held, on Wednesday evening, in the Wesleyan Schoolroom. There was a good attendance, and the chair was occupied by Mr. T. Gumersall. An excellent paper on "Palestine _ was read by Mr. R. Garnett, J.P., and much appre ciated by all present. A discussion followed. The meeting closed, after unanimously according a vote of thanks to Mr. Garnett.

div.head: CADISHEAD.
div.p: CADISHEAD.

WESLEYAN CHAPEL.—On Sunday, the foreign mission services were held in the above chapel. The Rev. B. Yates preached both morning and evening, taking for his evening subject" The Threshold." There was a good congregation, and .collections were made in aid of the foreign missions,

TEMPE RANCE ENTE RTAINMENT. —A public entertain- ment was held in the schoolroom on Saturday evening, when Mr. Firsh, of Manchester, delivered a pleasing and telling address. Solos were rendered by Miss M. A. Toft and Miss M. Johnson. The chair was occupied by Mr. G. Whitfield. The entertainment was well attended, and a collection was made at the close to defray expenses.

SniP CANAL MISSION HALL.—On Monday evening a temperance entertainment was given in the above mis- sion hall by the Oughtrington Drum and Fife Band. The band, in sailors' costume, marched through the village playing. The hall was crowded in every part, and a very pleasant entertainment was given. Mr. F. Foster was the chairman, and delivered a short temperance address.

div.p: LTMM.

WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMBNT SOCIETY.—The usual weekly meeting of this society was held in the Wes- leyan Schoolroom on Monday evening. A paper on "Socialism," was read by Mr. Simpson, and was dis- cussed by Messrs. F. 0. and E. Moston, Allen and Brereton. The lecturer made a very able reply to the criticism upon his paper. CONGREGATIONAL BAND OF HOPE.—An entertainment in connection with this band of hope was given in the Congregational Schoolroom, on Monday evening, the Rev. Charles Clay, 8.A., being in the chair. An address was given by the Rev. J. Davies, of Warrington. Two dialogues, entitled "Five bony blacksmiths " and "Tem- perance Birds," were contributed by nine of theyoungest members. There was also a laughing and crying sang by a chorus of the members, together with duets, reci- tations, &c.

GOOD THlstPLAnr.—Nineteen brethren of the Altrine- ham Crusaders',Lodge paid a visit'to the Towcr of Refuge Lodge, Lymtn, on Tuesday. WO. Berkerton presided, and gave an interesting address, and afterwards a pro- gramme of music was given. At the close of the enter- tainment Bro. Jenkins, of Warrington, proposed a vote of thanks to the visitors, which was seconded by Bro. Ellison, of Latchford, and carried. The company after- wards sat down to a sumptuous supper, at the close of which the brethren returned to Altrincham by convey- ance.

WESLEYAN SOCIAL TEA MERTING.—A social tea meet- ing of the inembrs of the Wesleyan Church took place in the schoolroom, on Wednesday evening. There were about 50 pre:3ent at tea, at the conclusion of which the Rev. A. Freeman assumed the chair, and gave a short address on the Christian life.—Mr. Brown spoke on spiritual growth and general civilization, and the coming week of special prayer.—Mr. F. 0. Moston spoke on spiritual sustenance, and Mr. Allen on the spiritual progression of practical Christianity. It was an interesting and profitable meeting.

div.head: LIVELY MEETING OF THE LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: LIVELY MEETING OF THE LOCAL BOARD.

The adjourned meeting of this authority was held on Tuesday night. There being present Messrs. H. Cameron (chairman), R. Dutton, D. Rogers, H. Harrison, Brazen- dale, Whitley, Holt, Thomason, Swallow, and Mr. Ridg- way (law clerk), and Mr. Mullard (clerk.) It will be remembered that the Board meeting on Thursday was adjourned under peculiar circumstances. A special. meeting to dispose of the business on the agenda paper was fixed for Tuesday night. Prior to the opening of the meeting, the Chairman said he should like to express his regret that anything should have arisen at the last meeting of the Board to finish the proceedings abruptly. On account of the course which ev3nts took, it became impossible for him to occupy the chair, and allow the business of the Board to proceed in the face of a very, grave accusation which was made by one of the mem- bers. He had been trying to take a charitable view of the matter, and he was sure that Mr. Brazendale, hav- ing thought over the subject in his cooler moments, would withdraw the charge he made against him. He really must decline to take the chair until the matter was disposed of.—Mr. Brazendale: If the Chairman of this Board is prepared to withdraw the charge he made against me, I shall be willing to withdraw anything which I may have said but not otherwise.—The Chair- man : lam not aware that I made any charge against you, at least I cannot remember that I said anything but what was perfectly correct and can be verified by facts. Mr. Holt thought that the subject which had caused that unpleasantness was a private matter, and had no con- nection with the Board at all.—Mr. Swallow: I am sure that Mr. Brazendale will withdraw.—Mr. Brazendale: I will do nothing of the kind. I will not withdraw anything unless the Chairman does the same.—After some further discussion the Chairman left the room amid dead silence.— Mr. Rogers proposed "That a vote of entire confidence in our Chairman be passed, to show our high apprecia- tion of his universal impartiality and straightforwardness in conducting the business of the Board."—Mr. Thomason seconded the proposal.—The resolution Was afterwards put to the meeting and carried, all voting in favour of it, excepting Mr. Brazendale.—The Chairman (Mr. Cam- eron) then entered the room, and the vote of confidence was read to him. In taking the chair,Mr. Cameron said: lam very much obliged tor the vote which you have passed. I have no object to serve by acting as Chairman of the Board. It is only right and proper that the busi- ness of this Authority should be carried on in a respect- able manner. If the Board is now satisfied I am, and I don't think that I am likely to refer to matters of that sort again, unless there is occasion. If there is occasion I feel that I can rely on the Board to support, if not me, at all events the chair. (Hear, hear.)—The several items on the agenda paper were then disposed of.

div.head: WARRINGTON TRADES AND LABOUR
div.p: WARRINGTON TRADES AND LABOUR
COUNCIL. *

The monthly meeting of this Council was held on Tuesday, at the B.orsemarket-st. Cocoa Rooms, there being 22 societies represented, and a good attend- ance of delegates, consequent upon the first meeting after the municipal elections. The re- port of the delegates Messrs. W. Bullock and J. Chrimes, who attended a preliminary meeting at Accrington, as to the federation of Lan- cashire Trades Councils, stated that the meet- ing was adjourned for the question to go before the different Trades Councils in Lancashire. A letter was read from Councillor T. Flood in which he conveyed his warmest thanks to the members of the Council for the manner they have acknow- ledged any services he had been able to render in the past, in the cause of labour. What is wanted in Warrington, is a strong labour party, as the Trades Council is formed to promote the interests of labour, and is not a political institution. Seve- ral candidates were referred to in connection with the municipal campaign. The Council's attention was drawn to the 'utterances of Councillor Bol- ton and Councillor Smethurst, the former making statements that "a few Radical fellows met in a back room," &c., to elevate themselves. As to that the Council wish to state, that they meet in as prominent a situation as they could desire; also that the questions put to the candidates were not introduced by a few "Radical fellows." but were the invention of his (Councillor Bolton's) own party. The Council then passed the following resolution: "That we express our disapprobation of the utterances of Councillor Bolton, made in public and in the Town Council; and to show that the members of the Trades Council look to Conservatives as well as Liberals, for their .support in the Town Council on the labour question, they will, with pleasure, by permission of the candidates, publish all the replies to questions put to them by the Council."

The price of flour was on Tuesday advanced is. 6d. per bag of 18 stone by the Leeds and District Corn Mil- lers' Association. This makes a rise of 3s. in seven days. A fire broke out on Thursday morning in Bethnal Green, London, and destroyed a timber stores, flock factory, and two houses. During the progress of the the flames many poor people in the neighbourhood re- moved their furniture into the street, and much excite- ment prevailed. A fireman was seriously injured, and while being removed to a house, a twin child died from shock or sudden exposure. The other twin child lay dead in a coffin upstairs.

THREATENING A. MAN WITH A PrsToL. At the Warrington Borougdi Police Court, on Monday, George Bostock was charged with threatening to shoot William Pugh, on Sunday morning, in Pierpoint-st.— P.S. Cheney said he was called to the house, and the de- fendant threatened to him to shoot Pugh, and pulled out a pistol loaded, but with no cap on it, and said witness ' had better lock him up or he would certainly do the complainant some harm.—lle was bound over in his own recognizances of £lO, and one surety of £lO to keep the peace for six months, and ordered to pay Bs. costs.—Mr. Hunt said he would take charge of the pistol at present.

THEFT OF CI:OTHES. At the Borough Police Court, on Thursday, before Captain Ridgway (chairman) and Mr. Councillor James Fairclough, James Preston, aged 17, son of William Pres- ton, formerly a lodging-house keeper, at22,Bank-st.,new a fish hawker,of 34, Dolman's-lane,and Harriet Dainteth, lately employed by him, were charged with stealing on the 20th ult. from the house of the male prisoner's father, one blanket, and one tablecloth, his property,also with stealing from the same place on the 10th inst., one pair of trousers,one vest,and one velvet overall, also his property. The articles had been pledged by several persons for the prisoners. Preston was sent to gaol for a month's hard labour, in each case; and Dainteth who is much older than he, and by whom the magistrates thought he had been led away, was sent to prison for a month's hard labour in each case. THEFT OF Supuns. At the Borough Magistrates' Court yesterday, before Dr. Gornall (chairman), and Alderman Wright, Martin Ford, forgeman .of 24,Ship Yard, was charged with steal- ing on Thursday afternoon, a pair of children's slippers, value is. 7id, from the shop of James Baker and Son, boot and shoe manufacturers,2o,Sankey-st. The prisoner pleaded guilty.—Mrs. Pritchaid, wife of the manager of the shop, saw him snatch at the slippers at the door, and followed him, sticking to him till the policeman arrived. She held him by the collar,thoug,h he attempted to strike her. At the station he stated that he only took one of the slippers. He was sent to prison for two months' hard ,labour.

AN ABSENTEE APP RENTIC B. At the Borough Magistrates' Court. yesterday, Ellen Logden was summoned for non-compliance with an or- der to-return to her work at Mr. Mill's fustian cutter's establishment. The defendant charged the complainant with making use of bad language, which he denied. She said he did so to others as well as herself. Mr. Hunt asked the complainant if he could not get on without us- ing bad language. The complainant said he did not do so. Mr. Hunt said a great many complained of it. Mr. Hunt had to rebuke the defendant for usine, disrespectful language to Mr. Mills, and Mr. Hunt rebuked her for do- ing so, telling her she should not speak in that way to her employer. Mr. Mills said that was nothing to the language she used at the works.—The ease was ad- journed for a fortnight, to allow her an opportunity of returning to work.

div.p: MINOIt CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Aleerman R. W. Fran- comb), Alderman Wright, and Councillor James

Fairclough. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—IOhII Rourke', 96th appear- ance, in Bridge-st., on Saturday morning, was fined 7s. including costs.—Mary Ann &argil!, of Manchester, in Sankey-st., on Saturday night, discharged on promis- ing to leave the town. Martin Berry in Bank-st., on Saturday night, sg.—Joseph Jones and Ellen Brown, Scotch people, were charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Bridge-st., on Saturday night. The male defendant was very disorderly and striking people in all directions. The female came up and tried to rescue him, and screamed and shouted. Twit police officers had great difficulty in'getting the male defendant to the Police Station. ' He pulled one of them (P.C. Roper) down. 10s. and costs.—Thomas Larkin, on Sun- day night, discharged on promising to quit the town.— Michael Hennessy was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Brid<.,e-st„ on Sunday night, and with as- saulting P.C. Hollingworth. He kicked the constable a number of times. The defendant said the officer struck him first. He kicked the officer under extenuating circumstances. A worm would turn sometimes. A very respectable man remonstrated with him and cried "shame." The defendant made a most voluble appeal to the Bench for mercy,and said the police followed him about like a modern Jack Sheppard. 20s. and costs.— Wm. Noon, drunk and disorderly in Bridge-st., on the 25':h of August last, 55. and costs.—Martha Williams, in Bewsey:road, on the 31st ult., 53. and costs.—Thomas Gallop, in Market-st— on the 31st ult„ 53. and costs. WIFE ASSAULTS.--William Humphreys, employed by Messrs. Fairclough and Sons, was charged with assault- ing Ellen Humphreys, his wife, on the 31st ult. Mr. Forshaw defended. Complainant said the defendant had struck her in the mouth, and kicked her in the side, and on the legs, and thrown her mother into the street for interfering. Dr. Cannell deposed to finding severe bruises on the complainant's body. Mr.Forshaw said the corni plainant was a very drunken and dirty woman, and on the occasion in question, threw a cup at him, and took a knife up to him, upon which he struck her,but did not' kick her. She was only prevented by a brother from running the knife into him. Richard Fairclough deposed that the defendant had been in his employ 12 years, and had attended his work well. Witness said the defend- ant was away recently from work, and told him it was because he had to go to the Infirmary through his wife hitting him with a poker. The complainant denied that she got drunk ; and addressing her husband, called him a murderin' little devil." A separation order was granted at her request, the defendant to allow his wife 10s. a week, and to go to prison for two months with hard labour.—Samuel Wilcher, canal labourer, was charged with assaulting Margaret Ann Wilcher,his wife, on Sunday night. Inspector Spinks found the defendant beating her near his house in Dial-st., and separat- ing them. The defendant afterwards beat her savagely in his house. Witness and P.C. Critchley had to burst the door open and apprehend him. The wife pleaded that her husband was t/rankat the time, and She had thrown a cup at him. He was fined 10s. and costs. DAMAGING A HEDGE. Arthur Rowland, William Yates, Arthur Lomax, and Walter Plumpton, boys, were charged with damaging a hedge in Howley Fields, the property of James Fairclough and Sons.—The lads had been pulling the hedge don and using a hatchet to cut it. Mr. Fairclough said most of the fences about there had been pulled down. They were usually destroyed about the sth of Nov. The boys were fined ss. each. INSANITARY PREMISES.—A FILTHY DEN.— Michael Joyce, 9, Dolan's-lane, was summoned by Mr. Norman, Inspector of Nuisances, for non-compliance with an order of Oct. 6th. requesting him to abate a nuisance of overcrowding at his house.—Mr. Norman said the house was filthy, and the defendant's daughter's face was so black that it could not have been washed for twelve months. The defendant had spoken to him about clean- .ng her, and.he had replied that the best thing he could do would be to black her all over, then she would need no washing.—Alderman Harzison : Make a blackamoor •of her.—The defendant's children witness believed, slept on the floor.—The case was children, a week to allow the defendant another chance of complying with the order, and he was enjoined to try to get his daughter to use some soap upon herself.—John Malony was sum- moned for a like offence, and was ordered to pay 225. due from him as the penalty previously imposed, and to abate the nuisance at once

OBSTRUCTING TFIE THOROUGHFARE.=WITI. -010Ver fo allowing a horse and cart to stand in Horsemarket-St. longer than necessary, on October 31st, and Benjamin Tasker were charged with a like offence in lkilarket-st.ion the 31st ult., and fined 2s. 6d. each.—Benjamin Single- ton, manager for the West of England Meat Co.. Butter- market-street, was charged with allowing mutton to hang oVer the footway so as to cause an obstruction, on the 31st ult. Mr. Hunt said the defendant had put out a board, for which he would also be summoned if he did not remove it. He was fined ss. BAD LANGUAGE.—EmiIy Hind was charged with using unseemly language at her bedroom window in Hill-st., at a quarter to 12 on the night of the 7th inst. 55." and costs. JUVENILE GAMBLERS.—John Fernley, Wm. Bradshaw, and Wm. Richardson, boys, charged with playing at a game of chance for money, on Sunday morning, were dismissed with a caution. CHIMNEYS ON FlRE.—Tinos.Craik, Thomas Cremptyn, and Patrick Toy, lodging-house keeper, were fined is. each for' having their chimneys on fire. TUESDAY.—Before Messrs, E J. Guest (chairman) and

W. Owen. A MILITARY OFFENCE.—Thomas Ross, charged, on his own confession, with having made a false attestation on enlisting in the militia, was sentenced to a month's im- prisonment with hard labour. ABSENTEES FROM ScsooL.—The following persons were dealt with at the instance of Mr. G. Riley, school atten- dance officer, for not 'sending their children regularly to school :—William Dagnall, fnrgeman, Warburton-st., 103 ; John Kermode; painter; 54, Marsh House-lane, 55.; Mary Hough, baker, 42, Howley-lane, 2s. 6d.; Henry Palmer, canal man, Alice-st., 55.; Frederick Pritchard, tanner, 17, Cartwright-st.. 55., the boy having been threatened with a birching if he came before the Bench again; John Sankey, joiner, 6, Jackson's Yard, 55.; Thomas Williams, soap maker, 10, Atherton-5t.,25. 6d.

OCCASIONAL COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. John White and Mr. Z. Armitage. DRDNIKENNESS.—rhornas Monaghan was charged with being drunk at Orford on the 7th inst., and fined ss. in- cluding costs. Michael Burke was fined 55., in default seven days imprisonment, for being drunk at Golborne, on the 7th inst. In default of payment he went to jail.

RUNCORN PETTY SES SIONS. MormaY.--Before Mr. C. Reynolds and Major Haziehurst. MISCELLANEOUS.—SeveraI persons were summoned for not attending school regularly, and the usual fine of 55., was imposed in each case.—Samuel Rawlins,a, black,was fined ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly.— Samuel Benson was mulcted in a similar sum for a like offence.—The license of the Lancers' Inn, Wellington-st., was transferred from David Crowther to James Shaw.

RUNCORN POLICE COURT. TIIESDAY.—Before Mr. Brundrit and Mr. Handley. DRUNKENNFSS.—WiIIiam Rowe and George Rowley, Ship Canal navvies, and Catherine McCann from London, in search of work, were each fined ss. and costs for being drunk.—Thomas Fladdock,a Ship Canal navvy, was charged with being skunk on the licensed premises called the Royal Hotel, Mersey-st. Inspector Cooper deposed to finding the prisoner at the bar of the hotel in p very drunken condition. Superintend-eat Large said the aublican would be brought before the Bench on Monday, and it would perhaps be as well to remand the prisoner , and hear both cases together. Tho prisoner was re- manded and admitted to bail.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THIIESDAY.—Before Mr. J. C. Gamble and Mr. J. Brock. • MISCELLANEOUS.—Thomas Lynskey, of Bold,was fined ss. and costs for drunkenness.—John and Jane Kelly, Legh-st., were each bound ever for creating a breach of the peace.—A number of persons were summoned for not sending their children regularly to school, and the usual fine of ss. was imposed. Ross KELLY made her 86th appearance and was fined 103. and costs for being drunk and disorderly. THEFTS.—Peter Bloughley (11) Pear-st., was charged with stealing a quantity of coal value ld., the property of the Globe Chemical Company. He was discharged with a caution.—A woman named Mary Ann Noon, of Nelson-st., pleaded guilty to stealing four pennyworth of coal belonging to Mr. 'Joshua Midwood, and she was fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days in default.--Sarah Hickey, of Wellington-st.; was committed to the Assizes for trial on a charge of stealing £2 10e., from the person of James Linnett, of Runcorn.

*** Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office. Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.
RUGBY.

FRODSHAM V. WIDNIS Amiramc.—This match was played at Frodsham on Saturday. The visitors won the toss, and elected to play uphill with the wind in their favour. Garner kicked off for Frodsham, a good return beinc, made, and play settled in the centre. Then T. Darlington secured ,and making a splendid run scored,T. Rogers failing at the place. The home team were now playing up well, their passing and tackling being very , accurate. T. Darlington again scored, but the place kick failed. Then T. Rogers scored twice in rapid suc- cession, but the place kick failed in each instance. Shortly after Brown scored, and the whistle blew for half time. The second half was of a much more even description, the visitors playing much better, and for a long time stopping all attempts at scoring by the home team. it last, however, Brown got over, and the game lended in a win for Frodsham by six tries to nil (12 points to 0). ASHTON Housn v. RUNCORN A.—Played at Woodchurch road, on Saturday, before a fair muster of spectators. C. Anderson started, and from a forward rush the visi- tors scored an unconverted try three minutes after the start. Continued pressure by the Runcornians resulted in a minor being forced. Coomber, getting hold,passed to J. Anderson. who ran, play being located in the visitors' 25. Wilson ran across the field, but from a combined rush the boys in green secured another minor. The House boys, who were playing up hill, pulled them- selves together, and good passing by J. Anderson, Cooraber, and Greenham, carried hostilities past the centre flag, where from a line out Williams distinguished himself by a smart dribble. Another attack by Run- corn was defeated by a magnificent dribble by C. Anderson. His brother James gathered up the ball, and after a grand run nearly the length of the field passed hack to his brother Charles Anderson, who scored a try. , Little improving the places, the visitors once more pressed, but half-time arrived with the result—Ashford House, one goal, Runcorn A. one try, two minors. Final , result—Aston House, one goal,Runcorn, four tries. WARRINGTON ST. MARY'S V. PARISH CHrßCH.—Played on the ground of the latter. The Saints kicked off, and at once took the ball into the home 25. The home team rallied, and by the aid of strong forward play took the play to the other end, where Howard got possession and scored, Morgan failing at goal. After the drop out the game was very even, both sets of backs kicking well ; but the home team came away with a rush and took play on the Saints' lines, and after several scrimmages Cliff got over, the kick failing. At half-time the Parish were leading by two tries to nil. After changing ends the home team pressed, but the Saints relieved to half- way, where the game settled down to a series of scrim- maces. Mellor eventually picked up, and, passing to Thomas, the latter re-Passed to Hampson, who dodged over the line,Helsby failing at goal. The Parish dropped out. The visitors, now playing better, attacked,but the home team defended well and took play to half-way. Hampson picked up and put in a nice run, but was brought down by the full-hack close to the line. -where the referee blew -hts whistle, the game ending in a win for the Parish Church by 4 points to 2. RUNCORN v. SALE. This match was played at Runcorn, on Saturday, both teams heir'', weakly represented, owing to the county match at Manchester. Gayter started for Runcorn and the visitors were first to attack, but Lewis saved, and returned to centre. From a scrimmage In the visit- ors' quarter,May got possession, and after putting in his kick, Pendlehury supplemented his efforts, and scored, Antrobus kicking a goal, and the home team again pressed the visitors' lines. But some smart passing by Evans, Robinson and Hampson resulted in the latter placing the ball behind the line in an easy position for goal, which was again kicked by Antrobus. Some splendid passing took place between May, Evans, Robinson. and Pendlebury, the latter dodging nicely over the line, and scoring a well-merited try, which, however, was not improved. Runcorn continued to press, and Sale had to make the ball dead on two occa- sions, to save further disaster. At half time the score was, Runcorn, two goals, one try, and two minors, to • Sale nil. After some scrambling play and careless pass- ing on the part of the home team, Reese scored, but the point was not improved upon. After a few' minutes' even play, Runcorn again broke away, a series of passes by May. Hampson, Massey, and Pendlebury resulting ina further try being registered. No goal, however, , was scored. No further point was scored, and when the whistle blew Runcorn retired winners by two goals, three tries, and four minors, to Sale nil. BARROW v. WIDNES. -

Played at Widnes before tliree or four thousand spec- tators. Brennan kicked off for the home team, and immediately forced Barrow back. The ball was soon back,but Brennan got possession,and after some fine play placed the ball in touch near the Barrow goal line, but nothing resulted, play being returned to mid-field. Play continued in ,the home quarters, and a free kick was' awarded Barrow, which Would have resulted in a score but for Barber, who relieved with a grand kick to mid- field. Widnes now ran the ball up the field. Drummond passed to Flumpton, who placed the ball over the line in fine style, but failed to improve. Immediately afterward Plumpton made a grand attempt to drop a goal. After a series of scrimmages, Gordon ran the ball over from mid-field, and scored another try, which Plumpton failed to improve. Play was even now for some time.but the ball was again in the Widnes quarter, and Drum- mond placed the leather over the line, and Plumpton
