div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 14, ls9l

converted. The whistle blew for half time, the score being—Widnes, 1 goal, 2 tries • Barrow, nil. On play being resumed,the visitors seemed determined to make up for lost time,and played a fine game,several fine runs and smart passing being witnessed; but nothing was scored for some time,when Bowker dropped a fine goal. A few minutes later Blezard placed the ball over the line,which, however, was not improved upon. Play was still centred near the home line, the Widnes men being unable to stand against their opponents. Before any further score was made time was called, the result being—Widnes, 1 goal, 2 tries; Barrow, 1 dropped goal, 1 try. WARRINGTON "A" v. STOCKPORT "A."—At Stock- port, on Saturday, before about 3,000 spectators. The visitors set the leather rolling; and Lawless was early prominent, but the home team quickly assumed the offensive, until Teare, Hampson. and Bailey, transferred the game to their opponents' 25. Some tall kicking was then indulged in, but Leggett, by smart play, effected a good relief, only to see Lawless throw to Potts, who sent the oval into Stockport territory. Massey at length cleared the danger, and Lomax on behalf of Warrington, ran finely, and was looking dangerous when stopped. By fine lacking Daniels and Lomax carried the scene of operations to the other end, when Potts nsade a grand' (run. Teare had to save a dangerous rush, and after some loose scrambling forward play, a fine punt by Webster force& Stockport to defend, a dribble eventually sending the ball to the centre. The contest was not destined to remain here, for the visitors, if lacking in combination, were playing most determinedly, and War- burton, Hampson, Davies, and Rowlands heading a 'grand dribble, repulsed their antagonists and a bout of passing between Lawless, Rowe, and Daniels only re- sulted in a minor. The drop out saw the team vying with one another in midfield, where Lally spendi ily stopped Mills, and some passing by the Warrington for- wards harassed the home defence, and from a free kick Lomax made a fine attompt at goal. After this a seem- ingly legitimate try by Warrington was for some unac- countable reason disallowed, but disaster quickly followed, as Lawless scored from Rowe's pass. A lot of fine kicking was then witnessed, and ultimately Teare, Forster, Hampson, and Warburton rushed down the field. Here Webster made a grand run to the line,,and from the subsequent scrimmage Lally got a brilliant try, but the easy place was a failure, and half time arrived with Warrington 0-2—s to nil. Resuming,Webster,by a tall punt and follow up,was ithia an ace of scoring, but Mills temporarily everted the impending danger. Teare, Bailey, and Russell dribbled finely back, and Lawless throwing to Rowlands, the latter galloped over the line, a minor quickly following. From the kick out Heath- coat got away, being- finely floored by Daniels, and it took the homesters all their time to keep their opponents at bay. At last the position was improved by offside, through the eagerness of Warrington, and in the ensuing loose play at midfield, Burrows got possession, and dropped a splendid goal. Re-starting, a flash of passinz by the visitors was supplemented with capital runs by Daniels and Russell, and some vigorous work by Hamp- son, Rowlands, and Bailey improved the advantage. Stockport were having all the worst of the play, Bur- rows time after time saving his side from disaster, ,but Warrington should certainly have scored after a dodgy run by Lally. .Davies, Forster, Warburton, and }lamp- oon were again notable, but Massey, getting possession, ran and kicked well into Warrington quarters. Potts saving grandly. Directly afterwards Warrington were caught napping, and Mills sent the ball over the visitors' line, and following up secured a try, and Stockport,after being pressed fully three parts of the game,luckily made a draw—Warrington having 0-3-3 to 1 dropped goal 1 try.

,WARRINGTON v. STOCKPORT. One of the most enjoyable games witnessed at Wilders- pool this season was that on Saturday, when the return match between the above clubs took place. Since their defeat by Warrington on September 21st, when our local team won by a try to nil, the Cheshire men have shown improved form week by week, and victory has generally been the order in the majority of their engagements. Stimulated by a large number of successes, it was no wonder that they fancied their chauce against Warring- , ton, but it must have been a hitter blow to the Stock- port supporters to see their defence so thoroughly routed and in the end defeated by two goals and one try to

ail. Warrington were minus some prominent forwards, Jolley being away assisting his county against Cheshire. Bate came in for a hearty reception as he appeared in his county jersey, and Ashton, losing the toss, deputed Fair. Turner to kick off towards the railway val. The open-

ing items although of a give-and-take nature, were highly interesting. After a bungle had been made with the return, Evans cleared his lines finely, but Stockport, packing the latter, rushed the oval back again, and J. Bate had to resort to daring saves to prevent progress. For a brief period the attack was kept up, the Stockport supporters being in high glee at the show made by their side. However, a damper was placed on this when " Smack " Bate came away, and Bandies, Heesom, and Evans being handy. The movement was seconded by Ash- ton, whose short enabled the homesters to reach the visi- tors' quarter flag. Grange kicked well, and slightly re- lievoid,but Warrington's superior combination was mani- fest, and another fine kick by the new county player again forced the Stockport men back near their lines. A huge penalty kick by Saville was but faintly responded to by Boscow, and a punt falling again from the Stock- port centre, the visitors again invaded. Barnes now gave us a sample of one of his old-time runs, and exchanges between the same player and Grange found Warrington aggressive once more. A fine exhibition of passing was next witnessed between the two tiatestand John got clear, Heesom slightly mulling the final pass. He retrieved his reputation immediately after, and from a free kick by Saville, the home centre, with a neat run and kick, had Murray defending his wing. Thornley, Ashton, and Turner were prominent in the dribble, and the attack now became fiercer than ever. Fair. Turner essayed a drop at goal on one occasion, with a futile effect, a minor being the result. Saville, who was the only back on the Stockport side who displayed anything like first-class form, showed up to advantage sooa after the drop out, but the effort was feebly supported, and ,Randles, Berry, and Evans with a concerted movement had the oval back to Grange's end, this custodian failing to repel the attack. Determination now marked War- rington's play, and, Heesom kicking well, Parrott had a kick charged by " Smack " Bate on the line, the Cestrians luckily saving.. A mark to Stockport was met by Barnes, who duly deposited the leather back at the Stockport quarters. Boscow, who had been almost a spectator nearly the whole of the game, was now called upon, and right well did he acquit himself, but on this occasion he showed up in another light, for running along touch he reached Grange, and passing when pressed, had the ill- luck to see the chance intercepted. Barnes again shone with a good run, and Murray was again tested. Morris saved on one occasion in surprising fashion, and the two Bates again passed finely. Berry charged a kick by Morris, and it was now evident that Warrington had aboutthe measure of their opponents. A rush was made for the line, and the oval being worked across to Murray, Ashton was well up, and charging the kick scored near ' the corner, Fair Turner's attempt at goal being a poor one. This was only the forerunner to a brilliant exhibi- tion a moment later, for after Barnes had responded to the drop-out" Smack " Bate dodged through, and a pass coming from the thick like shot to Evans.'rhe latter made tracks for the line. Being pressed into touch, he threw, to the open to Heesom, who took the chance in grand style, and scored under the posts, Barnes converting the point. Norris got clear soon after the drop-out, but the attempt to invade was staved off by Boscow, and Randles from some fine play by Evans got over the line, only to find the referee palpably in error, and the point disallowed. An effort was made near the close of this half, but Ashton passed a shade forward near the posts, and the score read at the interval—Warrington, 1-1-1 ; Stockport, nil. Heesom met the kick off, and Warrington at the onset had a spell of attacking. Morris was held a yard in play, and from some loose play, Noble kicked wildly, and Stockport recorded their first minor. Boscow was seen at his best immediately Ashton had dropped out, and in response to Saville's kicks changed the venue to the pavilion end, and although the Bates passed unselfishly, the chances were not taken. Saville was again the saviour of his side,s nd the home quarter flag was reached, but the Warrington forwards, who had not combined' well during this half, now displayed better form, and a rush being headed by Donohue, 'Buckley, Randles, and Berry, the visitors had all their work cut out to prevent disaster. The two Bates, Randles, and Barnes passed well, but Donohue failed in the finishing touch under the posts. The game tamed down somewhat now, and the monotony was only relieved when James Bate kicked finely down the open, and Grange mulling the leather, A. Barnes was in attendance, and snapping up the oval rushed over the line, not being satisfied until he had placed the oval behind the pests. T. Barnes converted. The remainder of the play was of a give and take nature and Berry claimed to have scored near the call of time. A minor to each side was all that was added, and in the end the scores road—Warrington, :2-1-2 ; Stockport 0-0-2. Teams :—Warrington : Bolcow, back; T., Barnes, Heesom, and Evans, three-quarters; James Bate and John Bate, halfbacks; H. Ashton, Fair Turner, Randles, Thornley, Buckley, A. Barnes, Molyneux, Berry, and Donohue. Stockport Orange, bask y Murray, Moine, and Parrott, three-quarters; Wickman and Norris. half backs; Dean, Norton, Beard, Bailey, Noble, McClure, Potts, Mills, and Downs. . •

added five goals, Robinson, in the centre,being too much for Ellis, who at this point began to play rather roughly. The game ended with Penketti 7, Lymm 1. McTear, as full-backfor Penketh, played a splendid game, as did Ellis for Lymm.

WARRINGTON V. Sr. ELPHINS.--zrhe local rivals met for the first time this season at Dalton Bank, before about 200 spectators.. The visitors came with a good record, as they have lost 4, won 3, drawn 2, while the home team are only just getting into their stride, hav- ing lost three and won 1. At 3.30, the visitors kicked off, but Turner and Tickle worked the ball nicely down, only to be robbed by Philips. Chantler then was called upon to save his charge, whic h he did magnificently The visitors gained two or three corners, but they availed nothing. The back play of Cook at this period was splendid. The game began to be of a very even character, theball going from one end of the field to the other. Chantler then had a handful from Clayton,which he got away; the visitors here played with great dash, but missing splendid opportunities of scoring. Half time arrived with a clean sheet. In the second half, the Saints took up the aggressive, but play continued to be of an even character till within ten minutes of time, when the Saints went with a rush. Williams scoring the first goal, followed five.minutes later with one from Scarisbrick. The play then began to be of a rough character, and the whistle sounded for time, leaving the Saints winners of a good game by two goals to none. The visitors did not play up to their usual form, there being considerable apathy among the players. Chantler, in goal, and Cook, Tickle, and Turner played a good game for the Saints, indeed to them their victory is 'due; for the visitors Philips, John Mather, Clayton, and Dutton were the best.
PRESENTATION TO MR. POWLSON.

A meeting of an interesting character was held in the Mayor's Parlour, in the, Town Hall, Warring- ton, on the sth inst.,at which the Mayor (Alderman Francomb), presented George Powlson with an album and a purse of gold in acknowledgment of his valuable public services as editor and publisher of the "Warrington Advertiser." The Mayor commenced the proceedings by saying: Mr. Powlson, on behalf af the subscribers I have very great pleasure in handing to you this beautiful album, and the cash received up to this date, namely, £ll7 Bs. Bd. lam not able to say much about your work in connection with the Press of this town. As you are

_ well aware, I was a very young man when you were perhaps in your most flourishing condition ; but I can safely say that I have always heard you spoken of in the very highest possible terms as being a gentlerrtan who ever upheld the truth in every possible form; a gentle- man of undoubted integrity ; and ene who at all times did his best to educate the people in every way that it was possible for a good and conscientious man to do. I shall be pleased if the gentlemen who are now present will say a few words, as I know perfectly well, that they have been intimately connected with you in your busi- ness transactions for a great number of years. Mr. JOSEPH DAVIES, J.P. said: I well recollect Mr-. Powlson coming to Warrington. The occasion of his coming was to take over the worn-out business of Messrs. Haddock and Son. But I believe that in connection with

it, the " Warrington Advertiser" was resuscitated as it were—a defunct press representative that had been started by Eyres many years before. It was a paper that I was always pleased to read. In that paper. I al- ways found truth :—I always found that Mr. Powlson did uphold all the Christian virtues, if I may so express it, which we know are so desirable; and in his paper we had beside the general news of the town. Mr. Powlson has lived after a good many worthy men in his profes- sion. There was Eyres who started the "Warrington Advertiser." Afterwards followed Messrs. Haddock and Son; and Mr. Powlson followed Haddock at Market Gate. There was likewise the firm of Messrs. J. and W. Booth, who were printers in Horsemarket-street. Then there was Toni Hurst, who represented the Radi- cal Press of Warrington in days long before your time Mr. Mayor. Then there was Tom Hope, who had a printing establishment in Buttermarket-street. He was an auctioneer as well. He was a good and worthy mem- ber of the printing profession in that day. I think he was uncle to Charles Chorley and yourself, Mr. Harrison? (Mr. Harrison : Yes.) Then there was Christopher Mather, and also Gardner, wile introduced lithography in Warrington. He published a very celebrated picture of the Warrington Regatta. Then there was Osborne in Bridge-street. Now the Press is represented by the " Guardian," the " Examiner, " and the "Observer," but amidst them all Mr. rowlson stands forward as a person we all regard with esteem, and we wish to make this little present as a memento, and to show our deep regard for him. (Mr. Powlson : Was there not also George Furnival ?) 0 yes, he was successor to Tom Hurst, and was some time at your establshment. (Mr. Harrison: He was.) Alderman HARRISON, J.P., said that, going back to the period when Mr. Powlson first came to Warrington , he had a distinct recollection of it. However, during the whole of that long time Mr. Powlson had never failed to inspire the public with confidence in his integ- rity and purity of motive, no matter how widely they might differ from him in the sentiments expressed in his journal. They all gave him credit for being honest and just. He was always straightforward and out- spoken. Mr. Powlson's paper was a medium for disem- inating Conservative principles, and that, he had done faithfully and well, at the expense, too, of his own pocket. And not only so, but the" Warrington Adver- tiser," was a journal most forward in its advocacy of everything that was calculated to improve the social condition of the people of Warrington. Mr. Powlson was one of the first who took up the ouestion of the Smoke Nuisance, and was mainly instrumental in Mr. Rawlinson coming down here and instituting an inquiry which proved of greet public advantage. Mr. JEANS said that with regard to his ownconnection with Mr. Powlson, it went back about 28 years. He had just come to Warringtou—to Marsh and Barratt's office— on trial. Looking for a news-room, he naturally went to Mr. Powlson's. Not being sure of remaining in Warring- ton, he offered to subscribe for a quarter, but Mr. Powl- son said he did not like to infringe the rules by taking other than yearly subscribers, but he was quite welcome to use the room. From that time to this, in all matters of business, and auything else, he had always found Mr. Powlson most generous. Eventually he stayed with Marsh and Barratt, and of course continued as a yearly subscriber to the Newsroom. He thought he was the last. —(Mr. Powlson: You and Dr. White). Mr. POWISON, in responding, said it was but Si mple justice to credit him, as they had done so thoroughly, with the faithful and zealous discharge of his profes- sional duties in connection with every event which had occurred, calculated to promote the interests and in- crease the prosperity of their common dwelling-place. The" Warrington Advertiser" could never be put in the category of "blind watchmen, dumb dogs, which can- not bark," nor its editor be derided for not having what is termed "the courage of his convictions." And his ' was only the common experience of journalists and jour- nalism in Warrington. During the existence of the "Ad- vertiser," the "Warrington Times," the Warrington Standard and Times," the "Warrington Mail," the "War- rington Daily Post," and the "Warrington Weekly Post," have all been discontinued. The appearance of the names of some of the donors had revived remembrance of pleasant intercourse in the past, and gave him en- coutaging evidence of the continuance of their mutual esteem.•
COLLIERY EXPLOSION AT ST. HELENS.

A SHOT-LIGHTER KILLED. The county coroner, Mr. Brighouse, held an in- quest at the Bamford Hotel, Parr, on Tuesday, on the body of William Millington, 260, Ramford-St, shot lighter and fireman at the Ashton's Green Col- liery, who was killed on Friday morning in the Florida Mine by the accidental explosion of a shot which had been charged for blasting purposes, Mr. Hall (Government inspector of mines), Mr. T. Penning- ton (certificated manager), and Mr. T. Glover (miners' agent) were present. From the evidence it seemed that a tunnel was being bored in the Florida mine through solid rock. During Thursday night two men, named William Roberts and William Joneo, were en- gaged in the work of boring holes in the rock for blasting purposes. Next morning when the shot lighter, Millington. arrived, they had bored five shot holes in the rock—two above, two below. and one at the side—and charged them all with powder by Millington's instruc- tions. Millington came in about five o'clock on Friday morning, and proceeded in the ordinary way to fire the shots. He fired off one of the bottom shots, and was returning to fire a second, when one of the top shots ex- ploded in his face, and killed him instantly. Jones and Roberts both stated that it was quite unusual to charge five holes at once and fire them one by one. Jones's (opinion was that wken the first shot went off the fuse flew up and dropped into the second hole.—Mr.Hall said he had examined the place, and he found that the shots which went off were 3ft. from each other. In his opinion, the second shot was lighted by the /lash from the first. One of the by-laws of the col- liery was that every shot shall be fired before commencing to stem or ram another. If that rule had been adhered to the accident would not have happened. It was a most dangerous thing to fire a hole in the midst of several others which were charged.—ln reply to Mr. Brighouse, Mr. Pennington, the certificated manager, could not say whether Millington had been supplied with a copy of the rules, but they were hung up on the pit bank.—Mr. Brighouse said a map might go in and out of the pit for years, and would never read thena there. The only safe way was to hand a copy to every man, and he could read them when he got home. The jury returned a verdict of accidental death, and they made a presentment to the effect that not more. than one shot should be rammed at a time; that the shot lighter should examine the holes before they were rammed and that shot lighters and other officials shonld on their appoint- ment be furnished with written or printed instructions as to their duties.
DEATH OF A N‘)VA. SCOTIAN CENr- TENARIAN.. THE OLDEST FREEMASON.

HALIFAX, TUESDAY.—The death Fs announced of the Hon. Samuel Chipman,at the advanced age of 102 years. Deceased had taken an active part in Nova Scotian poli- tics for sixty years. He was the oldest Freemason living, and was initiated into the Master's aegree in 1813.

Mr. George Lancaster, London editor of the " Dundee- Advertiser," committed suicide on Monday morning in his office in Fleet-street , London. The death is announced of P. W. Nally, a prisoner in Mountjoy Gaol, who was convicted for taking part in the Mayo conspiracy of 1882. A Calcutta telegram states that five convicts in the Rampore Gaol, who made a murderous attack on Major Vincent, vice-president of the Rampore State Council, have been executed. The Dublin police, on Monday, arrested the Rev. S. G.Cotton, incumbent of Caragh, county Kildare, on a , charge of manslaughter. -Mr. Cotton was founder and I manager of an orphanage in his parish; but the children were ill-treated, and one has died. Mr. Gladstone has intimated to M. Leon Say and other French gentlemen who proposed to entertain him at a banquet in Paris on his way to the South that his pre- sent state of health prevents him from accepting the honour.

- Monday was the fiftieth anniversary of the Prince of Wales's birthday, and the occasion was celebrated in Liverpool and many other towns by the display of the royal standard over public buildings and the ringing of balls.

The latter kicked off, and scored within half-a-ininute, but "hands" being claimed had to take the free kick. The score at half time was 2 to lin favour of Penketh. In the second half Lymm were penned, only threatening twice the Penketh goal, and the Penketh forwards had it all their own way, and

ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL.

_ Nothing seems to come amiss to the Bolton Wanderers just navy. Those who know them best confess surprise at their remarkable success in the League tournament. Their football is never of a very artistic order, and their style of play is not captivating to look upon. But the fact remains that they keep on winning both at home and abroad. luring the past week they have added four points to their record, and are now six in front of the other thirteen clubs. They lost their first game with Accrington, but won the return on Saturday by three goals to none. The forward play of the " Reds" was poor in the extreme, and the defence of the Wanderers was impregnable. The mistakes by the Accrington front rank were quite unworthy of a League team.

The holders of the championship had a narrow escape on their own ground. Their opponents were West Brom- wich Albion, who led at the interval by a goal. The second half was a fierce struggle, and in the end Everton won by four to three. The Albion were much annoyed at what they considered a serious blunder by the referee in awarding the home team a goal after ends were changed. The North End were again on tne right track, beating Stoke by a goal to nothing. The back play of the Prestonians was quite of the first-class. Sunderland's career received a check, and one, moreover, that was hardly lookeet for. They had been carrying all before them of late, but could not avoid defeat at Blackburn. The Rovers scored in the first minute and again in the first minute after the interval. They were often over- played by the clever Sunderland professionals, but Arthur's goal-keeping was admirable, whilst Forbes and M'Keown did excellent service at full-back.

Not a goal was kicked in the fixture at Wolverhampton between the Wanderers and Burnley, this being the first barren League encounter since the season Opened. Hill- man's goal-keeping saved the Turf Moor colours. Aston Vlila appear to have recovered the good form of a few weeks ago, as they made short work of Notts. A victory by tiVe goals to one against Oswald and his men speaks volumes for the skill of the Birmingham players,

Lancashire have come safely through their first two engagements, but they have not yet app,oached the form which won them the title of champion county last season. Their play at Cambridge last week left a good deal to be desired, and their exhibition against Cheshire on Saturday afternoon did not give entire satisfaction. Against the Light Blues the back play was not of the very best, and on Saturday the fervrards were no better than those on the opposite side, Another 'fault in both matches was the poor way in which the goal kicks were taken. Not one of the five tries obtained on Saturday was improved upon, but it must be admitted that the positions were not particularly favourable.

Stork acquitted himself creditably, on Saturday, as centre three-quarter, but he was no improvement on Marsh. Both Miles and M'Cutcheon were seen to advant- Age, the first try which the Salford player secured being a fine effort. Berry was very unequal, his passing at times being faulty and at others smart. Cross was steady and reliable without being brilliant. Tom Coop was as safe as ever at full back, his fielding and kicking being alike good. The forwards put in a good deal of honest work, P. Steel fully justifying; his selection. The forward department was the best feature on the Cheshire vide, every one of them playing with vigour and never shirking the scrimmages. Houghton was a success at full balk, and the three-quarters were well up to their work. They might have been better served by the half backs, neither of whom did anything great.

The team that has been chosen to do duty in the Yorkshire county engagements seems to be generally approved of. There are several new faces. W. Gold- thorpe, of ifunglet, who is to figure at full back, has been placing well all the season, and A. Goldthorpe, who will appear with Dyson and Lockwood at three- quarters, is possessed of qualities of a high order. Staddon and Bedford are two capable half-backs, and the forwards are a fine lot. Yorkshire are looking for- ward to the annual battle with Lancashire on the 28th instant, with their usual confidence.

With the exleption Af Valentine, whose knee is altnnst right again, Swinton departed on their Welsh tour, with their best men. They apparel at Cat diff on Saturday, and received a decided defeat. The Lancashire team could make no impression at all on their opponents' defence, and were beaten by two goals, and two tries. All the scoring was done after The change of ends, Arthur being conspicuous for the viciors.

There was a close conte3t bttween Wigan and St. Helens Recreation, the result of which was a try for each team. Pilkington put in sterling work for the " Recs." St. Helens were vanquished at home by Aspull. Gwynn did a good deal ' towards winning the Rochdale Hornets' fixture for Oldham, scoring a couple of tries in the best style. Runcorn had a comparatively easy thing on with Sale.
LOSS OF A STEAMER ITNID SEVENTY;

SEVEN LIVES A telegram from Fort Blair announces that on Sunday morning the steamar Enterprise, one of the ships of the Indian Marine,foundered in the harbour during a cyclone which raged with great severity throughout the day. Out of a crew of 83 only six were saved, the remainder going down with the vessel. The pilot brig Calleroon is also missing, but at present there is no reason to believe she has been lost. The Enterprise was an iron steamer of 540 tons and 150-horse power. A " Times " second edition telegram, dated Calcutta, Tuesday, states that the total lives lost in the wreck of the Indian marine steamer Enterprise, off Andaman Is- lands, were about 80. All perished except four Lascars, one fireman, and one native steward. The officers lost were Captain McCarthy, the first officer; Smith, second officer ; Shortlan, third officer; Andrew, chief engineer; Fennill, and assistant engineer, Joseph Gonsalves. The band of female convicts, opposite whose prison the wreck occurred; showed great heroism, and the survi- vors owe their lives to their efforts.

div.head: RAILWAY OUTRAGE. NEAR. WIGAN.
div.p: RAILWAY OUTRAGE. NEAR. WIGAN.

WOMEN THROWN ON THE LINE. The Wigan police were informed on Sunday evening of a dastardly outrage in a railway carriage on the London and North-Western Railway between Wigan and St. Helens. It appears that Ellen Critchley and her hus- band, along with a woman named Mary Cotterill,entered a third-class compartment. They were followed by three men, one of whom began to molest the woman, and when reproved struck her a brutal blow on the head, opened the door of the carriage, and threw her out of the train. The woman Critchlev now screamed "Murder," when the ruffian caught hold of her and pitched her out in the presence of her husband, who was powerless to assist, as he was held by the two companions of the man who had taken the most prominent part in the outrage. The train was meanwhile in motion, and both women were found in the six foot way, their escape from death being con- sidered marvellous. An express train was due on that line, and this train arrived within a few minutes of their being relieved from their perilous position. Information was at once given to the Wigan police, who despatched Police-Constable Alker to St. Helens, and he, in company with a railway detective in the latter town, apprehended a collier residing at Parr, named Robert Duckworth, who was brought to Wigan in custody.

div.head: " TOMMY " BURNS AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: " TOMMY " BURNS AT EARLESTOWN.

The champion diver, having announced his inten- tion of jumping from the railway viaduct, known as the Nine Arches, at Earlestown, a great crowd of people of all ages and conditions, assembled on the canal bank to witness the feat, on the afternoon of that day. The bridge crosses the canal,at the height of about 75 feet. and it was Burns's int'ention to dive from the ledge just below the parapet, into the canal, the depth of water at that particular spot be- ing somewhere about seven feet. During the week, however, the police became aware of what was to take place,and as they considered the feat to be too dangerous to attempt, they put themselves in com- munication with the railway authorities; with the result that instructions were given for the ap- proaches to the bridge to be guarded, and unau- thorised persons prevented from going upon it. Three o'clock was the time fixed for the exhibitiOn, and before that time, shoals of people were to be seen wending their way towards the canal, on foot, and in conveyances, until at the appointed time there could not be fewer than 3,000 people pre- sent. Sergeant Longworth and three policemen, with Detective Atkinson, of the London and North- Westean Railway Company, and a number of plate- layers were early on the scene, and took possession of the bridge in such a manner, as to render it im- possible for anyone to gain access to it. Burns. however, did not put in an appearance until 3-40. He was observed to emerge from a farmhouse close to the bridge, disguised as a collier, and ascend the embankment. On the way up, he stumbled and cut his hands. Arriving at the top, he was met by Sergeant Longworth, who inquired if he' was " Tommy " Burns, and on answering in the affirma- tive, he was told that he could not be allowed to go on the bridge. This was only what Burns expected, and on is making an effort to carry out his purpose, hi was promptly seized, and apprehended for trespassing. It was then seen that he was under the influence of drink, and it was deemed necessary to lock him up. He was accordingly given into custody by De- tective Atkinson, and marched off to the Police Station. and safely deposited in one of the cells, whare in less than fi7e minutes he fell sound asleep. He was liberated on bail at midnight, and will be brought before the magistrates at Newton, on Satur- day,on the charge of being drunk on the Company's premises, and with trespassing to the endangerment of life.

div.head: COLLIER DIVES.
div.p: A COLLIER DIVES.

About ten minutes after Burns had been removed a collier named'Dempsey, from Parr, got on to the unguarded bridge. and performed the feat which Burns had previously been prevented from doing. The performance was by no means satisfactory, as Dempsey was seriously injured.

TH-CTRSDAT.—Before his Honour Judge Ffoulkes. DAMAGE BY DUCKS. —John Frazer, farmer, Moore, claimed £1 10s. damage from Thomas Weir, also a far- mer at Moore, for damage caused by ducks and fowls on two of his fields. Mr. Unsworth (of the firm of Messrs. Jenkins and Unsworth) appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Arthur Browne for the defendant. It was stated for the plaintiff that the fields in which the damage was alleged to have taken place were separated from the de - fondant's stackyard and garden by a small brook. The defendant had been repeatedly requested by the plaintiff to keep his ducks and fowl off the fields as they were in the habit of trespassing and, doing dam- age to the hay grass. He, however, refused to prevent the nuisance. One shilling had been paid into court by the plaintiff as the amount of damage done. Evidence was given by witnesses called by the plaintiff to the effect that the damage amounted to fully 305., while for the defence there were witnesses who calcu- lated that the harm done by the ducks7could not be as- sessed at more than is. It was alleged that part of the damage to the crop had been done by rabbits. His Honour gave a verdict for 10s. damage. A COMPLICATID CASE.—James Sankey, of Newton-le- Willows, wheelwright, sued Charles and Thomas Pen- nington, Mill-lane, Newton, 'farmers, for £33 6s. 10cl., being the balance alleged to be due for work done. Mr. H. J. Longtoh appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. A. Browne for the defendants, who had paid into'court £22 19s. 2d., and proportionate costs £2 4s. 10d., but lie had filed a set off for £2 10s. for carting done for the plaintiff,and had also filed a defence,pleading, the statute of limitations to the item of £l7 16s. 10d. alleged to have been due for work done in 1879. His Honour said it would be as well to settle the point as to the statute of limitations first, and then Mr. Browne might take what other course he thought best. The plaintiff was then called and said that the account for the £l7 16s. 10d. was delivered on the 31st December, 187 g. and that on September, 1881, he received £lO on account. Cross-examined by Mr. Browne he admitted that he had sent in a number of accounts to the defendants but had never included the £7 16s. Md. of the balance until the present claim was commenced. On this admission his Honour then pointed out that the defence with regard to the statute of limi- tations held good, and that the only matter left to decide was as to the set off for £2 10s. which the defendants claimed from the plaintiff. Mr. Browne explained that the set-off consisted of two items of £1 ss. each, • for Mr. Pennington going to Liverpool on two occasions, one in October, 1889, and the other in June, 1890, at the plaintiff's request for a lurry laden with timber. It was admitted by the plain- tiff that the defendants had done this work, but he con- tended, in the first place, that it was done gratuitously; in the second place, if not done gratuitously, the charge was excessive. Evidence was given by witnesses on both sides, but ultimately his Honour gave a verdict for the defendants, both on the claim and counter-claim.
RESIGNATION OF THE -VICAR OF
HAYDOCK.

The Rev. A. M. Lewis, vicar of the parish of St. James' the Great, Haydock, placed his resignation of the lying in the hands of the patron, the Rev. W. J. Melville, rector of Downall Green, Ashton, on Saturday, and it was accepted. Mr. Lewis has also intimated to his churchwardens that he has resigned the living, and has in fact given up to the wardens, all papers connected with the parish and the church. Inquiries instituted on Thursday, elicited that "differences "of a more or less acute nature have for some months past existed between the Rev. A. M. Lewis and a portion of his parishioners, and as one difficulty was surmounted• add apparently forgotten, another would divide the councils of the church. Some of these differences, it is stated, have been traced to the period when the newly erected parish church, which still awaits consecration, was formerly opened for divine worship, by special license, in July last. For many years the Haydock parishioners worshipped in an inconvenient and altogether incommodious •church, and the new edifice, opened as stated in July last, was erected at a cost of £4,300. Towards this amount Mr. W. J. Legh, of Lyme Hall, Disley, the lord of the manor, generously contributed £2,000, in addition to a gift of the site, and it was felt by the worshippers that their long-expressed desires had been realised, and that, as a church, their future prospects were bright and encourag- ing. Unfortunately, however, the building committee of the church, which, it is stated, includes the prin- cipal parishioners, could not agree with certain re. commendations of the vicar. whqse tendencies are understood to have been of a Ritualistic character. From this point affairs seems to have gone from' bad to worse, and some singular proceedings were wit- ness at a meeting of the building committee, held in the vestry of the church on Friday night. The vicar attended this gathering,and a sequel to what transpired thereat was seen on Saturday morning, when the peo- ple's warden, Mr. Edwin Jackson, received a letter from the Rev. A. M. Lewis, intimating that he resigned the living and would no longer take charge of the services. He added that he had sent word to that effect to the patron of the living, the Rev. W. J. Melville, rector of , Downall Green . N The Rev. A. M. Lewis came to Haydock from Ash Vicarage, Martock, Somersetshire, in the early part of 1889. He and the then vicar of Haydock, the Rev. A. H. Kearney, mutually arranged for an exchange Of the livings, with the consent of their respective patrons. The present curate of Haydock is the Rev. R. S. Bartram, for whom the parishioners have shown much sympathy. The Rev. J. Chator, curate of Downall Green, and pro-

pective son-in-law to the rector has been appointed to the vacancy. In Mr. Chator, the parishioners of Haydock are fortunate, in securing a clergyman,who has not only the reputation of being an excellent preacher. but is known as a good organiser, and being a 8.M., he is qualified to take in hand and conduct the choir. In other ways the appointment is a good one, and it would have been difficult to make a better selection. It is ex- pected that Mr. Chator will preach at Haydock next Suuday.

The hon. secretary of the Irish Protestant Home Rule League has written to the " Dublin Press " stating that the League is Anti-Parnellite, and intends to issue a manifesto to that effect. The "Yorkshire Evening Post" is officially informed that Mr. Jackson has accepted the Irish Secretaryship. Mr. • Jackson's appointment will cause an election in North Leeds, where in 1886 he defeated Mr. Rutson by 619 votes. A jeweller named William Slater was on Tuesday re manded at Clerkenwell Police Court on a charge of at tempting to poison Anne Bowden. Counsel for the Treasury, who prosecuted, stated that the prisoner would also be charged with poisoning Ellen Denworth at Lam- beth.

div.head: DISASTROUS GALE.
div.p: DISASTROUS GALE.

GREA.T DESTRUCTION OF SHIPPING AND LOSS OF LIFE. ACCIDENT TO A LIFEBOAT. Wednesday's gale was of a most disastrous char- acter, both at sea and on land, ani the loss of life will in all probability be much greater than that already reported. The list of shipping easualties is a heavy one. The cyclonic disturbance which was approaching our islands on Tuesday evening proved to be far more serious than originally ap- - peareti ; and in the courses of Wednesday when the system travelled north-eastwards across the kingdom a severe gale from varying directions was experienced over the entire country. Continit- - ons rain was reported over nearly the whole king- dom. WRECK AT SA.NDGA.TE.—MANY LIVES LOST. At Sandgate a three-masted vessel stranded opposite Wellington Terrace on Wednesday morning, and the - crew took to the rigging. Ths rocket apparatus was at once got out, and the lifeboat attempted a reseue. The- vessel was found to be the Beuvenue, built at Dumbar- ton in 1884, and owned by Messrs. Watson Brothers, of Glasgow. She had a valuable cargo with which she left London on Tuesday for Sydney. When the serious condition of thingr,s became recognised, the excitement- on shore was intense. The seamen could be distinctly seen in the rigging, and as the hull of the veisel had been under water since about seven in the morning, there was a general fear that she would go to pieces. To add to the general terror of the spectacle, the 9ea began to cast up wreckage, whilst several dead bodies were observed. Opposite the Marine Parade a heart- rending scene was witnessed, a sailor being all but rescued by a boatman who had bravely plunged into the sea. The latter hads ordered a friend to procure some nourishment for the sailor in case be should be - rescued, but when the poor fellow was within almost arms' length of the boatman he became exhausted and sank. The military were called out, and rendered what assistance they could. In attempting to launch the life- boat at Hythe it capsized, and a man named Doolan was drowned. He leaves a widow and five children. At nightfall beacons were lighted on shore, with the idea that they might encourage the poor fellows still hanging in the rigging between life and death. Tele- graphing on Wednesday night a correspondent saysro— Twenty-seven of the unfortunate crew, have been eal- lantly saved by the Sandgate lifeboat and taken to Folkestone. The crew numbered 32 all told. The five who have perished are Captain Maddrell, who was in command of the vessel, Pringle Bruce, of Gravesend, and Edgaid Ironmonger, the two apprentices, the steward and an able-bodied seaman. a- This was not theonly fatality which has to be recoided as occurring near Bandgate. In the forenoon the schooner Eider' of Bordeaux, was blown ashore between that place and Elythe. After waiting for sotne, time the crew resolved to try said reach the shore, only a few yards off. There were on board, besides the captain and four seamen, the captain's wife, and a lad, the captain's nephew. They had taken off their clothes, when the vessel gave a lurch, and all were washed info the sea. The four seamen saved themselves, but saw no more of the captain, his wife, and nephew. The body of the latter was subsequently washed ashore at Sanagate.

div.head: WRECK OFF FORMBY
div.p: WRECK OFF FORMBY

It was ascertained on Thursday morning that a small steamer had gone ashore off Formby during the gale the previous afternoon,and that the crew had been drowned owing to the lack of life saving appliances. It will be re. membered that some time ago the lifeboat at Formby was withdrawn, and it is asserted that since then three wrecks have occurred under circumstances similar to the latest. A. group of fishermen on the shore observed four men in the rigging, and although the distance was not more than three hundred yards they were powerless to aid. The steamer was the Hawarden Castle, of Liver- , pool. The Southport lifebqat was out all night, but saw nothing of the ill-fated craft.

A telegram from Lowestoft stated that a large fish?ng boat, Star of the East, has been lost. The crew consisted ef eight men, one of whom only was got ashore, and he died subsequently. The Lowestoft boats John Jane and Hannah were driven ashore, but the crews escaped with their lives. A vessel loaded with coke for Norway was wrecked be- tween Lancing and Worthing, but the crew of eight men and the captain were rescued by the lifeboat. A wreck was also reported at West Brighton. The pilot cutter Venus, with three men went to the rescue of a man who was observed holding on to the keel of a small boat that had been capsized near Cardiff. Two men put off in a punt, but the sea capsized her, and the three men were drowned. At Penzance a schooner got ashore on one of the eastern islands of Scilly, and the lifeboat from St. Mary's went to her assistance. A number of small boats in the harbour were sunk. From Poole it is reported that the brig Solertia, of Tons nerg, laden _ with deals, from Soroka for Poole, stranded in Studland Bay. Her crew of eight were Dee- med by the lifeboat. Two steamers got ashore at the mouth of the Avon. In the afternoon a lofty chimney stack at the Feeder Saw Mills fell through the boiler house, crushing one man. Benjamin Smith, and killing him on the spot, and injuring two others named Ford and Cantle. An Aldeburgh telegram states that four vessels had been wrecked there, but that their crews were saved. At Southend a schooner, name unknown, was seen to go ashore on Shoebury. Four boats from Southend put off to render assistance, and a fishing smack coming' UP from below the Nore lowered her boat with two men, but the heavy sea struck the boat and capsized it. The men were thrown into the water, but one of them, named Murrell, held on to the side of the boat. The other named Cotgrove, held on to Murrell's legs, but the saa washed hint away, and he was drowned. He leaves a wife and five children. Early on Wednesday morning a schooner belonging to Padstow, which was on a voyage from Cork to Poole with oats, was driven ashore on the Eastern Islands at Scilly. At Axminster, in East Devon, the rivers Axe and Tarty are flooded to a greater extent than has been known for years, and in many places the roads have been converted into lakes of water. There is reason to fear that large numbers of cattle and sheep have been drowned. At Eastbourne the gale was very fierce and much deS- tructioe was done to house property. The most serious casualty was at a village residence known as Gothic House, in Lismore-road, where tons of debris came crash- ing through the upper and lotver rooms, killing a servant . named Ames on the spot. At the residence of the mayor damage to the extent of £2OO was done. The smack Gemini was assisted into Ramsgate har- bour on Wednesday, and reported that John Causton, George March, Frederick Plummer, and George Plum- mer were washed overboard and drowned off Dover yesterday. Lloyd's report the following casualties :—Londea schloner Caroline, from Swansea for Wells, ashore at SPurnhead ; the lifeboat landed the crew. A. schooner sunk at Bembridge Ledge ; name unknown; crew miss' ing. The Deal lugger Success foundered off Dymchurch, Deal; two men, Grigg and Philpot, were drowned. The British brig Blanche, from Cardiff for Rio, foundered on the 2nd inst. ; crew landed at Teneriffe. TWO LIFEBOAT MEN DROWNED. The coxswain of the Dungeness lifenoat telegraphs tlaat five men were washed out of the boat, but that only two were drowned. Their bodies have been recovered. A STEAM LAUNCH' WRECKED: FIVE LIVES LOST - MADRID, TIIINISDAY.—A terrible storm is raging on the coasts of Galicia. A steam launch belonging to the Spanish squadron, now in Arosa Bay, has been wrecked at Villagarcia, and of the seven men on board all buttsvo were drowned. WRECK AND LOSS OF EIGHT LIVES. eked BILBAO, THURSDAY.—The sloop Julio has bee near this port: Eight n of the crew were drownedv:brue e but th remaining three were rescued.

div.head: MURDER .OF A Arusw ITALL
div.p: THE MURDER .OF A Arusw ITALL

SINGER. The deputy-coroner for Central London and Middlesex opened an inquiry,on Thursday afternoon,at t,!•-e Coroners' Court, Clerkenwell, relative to the deaths of Frederick Wolstenholme, aged 31, dresser to a music hall artiste, and his wife. Mary, aged 29, a dancer, known profes- sionallv as "Polly Newbury." Wolstenholme shot his wife at their apartments on Monday, and afterwards committed suicide by shooting himself. The woman died shortly afterwards from the effects of her injuries. Mrs. Emma Carpenter, the mother of the deceased woman, said five years ago the husband threatened to take her life with a revolver. There was some jealousy on his part then. -.---

- At Clerkenwell, on Friday, a beerhouse-keeper named Dove was remanded charged with attempting to murder his bar boy named Kanes. Mr. Butler (Liberal Unionist) and Mr. Lambert (Glad- stonian Liberal) were on Friday nominated to contest the South Molton Division, to fill the vacancy in the Parliamentary representation caused by the elevation of Lord Lymington to the peerage.

div.head: SELECTED READIN GS.
div.p: SELECTED READIN GS.

ktrTtIORS AND. THEIR Ways.—Carlyle was one of the most painstaking of writers, almost every other word he wrote being erased and another put in its place. One day he went to the printer to large hint to push on with the work. "Why, sir," id the printer, "you really are so very hard upon as with your corrections. They take -up so much time, you see." Carlyle replied that he was accus- tomed to that sort of thing; that lie had had .works printed in Scotland, Sand—" "Yes, indeed, sit," interrupted the printer; "we are aware of that. We have a man here from Edinburgh, and when he took up a bit of your copy he dropped it like a red- hot cider, and cried out, Oh; preserve ! have you got that man to print for? Goodness only knows when we shall be one with all his correc- tions.'"—The callousness of Thomson, the author of "'The Seasons," about money matters, was truly wonderful, even for a poet. One day, while paying a brewer's bill, he inadvertently handed the man two bank-notes 'rolled together instead of one. The brewer did not discover the error until next day, when he honestly returned the second note. As may be supposed, the worthy tradesman was considerably astonished at seeing Thomson pocket the note with supreme indifference, and with the cool remark. that "could have gone on without it."—Samuel Rogers, the poet, was a very slow writer. One day several of his friends were talking about him, and one asked whether he had written anything lately. "Only a couplet," was the reply (this couplet being his celebrated epigram on Lord Dudley)."Only a couplet!" exclaimed Sydney Smith, who formed one of the party; why, what would you have? When Rogers produces a couplet, he goes to bed, and the knocker is tied, and straw is laid down, and candle is made, and the answer to inquiries is that Mr. Rogers is as well as can be expected." —No author has been made the subject of more amusing anecdotes than Dumas the elder. The following is character- istic :—On the morning of his daughter's wedding. day, Dumas said to his future son-in-law, with all the habitual affability for which he was famous, "Yes, I guarantee my daughter In income of 18,000 francs a year." The bridegroom, who was quite indifferent on the subject, his marriage being one entirely of affection, began protesting that his generous father-in-law was taking too much upon himself, when he was interrupted by his Ands whispering. "Oh, let him be, let him be; he can well afford to pay the first month's instalment." The comment of his daughter is very suggestive of the wide margin between promise and performance which characterised Dumas in money matters. •

CAN ANIMALS COUNT ?-110T1ZeIMI cites facts showing that some animals can count the number of similar objects or acts, provided the numbers are not too high. When a magpie is watched by a company of hunters it will not move till they go away. If they go one after another it cannot be deceived by one of them staying behind, unless there are more than four of them. Another story of similar bearing is that of the tramway mules at New Orleans, which are relieved and fed after mak- ing five trips. They make their trips patiently and quietly till the end of the fifth, when they give evi• dent signs that they expect their usual refreshment. The horses in the coal mines of Hainault make 30 trips a day, taking their places again, after every trip, at the head of the train, in readiness for the next trip; but at the end of the thirtieth trip they turn their heads in the opposite direction, or toward the stable. Facts of this kind ought to be tested by most preeise experiments. Are not the horses warned at the end of their stint by some exterior signs ? Is not the conclusion that they count the number .of their trips arrived at tco quickly? It would predicate n very high degree of development to.suppose that a horse could count up to 30 in any given number of hours. A man in such case would nearly always make mistakes, unless he had some means of registering the trips as they were com- pleted. It is nevertheless established that some birds and quadrupeds are capable of counting up to four or five, and perhaps more,- The Popular Science Monthly. IT is needless to say that the cat has never adopted itself to either snow or water. And yet the foot of the cat has been modified from its most perfect form, as found in the lion and tiger, where the formation is so beautifully fitted to leaping and alighting, In tbe latter particular, the adjustment of the muscles and bones to a minimum of shock is marvellous. The man who jumps down but a few feet, and, despite his utmost efforts to save himself, neverthe- less jars his whole frame, can best marvel at the ease with -which the members of the cat family alight from great heights. Even the ponderous body of the lion or tiger makes hardly more noise than a rubber ball 'coming to the ground. From the lion to the cheetah the foot is essentially the same, but it is nevertheless modified, in minor par- ticulars to suit the differing oonditiong of Ow. vnr;nng members of the great family. ; SOME thoroughgoing democrats may look with complacency on a mob of mediocrities, but to most other persons they are the reverse of attractive, The absence of heroic gifts.is a heavy set-off against the freedom from a corresponding number of very de- graded forms. The general standard of thought and morals in a mob of mediocrities must be medi- ocre, and, what is worse, contentedly so. The lack ofliving men to afford lofty examples, and to educate the virtue of reverence, would leave an irremediable 1: All men would find themselves at nearly the ~d average level, each as meanly en- dowed neighbour.—F. Galton. THE average life of woman is longer than that of man, and at equal years woman's expectation of life is greater. But, by way of compensation, more males are born than females, and of late years the disparity between the average life of the two sexes has been disappearing, perhaps because women are hetaking themselves more to those active em- ployments which expose them to aocident, wind and weather.

DEAR to us are those who love us; the swift moments we spend with them are the compensation for a great deal of misery; they enlarge our life; but dearer are those who regret us as unworthy,-for they add another life; they build a heaven before us whereof we had not dreamed, and thereby supply to us new powers out of the recesses of the spirit, and urge us to new and unattempted performances. —E. W. Emerson.

OUR bodies are continually wasting or weiring any, and are repaired by the food and drink we consume. The fleshy particles of our bodies are renewed about once a year, and the bones about once in seven years. So in every period of seven years we have possessed seven bodies of flesh and blood and one frame of bones. In all probability you have not one particle of flesh and bones you had moven years ago.

A HUNGARIAN who had been 15 years making a coat-of-mail entirely of wood, wherein not a single link was wanting, carried it to Hunniadee, the war- like King of Hungary. The monarch, instead Of praising his ingenuity, as he had expected, sentenced him to be confined in prison for 15 years for wasting so much time and ability in so useless an employ- ment.

IN all business delay is disastrous. Each day brings new problems to solve, new decisions to make, new duties to perform. Each one of these demands a certain amount of careful thought, but it also demands a final conclusion and prompt action. He who does not learn how to apportion these to the hourly necessities cannot hope to succeed in his business, be it what it may. TRUTH is naturally so acceptable to man, so charming in herself, that to make falsehood be received we are compelled to dress it up in the snow- white robes of truth—as, in passing base coin, it must have the impress of the good ere it will pass current. Deception, hypocrisy, and dissimulation are, when practised, direct compliments to the power of truth.

SIR WALTER SCOTT never considered any amount of literary distinction as entitled to be spoken of in the same breath with mastery in the higher depart- ments of life. To have done things worthy to be written was in his eyes a dignity to which no man made any approach who had only written things worthy to be read.—J. G. Lockhart. IT is the curse of every evil nature and evil crea- ture to eat and not be satisfied. In order to teach men how to be satisfied, it is necessary fully to understand the art of joy and humble life—this at present, of all arts or sciences, beim the one most needing study.—John .Ruskin.
