Sir,—We have received in formation3from various places in the district—Ashton, Bury,Marple,Stalybridge, and others—that certain persons are going about repre- senting that they are connected with this hospital or its surgeons, and have been'sent to change or supply spec- tacles or other articles, and, in this way many persons have been induced to purchase unsuitable and worthless glasses at an extortionate price. We shall be glad if you will enable us to make it known as widely as possible that all such persons are impostors, and that at no time and under no condition is anyone sent to see patients at their homes for any purpose. Any persons whom the surgeons wish to see again will be sent for. The whole work of the hospital is done at the hospital, and the only recognised Optici- ans are Messrs. Thomas Armstrong and Brother, 88 and 90. Deansgate, Manchester. I am, dear Sir, very truly yours, November,:lB9l.
W. R. BURGESS, Sec.
THE WATCH COMMITTEE OF THE WARRING-

TON CORPORATION. Sir,—l am glad to see that the Warrington Town Council,has at last seen the error of its ways,and decided that it will no longer have a brewer, or a publican, on the Watch Committee. Councillor Bolton thought he was a fixture, but he has 13,-en removed, thanks to the temperance party, for their action, during the election, and the sense of fair-play of the Liberals, and of those Conservatives who thought of principle before party. I don't understand, Mr. Editor, how it is that anybody thought it as reasonable to object to a teetotaller as to a publican, in forming the Watch Committee. A publican has a personal interest to serve, but how can it be said, that the abstainers interest is a personal one ? The difference between the two is that the publican has an interest in checking the enforcement of the law, while the abstainer simply wants the law carrying out, as he ends it on the Statute Book. It seems to me that it is just as ridiculous to object to a teetotaller being on the Watch Committee as it would be to object to a man because he was a moderate drinker. Indeed, if one wanted to stretch a point, it might be said that the Councillor who took any drink at all must be more or less in sympathy with drink-sellers. But I don't want to stretch a point : all I want is fair-play. Yours truly, A LOOKER-ON. Warrington, Nov. 12th, 1891.
THE RECTOR OF WARRINGTON ON BAPTISM, &c.

Sir,—The Rev. F. W. Willis is reported as saying at the Diocesan Conference in Liverpool last Wednesday : " That the church was the whole company of the bap- tised. He would speak strongly on baptismal regenera- tion, he would point out to children the great meaning of confirmation, that they did not go to confirm vows, but to be confirmed by the Holy Spirit. He would speak (to childrea) of episcopal ordination as absolutely neces- sary. He would show the limits of confession to the priest, and of absolution. He would show to them (children) the doctrine of the real presence." I beg to differ from the Rector. The church is not the whole company of the baptised, but believers only. Now in the Church of England a person as a rule is never bap- tised ; sprinkling or pouring of water is not the meaning of the Greek word baptize. It means to dip, to plunge, to bury, to overwhelm. Further, the following divines are against Infant Baptism :—Bisliops Burnet,Lightfoot, Archbishop Seeker, Deans McNeil, Stanley, and Howson. Conybeare, wrote :—" It is needless to say that baptism was administered by immersion; the convert (not.infant) being plunged beneath the surface of the water, to re- present his death to a life of sin, and then raised from his momentary burial to represent his resurrection to the life of righteousness. It may be a subject of regret that the general discontinuance of this original form (not modern) of paptim has rendered obscure to popular apprehension some very important passages of scripture. Confirmation is unscriptural. The following say it was never instituted by Christ or His Apostles :—Bishops Jewel, Burnet, Mant, Cheyney, Drs. Blakeney, Jacob, Wycliff, the late Dean of Bangor. Dr, Smith's Bible Pictionary is silent on it and many others are. Episco- CoPiession and priestly absoiutoin are not in the New Testament. As to the real presence, this Romish doctrine is contradicted in Hebrews Bc. 4v., the service for Ascension Day, the Litany, and the Creeds, "This de in remembrance of me, till he come," all imply the bodily absence of Christ, whenever the Lord's Supper is celebrated. See also the last rubric in the Communion service. Hooker says, "The real presence is not to be sought in the sacrament, but in the worthy receiver." We live spiritually by faith not by sight. ROBERT FOULKES. Frodshami Nov, 101 1891,

DRINKING AND VOTING. Btr,—That drink and voting, like fire and ruin, lowed the hideous host of a notorious brewer in Warrington, on the 2nd inst, is no secret, in his success. I am told by some young women, who have suffered privation almost from infancy, and to my knowledge for many years have had to keep a shelter over their young heads with- out the aid of their unfortunate father and mother, who are both pitiable victims of the traffic, that when the brewer solicited the vote held by one of them he was told he would not get it. He inquired "Why ? You voted for me the last time ; why not give me your vote again ?" "Why !" she replied, "because we don't in- tend to give any brewer or publican a vote again." Those who havehelped to nut brewers, Ice., in possession of the ruling power of the town cannot escape the respon- sibility for so doing; for assuredly "Birds of a feather lock together "in both this world and the next. It is more honourable to suffer defeat, resisting a bad cause, than be "like dumb driven cattle," regardless of social and moral principles. When I see the children hungry, shoeless, and almost naked, and begging for bread, my youthful history rushes with many very painful scenes (which I may not now relate) through my mind and heart. I am amazed to notice how any persons calling themselves Christians can vote and take the drink themselves,or do anything to side with the cursed traffic which they know ruins its thousands yearly. They vainly seek to shield them- selves behind the example of Jesus Christ. Suet) men Ignore all the life of Christ—save one act at the marri- age at Cana of Galilee. All the rest of His self sacrific- ing life is lost upon them. If Christ had done nothing more than turn the water into wine, we could reasonably conclude that millions of men would not be attracted tc-i- -wards Him. Pity and love gushed from Him like streams from the fountain ; cleansing th 2. leper, healing the sick, raising the dead, weeping over the doomed city, forgiv- ing the dyinc, thief; and at last forgiving His murderers. What a striking contrast this to the selfishness of such as grow rich at the expense of the social and moral ruin of others through the drink traffic. The clergyman and minister, as well as the layman, brewer, or publi- can, who cling to the bowl, miss the grand principle in Christ's life and teachings : they follow Him only to the Marriage feast for wine not love; for filthy lucre,not self- sacrifice ; and therefore they stop in the Christian course where they started. Yours, Zcc. Warrington, Nov. 3, 1.891.
DO YOUR DUTY.
THE WARRINGTON TEMPERANCE FEDERATION AND THE RECENT MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
MR. HAMPSON'S LATEST EFFUSION.

placard printed in blue ink, bearing the Signature of " John Flampson," is a fair specimen of the attempts which this worthy occasionally makes to throw dust in the eyes of the public, by distolting facts, and grossly aspersing the motives of his opponents. No doubt Mr. Flampson is considerably distressed by the results of the last two November Elections, and let me tell him, in passing, that if he and his party leaders are so blind as to persist in associating the Conservatism of Warrington as intimately as they are at present doing, with the drink interest, so surely will they detach from their party the support and allegiance of those Conserva-

tives who decline to be parties to an alliance of so demoralising a nature. Mr. flampson has thought fit to placard the town with a very brief extract from a letter recently published by the Rev. J. J. Langham, in which the latter gentleman states that he did not authorise his name to be appended to the circular issued to all the candidates at the recent election by the Temperance Federation, but Mr. Hamp- son completely ignores a far more important statement made by the clergyman in question in the very same letter. Mr. Langham says
" The questions themselves I regard as very proper ones, and no reasonable objection can be taken to the action of the Federation in seeking information thereon as to the views of the candidates."

If Mr. Hampson is so desirous that the public shall know the facts, why does he not publish the whole truth and nothing but the truth ? Now, sir, as I was one of the persons present at both of the meetings of the Temper- ance Federation, at which this question was discussed and action decided upan, let me put the full case before your readers. The Rev. J. J. Langharn has been one of the hon. co-secs. of the Warriugton Temperance Federation for some years past. All notices issued by the Federation have during this period borne his signa- ture. A meeting of the committee of the Federation was convened by the hon. secs. in the usual way for October 21st, to "consider the question of the forth- coming municipal elections, and to decide what action should be taken in regard thereto." The meeting was held, and it was decided to submit the same two ques- tions to each candidate, and to hold a further meeting a few days later to receive the replies and to decide what further action should be taken. The Rev.J.J. Longhorn and the Rev. J. Yonge were neither of them present at the meeting, so that Mr. Hampson's further statement that the Rev. John Yonge "drew up the circular which was sent to the candidate" is a pure fabrication. A letter enclosing a printed copy of the circular,which was sent to each candidate, bearing the names of the hon. secs. (Rev. J. J. Longhorn and Mr. W. Roberts) was sent to Mr. Lanham by the same post ; and the rev, gentleman replied on October 23rd as follows : " Thank you for your letter. I think the questions are very proper ones to put.—J. J. L." Probably Mr. Long- horn had overlooked this acknowledgment when he penned the letter from which Mr. Hampson has culled so misleadinr, an axtract.

A further ineetinz of the Federation was held on Oct. 25th, to receive the replies of the candidates.and having considered the same, it was decided to issue a manifesto in the name of the "Committee of the Warrington Tern- perauce Federation" calling upon the temperance elec- tors in ths various wards to support those candidates only who were favourable to our policy. As a member of the committee, I venture to assert, that our action throughout has been per- fectly honest and straightforward, and we are proud to think that it has so strengthened the public opinion in the town as to lead to the consummation we desired, in the expulsion of Councillor Bolton from the Watch uommittee, at the Council meeting on Monday ast.

In conclusion, let me advise Mr. Hampson to spend a little time in extracting the big " neam " which at present obstructs and distorts his vision—possibly the gentleman who announces himself as a member of the British Medical " Journal " would assist—and he will then find that the " mote " which he fancied he had dis- covered was merely the reflection ot his own jaundiced oculars.—! am, Sir, your obedient servant.
A MEMBER OF THE WARRINGTON TEMPERANCE FEDERATION.

div.head: PESTERING TUE LORD. "God helps those who help themsel. es." Old English Proverb.
div.p: PESTERING TUE LORD. "God helps those who help themsel. es." Old English Proverb.

Sir,—" Gnostic" tells us he has been abroad. This is needless. Many of his statements could only come from one who not only has been, but is pretty constantly abroad, at sea, and hopelessly adrift. He says nothing of Timbuctoo, although I should imagine he got his logic from thence. Take as a sample of this travelled logic what he says in his first paragraph. If any meaning at all can be attached to it it is this—that the man who professes not to know everything is an ignoramus ! And conversely I should suppose that he who does profess to know everything must be a philosopher. I should be much inclined to attach another label to the last specimen—ie. a fool, a knave or a gnostic. This precious paragraph winds up with a quite charac- teristic misquotation of my words. I did not " place the agnostic at one end of the scale and the gnostic at the other." What I did say was that Professor Huxley, as an agnostic, might be regarded (by such as " gnos- tic ") as an ignoramus, while gnostic at the other end of the scale, &c. Now this makes a most wonderful differ- ence. For if Professor Huxley at one end of the scale is an ignoramus, "gnostic ".at the other, must be a savant— a philosopher. I need not say that the one supposition is about as true as the other.

The thoroughly unscientific cast of mind of your not- too brilliant correspondent is shown in his treatment of the question of personal knowlege. To know a fact we must have had personal experience of it. Book learning is not admissable • such being merely the record of the experience of others, and the statements so made re- ceived orrejectedin accordance with the evidence, but can only be admitted to the rank of personal knowledge upon personal verificarion. Where then is " gnostic's " stand point for the assertion that the laws of chemistry are not universal ? Has he been there—all over the shop —has he read it or dreamt it. But I see in his last effort in the scientific treatment line this luminary now gives us to understand that when he denied the universality of the laws of chemistry, "it had no application to distance." Now, it would be past the wit of man to dissociate the idea of distance from that of the universe. Perhaps " gnostic" will explain and give us the logic of it, de- ductive or inductive, along with that which counten- ances prayer for a rise in the barometer, an alteration of the dew point, thermometric changes and other causes tending to a cessastion of aqueous precipitation. As in science so in literature. Passing over such trifling slips—as one thing being different to another— although that is a piece of graminer I can't get round— the use of such phrases as" the modification of the law of gravitation" is merely a bit of rant; cant phrases unthinkingly scribbled. I can understand chemical reagents modifying matter, but I have never met with any instance in any record of a " modification of the law of gravitation." When C. combines with two oquivalents of 0. to produce CO,. the total weight of the resulting compound is of course greater than that of its constituents, but the atomic weights remainthe same. Take another view of this :—When Adolphus and Angelina determine upon marrying and finally do so, is thereby the law of marriage in any way altered or affected? I iina,gine it to be within the mental grasp even of a " Gnostic " that it is Angelina with her Adolphus that are affected by this ceremony, while the Matrimonial Law remains unchanged. Again, take this man's idea of a just literary parallel. Because I deny the reasonableness of an erring mortal pleading with an Infinite Omniscience for a change of His plans and designs, " Gnostic " compares this to Portia pleading for mercy from the revengeful Jew Shy- lock ! His logic, like his science, is all abroad. See tie following piece of fatuity. " Gnostic," referring to me says—" Now, in so far as he does not know them they are unknowable." Here the" them," applies to " the things." I candidly acknow- ledge " I do not know." Hence it would appear that what I do not know is unknowable; in other words what I do not know nobody else does or can know; a manifest absurdity. But this is quite in keeping with the man who can see no difference between my phrase " the logical position of prayer" and his own "the logical position of the laws of Nature." Now prayer being man-made—the expressions of mere human wants and wishes may be regarded either as reasonable or the reverse. But whoever heard of an unreasonable law If Nature? Science being founded upon good common sense, of which it is merely a refinement, I would sug- gest to " Gnostic " that he study the rudiments ere he tries his unfledged pinions in the cerulean heights of pure science. With regard to prayer for material benefits, my posi- tion is essentially that shown in Esop's fable of Jupiter and the husbandman. When the latter applied to Jupiter for help to get his cart out of the ruts, the god's reply was " Put thy shoulder to the wheel." I much admire the practical wisdom of the parson who, when asked to pray for rain, replied, "Very well, but wait until the glass falls." Prayer for such objects, if not all prayer, only possible with people densely ignorant of their ' utter insignificance in the scale of nature. It is the 2me of an exaggerated estimate made by man of his place and importance in that scale. He is like the fly on the knave of the wheel who said "What a dust we are raising !" The fact being that he is whirled round by the earth and carried through space with as little thought or regard for his wants and wishes as the mite in the cheese gets when this, its place of abode, "upon which it lives and moves and has its being," is rolling down hill in strict obedience to immutable law, to be inevitably dashed to pieces at the bottom. And it is quite within the bounds of possibility that, could we but interrogate his mite-ship, asto his place and import- ance on the cheese, he might give us to understand that that cheese had been made with special reference to the requirements of himself, his ancestors and descendants; and that a tradition to that effect had been handed down from said ancestors, time out of mind, beyond the memory of mites. And the mite has just as much reason to suppose the cheese to have been made speeially as his habitation as we have, who are but comparatively greater mites, to arrogate to ourselves the idea that this earth was created with special reference to our use and benefit. Man is here solely as the result of the operation of natural laws. If he conforms to these laws, it is well with him; if not, he suffers, for they are far-reaching inevitable, and immutable in a sense undreamed of by the Medes and the Persians. The greatest wisdom man exhibits is when he pits law against law. In this way all his greatest physical achievements have been effected, achievements which all the praying of all the ages would never have brought about. In the matter of answered prayer, a good friend of mine—otherwise of undoubted sanity—has promised to give an instance of the altera-
VP" . 1

div.head: 111 E EXAMINER, SATU_RD
div.p: 111 E EXAMINER, SATU_RD

tion of a law of nature by prayer! When he has suffici- ent leisure ! ! This was in 1891. I am thinking these figures will be reversed ere I am afforded this treat, and then alas! it will be of little use to me! Awaiting this further enlightenment, I remain, &c., ' JOHN PEERS. Penketh, Nov. 8, 1891.
BRIMSTOO.A.N AN' TRA.YCLE. (MIXED.)
BI Tum o' DICK 0' BOBS.

Aw mentioned last week about the burning ques- tion o'th' day bein' Cremation, an' as aw were studyin' id wi a view to be cremated. One or two mates as knows me varra weel tell me as aw'm sure to come to erema.tion at last, wodever aw may think neaw ; an' as there'll be no traycle then, but ony quantity o' brimstooan. Onyway thad con pass. " Ashes to ashes "may mean cremation, or id may nod, but aw look on id as a varra ancient art, an this is proved bi th' ancient form o' invitation con- tained i' th' words "Go to H— !" No deawt in a, tooathri year fro neaw, when Eddication an' Beha- viour ged a bit moore popular, fooak'll awter th words to "Go to Woking." Aw r'aly think aw shall be cremated, after o', be- cose its so varra healthy—nod for me, but for them as is left. Yo' know aw could ne'er fancy bein' t'en to the Cemetery, an' shoved in a hoyle wi' a tooathri' inch o' wayter in id, an' th' idea o' worms mek mi flesh areep. There's nowt o' thad soort abeawt Cre- mation, for after comin' eawt o'th' oon yo'r remains con be put in a bottle an' labelled an' put keerfully ! away. Aw like thad idea for some things, an' aw dorn'd like id for others. Id wod be easy enough willin' th' bottle an' contents to yo'r relayshuns an' friends, an' happen th' pro'oatO duty wodn'd.be varra heavy; an' th' treasure could be left to a local Museum : or,—i' my case—to th' British Museum, soon as mi admirers on th' Continent., an' in America, could come o'er bi a trip to see wocl were left on me. But there's this abeawt : Suppooase some good-for-nowt owned th' remains an' took id in his heead to tek 'em reawnd th' country as a show! Or popt 'em!! Fancy one lot at a sale bi auction o' unredeemed pledges bein' catalogued like this: "Lot 87. Glass bottle, with contents, being the cremated remains of Tum o' Dick o' Bobs." Imagine thad lot baize knockt deawn at tuppence! Yigh, an' one con imagine th' brokers comin' in an' th' bottle bein' atown ; or a descendant's child tekkin id for a plaything, an' lettin id fo'; or some wedgeheyd mis- takin id for a snuffbox, or for a scent bottle!

Th' Lord Mayor's Show seems to ha' bin a bit ov a wet fizz this year, an' o' through th' bad weather ; well, it's a pity. becose his Wership hed done his level best to mek id a best on record, but th' rain 'll put a damper on owt. Th' Lord Nlayor's a Welsh mon, an' gallant little Wales wor " on th' job," an' no mistake ; th' procession were real peasants, an' bards, an' miners fro' \Vales, an' th' rain fairly dud pelt deavrn on 'em. Talk abeawt th' Leek bein' i' evidence, id were all o'er th' shop; evenih' cleawds were full on 'em (leaks ; see ?) Yigh, an' there were Welsh airs to dinner, an' happen Welsh rapput, for owt as aw know.

Aw see there's just bin a book publish t bi a factory inspector o' th' name o' Taylor co'd The Modern Factory System; it's rayther too dear for th' fooak as owt to buy an read id, but aw hooap th' author 'll bring eawt a chep copy at—say a shillin', an' then he'll hey a big sale. Th' book shows as i' owden times th' main object o' th' operatives were to find a spot on th' oppen heath, wheere land could be getten for an owd song, an' werk could be done beawt ony interference fro' th' trade regulations o' th' teawn guilds; here he bed his cot, nn' grew his pratoes an' other green stuff when he worn'd weavin' or spinnin'. An' th' book tells abeawt an owd Berkshire manifact'rer co'd John Smallwood as lived four hundeld year sin' ; he hed two hunderd looms i' one reawm, a hunderd carders, two hundred spinners, a hunderd an' fifty childer to pick wool, fifty shearers, eighty "rowers," forty dyers, an' twenty fullers—oltoget- her welly a theawsand hands. Yigh, an' he fed 'em o' "ten good fat oxen" bein' killed every week for 'em; quite a co-op concern, eh? A hunderd o' th' werkmen mercht wi' him to Flodden Field to show as they could feight, as wed l as werk. Aw do hooap a chep edition 'll be browt eawt, becose theawsands upo' theawsands o' werkin' chaps wod spend scoores o' heawrs o'er id, wi' pleU- sure—an' benefit.

Its herdly possible for fooak as loves childer to realize th' truth o' some o' th' cases repoorted th' noospappers, o' parents bein' so inhuman wi' their own flesh an' blood ; they leave 'em deein' like dogs i' their filthy hovels, an' off they gooa slotchin' an' drinkin' at th' nearest jerry-shop. Sich like are nowt but brutes —nay, it's insultin' some o' th' brutes to compare 'em wi' sich waistrels ' an' it's a pity they con ged off wi' owt less nor th'eat. Some day we may hey institutions as'll he peawer to tek th' childer fro' em,an' then there'll be no excuse for keepin' th' parents eawt o' jail ; at th' present time a chap as ill-uses his wife has to support her when hoo leevos him—or welly sooa—an' why nod some law to protect th' chiider, an' at th' same time provide for their keep. We dorn'd seem to ha' progressed mieh sin' 3lrs. Browning wrooat " The cry of the children" an' towd us as
"The child's sobin the silence curses deeper Than the strong man in his wrath."

There's two items o' news i' th' pappers this week asle bide thinkin' o'er, an' th' fost is thad abeawt th' life boat men at Blackpool bein' on th' strike for better pay, an' a better booat ; well, fro' wod aw know o' them chaps—an' aw've spent seven year among 'ern—they're th' reight. We corn'd spent too mich brass i' mekkin' th' booats as good a, they con be tried, an' we corn'd fir a standard rate o' pay for sich werk as they do. It's to eawr shame iv th' society hesn'd enough brass i' hand to pay 'em gradely ;we gooa to th' seeaside every year, an' gi' to th' niggers, an' Punch an' Judy, an' to th' Salva- tion Army—becose we're religious! We mek eawr- sels ill wi' eytin' an' drinkin', an' enjoy eawrsels o' we con —but we ne'er think o' droppin' a penny i' th' lifebooat boxes. Why? Aw con only suppooase it's just becose id doesn'd come up to us an' bully us till we give, same as th' Punch an' Judy women does. Th next item is thad abeawt owd sowjers bein' gi'n a chance at vacant country pooastmonship after passin' a civil service examination! But we'll hey another word on this subject next week; th' mean- time it's wo'th thinkin' o'er, is this consideration fro' heydquarters.

div.head: FATALITY AT MORRIS BROOK
div.p: FATALITY AT MORRIS BROOK

\lr. H. C. Yates held an inquest on Wednesday afternoon, at Latchford Hospital, relative to the death of Joseph Tilsley, deputy foreman engine cleaner, 3, Toft's-yard, Hall-st., Warrington, whose body was found in the bottom of the Ship Canal cutting, at Morris Brook, a depth of thirty-five feet, on Monday morning. The evidence given was that deceased had left his work at eight p.m.on Saturday night, and went into Warrington, where he had some drink. He was last seen at eleven o'clock,at the end of Thelwall-lane, returning to his work. He was never missed until his body was found by a lad named James Jeffries. Mr. Ewart,agent for the Ship Canal, said deceased ought not to have left his work,as he was on night duty. Nothing suspicious was seen about the spot, and over 30s. was found on the body. Verdict of "Found dead" was re- turned.

div.head: FIRE AT WARRINGTON BARRACKS:
div.p: FIRE AT WARRINGTON BARRACKS:

On Thursday night a fire occurred at Orford Bar- racks, Warrington, but was got under before much damage was done. The fire was discovered by Sergt. Wilkes, and occurred in the office of Col. Kennedy, the paymaster of the military stationed at War- rington. District-Sergeant Wilkes, who is one of Colonel Kennedy's clerks, went to his office about a quarter to six and discovered some boards near the fireplace to be_alight. With great promptitude he summoned a couple of the pay office orderlies and despatched them for water, in the meantime re- porting the fire to the commander of the guard and Sergeant Majors Bailey and Day. The latter soon got a body of men at work, and, in a short time wholly extinguished the flames. Much credit is due to Sergeant Wilkes for his promptitude in reporting the fire, and also for his efforts in extin- guishing it. Among others Quartermaster-sergeant Considine and Sergeant Ward gave great help. A court of inquiry will probably be held in reference to the fire.

div.head: FIRE IN PORTER-STREET.
div.p: FIRE IN PORTER-STREET.

On Tuesday evening, about 5 o'clock, a fire was discovered to have broken out in a house occupied by Arthur Deeley, a lamp lighter, of 15, Porter-st. Two children aged 4 and 212- years respectively, had been left in the house by themselves. A man named Wm. Bennett, Deeley's father-in-law, was sent for, and he burst open the door,and,creeping in through the dense smoke that filled the house, found the children in a state of semi suffocation in the kit- chen. He got them out, but ;was almost himself overpowered by the smoke, and had to be assisted to the door by a man named James Unsworth. The mother of the children presently made her appear- ance with her baby in her arms, and entered the house to try to save some of the furniture, very foolishly carrying the infant in with her. She also was overcome by the smoke,and Police-Sergeant Jones had to release her from her dangerous position. That officer, with the assistance of some persons living near, managed to subdue the fhmes, but the furniture and a Cupboard in which the fire is sup- posed to have been accidentally originated by the children, were almost entirely destroyed. It ap- pears that the mother on leaving the house had locked the children in. There was a fire in the grate, but no matches were left lying about.

div.head: INDEPENDENT ORDER OF RECTIA.BITES. THE MAGISTRATES AND THE WATCH COMMITTEE.
div.p: INDEPENDENT ORDER OF RECTIA.BITES. THE MAGISTRATES AND THE WATCH COMMITTEE.

The annual tea party and concert in connection with the Independent Order of Rechabites, Charity Tent, were held in the Brick-street schoolroom, Warrington, on Tuesday evening. The entertain- ment was presided over by Mr. John Walker, but previeus to this there was an interesting ceremony, consisting of the formation by Bro. John Dimond, P.H.C.R., of Southport, of a juvenile tent and the imitiation by him into this of some 20 members. The ceremony having concluded, The Chairman, prefacing the entertainment, stated that the Charity Tent was founded in 1836, and was the fourth in age in the whole Order. The number of members at present was 84, 30 of whom had joined within the past two years. He also referred to the juvenile tent just formed, and the means of increasing its numbers. There was, he said, no Friendly Society that offered the advantages that the Order of Rechabites did. They kept their heads clear, and were able to do their work better, and ran less risk of accident than other bodies of men. Apart from that they had the satisfaction of feeling that they were free from alcohol, which, however diluted it might be, was more or less a poison, and this fact gave them more exemption from disease than those had who took drink even in small quantities. He was speaking a ' physiological truth when he said that the latest dis- coveries of science shewed that the beginning of disease in most cases, especially malignant and virulent disease, Proceeded from germs, bacteria, or bacilli, whatever you chose to call them. These very infinitesimal things were like seed sawn in a particular spot, so that the re- sult was that in a system weakened by exposure,neglect, or indulgence in intoxicants, these germs found a suit- able spot for development, and disease was more likely to be brought about. Statistics went to show that there ' was mole sickness and a larger percentage of deaths in all classes of Friendly Societies than in the Order of Rechabites. As to the branch in Warrington, it had more than deubled its number of members in the last two years : its sick fund was about £lOO and its death fund £5OO, which put together amounted to £6OO, equal to a little over £7 per member. He had now to say a word or two on the local side of the temperance question. They had, unfortunately, to remark that there was a very large field indeed for their exertions in Warrington. Somehow or other drink had got possession of this old town, and it was their business to do all they could to induce the people to take a turn for the better. 'Unfortunately, some of their rulers themselves, who Ought to set a good example, were doing, he was afraid, at times,just the reverse. Only the other day a question was raised, in the Police Court, as to whether it was de- sirable or not to extend the Lion Hotel, so as to give an opening into Ship-yard. The Chief Constable said that Ship-yard was a place noted for its disturbances and rows, and yet,in the face of that public statement,which ought to have impressed any body of men, the magis- trates decided, by way of quieting the disturbances and lessening the rows in Ship-yard, that a door should be opened out of the public-house into that yard. (" Shame.") Yes, it was a shame. (Applause.) It was a discredit to those who sat upon the Bench—(applause) and it was the duty of the citizens to protest against it. Pie had given the dark side of the picture, but they had a bright side to it. Some of those who had bean work- ing in the temperance cause felt it was wrong that any person connected with the drink traffic should have a seat upon the Watch Committee, whose duty it was to carry out the licensing laws. It was admitted in every town where public spirit was high that you could not do bettor than have the very best men in the Town Council on the Watch Committee. but in Warrington, through some carelessness,or indifference to the public welfare, a gentleman who was a brewerand was the owner of some 17 licensed houses had been allowed to take a seat upon the Watch Committee It was a scandal and a dis- credit to the town that it was ever permitted. (Ap- plause.) They had stirred in this matter and brought it before the public in the last municipal elections ; and he was pleased to say that, as the result, that person who held the seat his ought not to have held on the Watch Committee was on Monday removed from that Committee. (Renewed applause.) Although they had their seasons of discouragement, they had their occasions for congratulation, and they had always the consciousness of moving in the right direction. (Ap- plause.) Brother Dimond subsequently addressed the meet- ing. He said he was not there to advocate the theory of teetotalism: it had passed beyond the point of theory. He was there to strengthen their hands so that they might create a revolution of the right kind in War- rington. The drinking austoms were very strong there, but the strength of the teetotal movement was so great that it was able to carry sll before it. The speaker ex- patiated on the growth of Rechbitism,stating that it had now 100,000 members. Referring to the business carried on by Sir A. B. Walker, he remarked that the profits he obtained every Sunday from public-houses he owned in Liverpool would found an art gallery there every year at a cost of £30,000. Was it not a shame that su.th pro- fits should be built upon the wreck and ruin, the misery and degradation of the vast masses of people who inhabited the dark spot on the Mersey it The entertainment, consisted of a song by Mr. R. Broomhead, duets by Messrs. J. and W. Critchley, H. Dutton, and Flazledine, and Broomhead and Lightfoot, a reading by Mr. W. Wright, a recitation by Mr. B. Few, a round by a glee party and a dialogue entitled" Apart- ments to let," by James Shaw, W. Wright, R. Henshall and R. Hazeldine. Votes of thanks were accorded to the Chairman and to Bro. Dimond.

Mr. Whymper, Chief Inspector of Factories, in the course of his evidence, on Tuesday, before the Royal Commission on Labour, complained of the inadequacy of the inspecting staff for the proper administration of the existing Factory Acts.

div.head: CONSERVATIVE WARD MEETINGS.
div.p: CONSERVATIVE WARD MEETINGS.

A meeting of the Conservative Committee of the Town Hall Ward, in accordance with a resolution passed at a meeting of the Council of the Association on Friday evening, was held in the Committee room of the Conservative Club, Warrington, on Tuesday evening, "for the purpose of appointing six dele- gates to meet the Council on the 27th inst., to con- sider the selection of a Conservative candidate to contest the borough at the approaching general election." Councillor Smethurst presided, and thanked the • burgesses of the ward for having returned him as their representative at the recent election by a majority of 41 votes. They had had to meet two oppos- ing elements. The Trades Council asked the candidates certain questions, and he believed that he answered them fairly. He published the questions and his answers on the walls, to enable the public to judge between himself and the Council, and the public decided in his fav- our. He did not like bigotry, either on the part of teetotalers or publicans. A temperance circular had boen sent out signed by two gentlemen, but one of them denied that he had authorised his same to be attached to it. To issue a circular under such circumstances was disgraceful. However, he had come out of the fight successfully, and the Conservatives could afford to be generous. Referring to the Watch Committee Council- lor Smethurst said that at his first appearance in the Council Chamber he endeavoured to be fair, and refused to vote for Councillor Bolton being elected a member of I the Watch Committee ; with all the energy he possessed he should equally object to the appointment of Council- lor Henry Roberts or any other strong partizan. The meeting then appointed the following gentlemen as the delegates to meet the Council of the Conservative Associ- ation :—Messrs. William Johnson,James Woods, William Watson, John Titchard, Captain J. C. Ridgway, and the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton. Meetings have also been held in Whitecross and Bewsey Wards. The delegates for Whitecross Ward are Messrs. Walter Milner, lienry Rent, Benjamin Kenyon. Henry Isherwood, R. G. Woolacott, and Saul Mason, and for Bewsey Ward Messrs. E. M. Crosfield, T. H. Pearson, George Bobbington, Alfred J. Jolley, William Atherton, and John Baird. At meetings held at the Conservative Club on Wednes- day and Thursday evenings the following delegates were appointed for the wards named :—Town Hall Ward.— Messrs. W. Johnson, and James Woods, the Rev. E. C. E Carleton,Messrs. William Watson,and John Titchard,and Captain J. C. Ridgway. St. John's Ward.—Messrs. W. D. Jeans, D. Bawling, Thomas Cuppage, J. C. 6'utton, T. C. Brookes. and Ralph Clarke. Fairfield Ward.—Cap- tain T. E. Withington; Messrs. John Brown, H. S. Essenhigh,L. W. Reynolds, and Wm. Johnson,and Major Pickmere. Orford Ward.—Messrs. William Carson, Wal- ter Jones, C. D. Parkinson, Vere R. Davies, Gilbert Greenall, W. B. Greener. Howley Ward.—Messrs. Joseph Burchall, John Dewhurst, L. W. Reynolds, R. W. Marsh, George Jones, and John Whitly. St. Austin's Ward: Messrs. J. Bailey, H. R. Horrobin, John Skelton, Charles Skinner, H. N. Houghton. and G. Nunnerley. Latchford: Messrs. D. W. Finney,Walter Jackson, Thos. Jackson, W. H. Young, and J. Wesley Tauranac, and the Rev. F. L. Good.

div.p: A FLOODED TOWN.
The River Paraett, n3ar Langport. Somersetshire, has burst its banks. The main streets of Langport are sub- merged.
WRECK OF A SCHOONER.
The Norwegian schooner Forgarit was wrecked outside West Wymss Harbour, Fifeshire yesterday. The crew were saved. THE FIFTY-THREE MARBLES BOY.
The Cardiff Joy who, a few days ago, swallowed, for a wager, fifty-three marbles, has been discharged from the infirmary, the marbles having been extracted.
NAILNIAKERS GET 10 PER CENT. ADVANCE.
The wrought iron nailinakers in Staffordshire and East Worcestershire returned to work yesterday, the employers having granted them 10 per cent. advance.
SOUTH MOLTON ELECTION.

The polling commenced in the Scuth Alolton Division yesterday, the candidates being Mr. Buller (Liberal Unionist), and Mr. Lambert (Gladstonian Liberal.) Both parties seem equally confident of success. The result will be declared this afternoon. DEATH OF A CHESHIRE MAGISTRATE.

Yesterday morning, Mr. F. G. Symonds, J.P., died at his residence at Sale, from a fit of apoplexy very sud- denly. He took a very active interest in local affairs. In politics, he was a Conservative,and until a fortnight ago, when he was presented with an illuminated address he was chairman of the Sale Conservative Association. DESTRUCTIVE FIRES.
The premises of Messrs. Evans and Co., wholesale druggists, Liverpool, were burned down yesterday morning. .
A large cotton mill was burned down at Stockport, yesterday. The mill belonged te Messrs. Balfe and Co., Corporation-street. WRECKS AND LOSS OF LIFE.
Lloyd's state that the fishing ketch Test arrived at Brightlingsea on Thursday night, and reported the mas- ter and one man washed overboard.
The barque Gylfe, for Liverpool, was stranded on Thursday night west of Old Head, Kinsale, and was wrecked. The captain and four of the crew were saved, but seven of the hands were drowned.

FATAL FIREDAMP EXPLOSION. ELEVEN MINERS KILLED. ESSEN, FRIDAY.—An explosion of firedamp occurred yesterday at the Koenig Ludwig Coal Pit, by w hich eleven miners were killed and two injured. ARREST OF A GERMAN BANKER. BERLIN FRIDAY.—Herr Maass, a well-known banker at Charlottenburg, has been arrested on charges of fraud. The arrest has caused great sensation.

div.head: MA ItKET.S.
div.p: MA ItKET.S.

LIVERPOOL PROVISIONS. FRIDAY.—Beef is quiet, an buyers have a slight advantage. Pork has a slow sale at th quotations. Bacon met a steady demand, and previ ou values are maintained. Hams sell steadily at the quotations. Shoulders rule firmer, especially fresh landed parcels of New York cut, same being in limited supply. Butter shows no change. Lard is very firm, and only few sellers. Imports of fresh Beef from New York, 4.411 cwts. Imports of salted provisions :—Bacon, 238 boxes; Hams 191 boxes; Cheese, 3.230 boxes; Butter, 140 packages; and Lard. 3 tons.—Cable advices from America received to-day quote Hogs, Lard and Bacon without material change. MANCHESTER TRADE, FRIDA.Y.—Cotton is not in good form, futures to not improve, and spot transactions are covered by the first estimate of 6,000 bales, Brown Egyptian some Brazilian being quoted 1-16 lower. Bundles are in a bad way, and stocks that have not looked well for some time look less attractive to-day. Printers are difficult to move either in good or common qualities, and prices favour buyers. China demand does not improve, and few lines of magnitude are moving in India goods. CORK BUTTER, FRIDAY. Ordinary : Firsts, 115 s; seaonds, 100 s. ; thirds, 93s ; fourths, 82s. div.head: EtA.L CLUB.
div.p: EtA.L CLUB.
ANNUAL MEETING
TON LIBE
OF THE WARRING-

On Tuesday evening the annual genetal meeting of the members of Liberal Club was held in the large billiard-room, the chair being occupied by Councillor J. H. Fleming, president. There was a good attendance, amongst those present being Coun- cillors G. Plumpton, Arthur Browne, S. J. Beaman, and J. Garner; Messrs. William Pierpoint, J. Rymer Young, Joseph Albinson, D. Tinnion, Alfred Perris, and Thomas Pemberton (hon. secretary). The Secretary presented his annual report and balance- sheet, from which it appeared that a handsome profit had been made during the past year. The report and balance-sheet were yaanimously adopted, on the motion of Mr. Pierpoint, seconded by Mr. Tinnion. The following officers were elected for the ensuing 12 months, viz., Councillor Fleming, president; Messrs. W. Pierpoint, Thomas Morris, and William Roberts, vice-presidents; Mr. John Crosfield, hon. treasurer; Mr. T. Pemberton, hon. secretary; Corn- mitt ee,Messrs.D. Tinnion,C. Jackson Holmes,J. Albin- son, J. R. Calvert, W. Gilbert, S. J. Beaman, T. Critch- ley, A. Browne, J. E. Warren, and Robert Bennett; auditors, Messrs. J. W. Bouchier and John Harrison. Votes of thanks were accorded to the president, officers, and Committee, special references being made to the valuable services rendered by the Secre- tary during the past five years. It is, we understand, intended to present a handsome testimonial to him; and a substantial sum has already been promised.

A man named Edward Osborne, aged 51, was on Wed- nesday remanded at the West Ham Police Court, on a charge of attempted wife murder. The woman, who has fourteen scalp wounds and a fractured skull lies :in a oritical condition.
WARRINGTON.
"THINGS THAT ARE PERFECT."
The Rev. J. Warnock occupied the pulpit of St. John's Presbyterian Church, on Sunday, taking for his subject "Things that are perfect." There was a good congregation.

div.head: MAGISTERIAL DELAY AGAIN.
div.p: MAGISTERIAL DELAY AGAIN.

At the Borough Police Court, on Tuesday morn- ing, Mr. E. J. Guest was the only magistrate pre- sent at the hour for commencing the business, and a ease of attempted suicide having been disposed of by him, there was a delay of over ten minutes,as the remainder of the cases necessitated the pre- sence of two magistrates, when Mr. W. Owen made his appearance and the court was resumed.

div.head: DRUIDS' PRESENTATION.
div.p: DRUIDS' PRESENTATION.

On Saturday a presentation took place in connec- tion with the Isle of Mona Lodge of the order of Druids. The presentation took the form of an emblem of merit to P.A. David Percival, for the services he had rendered to the lodge. The pre- sentation was made by the treasurer of the lodge, before a large number of members. Several short, speeches were made, and the proceedings passed off in a most successful manner. STARR-BOWKRTT APPROPRIATION.

An appropriation meeting of the second War- rington Starr Bowkett Society was held in the Legh-st. school-room, on Monday eTening. Mr. E. Aukland presided, and there was a fair attendance of members. Mr. Longshaw and Mr. Hassan acted as scrutineers, and a girl named Maggie Hill drew the ballot balls. As the result of the ballot, Mrs. Mary Broughton, of Market-st., was entitled to the use of £4OO free of interest for 112- years.

div.head: Z.T. PETER'S CHURCH.
div.p: Z.T. PETER'S CHURCH.

At the last meeting of the building committee, held in St. Peter's vestry, Mr. John Murray (hon. treas.) submitted a balance sheet from which it ap- pears that the receipts for the church building fund amount to £4,359 7s. 4d., and the cost of structure to £4,353 148. 3d., leaving a balance in hand of .25 13s. id. The total cost of the chuzch and fittings amounts to £4,508 19s. 2d. All the bills have been paid, the accounts audited, and the church is free from debt.
WESLEYAN MUTUAL .13IPROVEMENT SOCIETY,'
BOLD-ST.

On Monday a musical evening was held in con- nection with the above society. Miss N.Picton and Miss A. Bawling charmingly rendered the songs al- lotted to them, and Miss A. Toft played two violin solos in a pleasing manner. Miss Pigot, Miss Toft, and Al r.Sleigh acted as accomparnsts,and were very efficient. During the meeting Miss Perkins read a capital paper on "Courtesy." Mr. C. 11. Kerry,one of the vice-presidents, occupied the chair. The room was full, and a most enjoyable evening was spent

THE YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION DEBATING SOCIRTY.

This Society held its meeting on Thursday night, Mr. H. Horden in the chair. Impromptu speaking was the order of the evening. The subjects, which were ballotted for, were "How to be happy though single" the introduction of which fell to the lot of Mr. Ainsworth, and "Temperance a stumbling block to sociability" the introduction of which bill to the lot of Mr. Stringer. Discussion upon each topic was heartily engaged in, the meeting coming to the conclusion that it is possible to be happy though single, and that though there are no doubt many failings in connection with temperance reform, we ought not to condemn temperance reform on that account but try to remety its faults.

div.head: GAPPENHALL SCHOOLS.
div.p: GAPPENHALL SCHOOLS.

The little village of Grappenhall has been mind- ing i..s own business in a very satisfactory way. Advantage has recently been taken of the Govern- ment grant to reduce the school fees and make the school self-supporting. Under the old system a debt of about £B5 has accumulated, and an attempt has made to clear this oft by private subscription, with such success that within a fortnight the whole amount has been promised. Mr. J. Charlton Parr has, as his share, doubled the amount of the largest subscription, and two out of every three to whom circulars were sent have contributed.

div.head: SOCIAL EVENING.
div.p: A SOCIAL EVENING.

Last night week the agents of the Refuge Assur- ance Company in this district, with their wives, held a social meeting in the Academy-st. Mission Chapel. After a splendid tea the room was cleared and Mr. Thornton tcok the chair. In a few words he expressed the pleasure it gave him to meet in a social manner with those present. He also spoke in a complimentary manner of the Warrington agents of the Company. An excellent musical entertain- ment was then given, the following taking part: Mr. Richardson, Messrs. Thornton, Mr. Robins, Mr. Atkinson, Mr. Rutter, Mrs. Dutton, Mr. Critchley, and Mr. Williams. THE SONGSTRESSES OF SCOTLAND.

On Monday evening at the usual weekly meeting of the Wycliffe Young People's Society, Mr. Corney read a paper on "The songstresses of Scotland." There was a good attendance, the Rev. J. Yonge presiding. Mr. Corney in the course of his paper gave the history of some of the most popular songs- tresses ot Scotland, and several of their songs were sung as solos during the evening by the following: Mrs. Jeffery, lis & Bali, mtss B. bllbuLle, Miss Payton, Miss Kershaw, and Me6srs. Browne, Booth, J. H. Yonge, and Knowles. Mr. Payton accompanied on the piano. At the close a vote of thanks to the essayist for his excellent paper, and to all who had assisted him, was passed. Mr. Corney responded, and the meeting terminated.

div.head: TEA PARTY AT MOORE.
div.p: TEA PARTY AT MOORE.

On Monday a tea party in connection with the Band of Hope Sot;iety was Iheld in the Wesleyan Chapel schoolroom. At 5.30 the juvenile members, numbering about 50,sat down to tea,and afterwards the adult members were entertained. Tea being over, an entertainment consisting of songs, duets, recitations, and readings was given by Mrs. Birch, MiE ' Dolling, Miss Hambling, and others. Mr. Roy- lance presided, and the songs,&c., were accompanied by Mr. S. B. Hambling, and by Mr. Wm. Cartwright on the violin. Miss B. Dutton, lion. secretary for the district Band of Hope, made a statement res- pecting the condition of the society,and was pleased to inform them that at the present time they had over 100 members on the books. The singing of the Doxology about nine o'clock terminated the even- mg's pleasant entertainment.

div.head: INFIRMARY CONCERT.
div.p: INFIRMARY CONCERT.

The annual concert promoted by the Working men's Infirmary Committee was held in the Public Hall on Saturday. There was a large attendance. The Mayor (Alderman Francomb) presided, and mentioned that he had received letters of apology for non-attendance from Mr. P. Stubs, Mr. J. C. Parr, Mr. Bleckly, the Rector, Mr. R. Pierpoint, Mr. J. Marson, Captain Withington, Mr. J. White, Mr. Buckton, and others. That concert, he said, was got up by the working-men of the town who in ten years had subscribed to the Infirmary at their works £4,289 3s. Op., and the concerts for the ten years had realised the very handsome sum of £455 Ms. 10d. (Applause.) Ile thought it was the duty of every one of them to do all they could for the Warrington Infirmary, and he believed it was the determination of every one present that the Infir- mary should be kept in an efficient state. (Applause.)—An excellent programme of music was then rendered. It included several performances by the band, conducted by Mr. T. J. Down, which was much appreciated. Thpre were also songs by Mr. R. Eccles, .Miss Fanshawe, Mr. Pierce Hughes, Madame Ashworth Hughes, and Mr. Harry Collins. The concert was a success from a musical point of view. Mr. Riley again efficiently acted as pianist. The receipts from the concert were £49 Bs. id., and the expenditure was £2O is. 4d., leaving a balance of £29 6s. 9d., which has been handed over to the Infirmary authorities by the treasurer of the workingmen's com- mitte, Mr. E. M. Crosfield.
ORANGE BALL.-SIR GILBERT GREENALL AND THE
ORANGEMEN.

The twenty-second annual ball was held on Mon- day evening at the assembly room of the Conserva- tive Club, in aid of the Benevolent Fund of the Loyal Orange Institution of Warrington, and in commemoration ot the landing of William 111., Prince of Orange. Bro W. Bloomfield, D.M., was present, and the officers of the society, who appeared in full regalia. Bro. Watmough acted as M.C., and the music for dancing, which commenced at eight o'clock, and was kept up with spirit for several hours, was supplied by Mr. J. Buckland's quadrille band. About 200 persons were present. The catering was in the hands of Mr. and Mrs. Higham.—During an interval in the dancing, Bro. William Bloomfield made a short speech, in which he referred to the refusal of Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., M.P., to be the Conservative candidate at the next general election. As a body of Orangemen they were sorry to hear of his resignation ; and all of them would support him if he again contested the borough. It would be safe in his hands. At, the last general election five questions were submitted to Sir Gilbert, all of which he answersd to the satis- faction of Orangemen, and they expectedsimilar answers to be given by the next Conservative can- didate. It was not necessary for him to state what the answers were, but Sir Gilbert's refusal to serve again was very much regretted by the Orangemen thr)ughout the borough.

div.head: CHAIRMEN OF COMMITTEES.
div.p: CHAIRMEN OF COMMITTEES.

During the week the following chairmen and vice-chairmen of Committees of the Town Council have been appointed. Watch Committee: Mayor, chairman, and Alderman Harrison, vice-chairman; Town Hall, Park and Baths Committee : Alderman Chandley, chairman, and Councillor Bolton, vice- chairman; Gas Committee: Alderman Holmes, chairman, and Councillor R. T. Fairclough, vice- chairman; School Attendance Committee: Coun- cillor Fleming,chairman,and Councillor Sha w Green, vice-chairman. The School Attendance Corn in itteo also decided in future to hold their meetings every alternate Thursday at 7 o'clock instead of at three o'clock in the afternoon as heretofore. At a meet— ing of the Nfuseum, &c. coarnittee, yesterday, Mr F. Monks was elected chairman, Councillor H. Roberts, senior, vice-chairman, and Councillor L. Greening, junior, vice-chairman.

div.head: WARRINGTON DEBATING SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON DEBATING SOCIETY.

The weekly meeting of this society was held on Wednesday evening in the Masonic Rooms, Sankey- St. Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins presided, and there was a good attendance. Mr. A. Bennett introduced a dis— cussion on the subject," Why change the Govern- ment?" in which he strongly upheld the view that there was no need for a change. He made a com- parison between the achievements of the present government and that of Mr. Gladstone's government of 1880, very much to the advantage of the present government. He argued that even with regard to the Liberal cry of "Peace, retrenchment, and re— ..

form," the policy of Lord Salisbury had been much more successful than that of Mr. Gladstone. The de- bate which followed was an interesting one, those taking part in it being Messrs. Dutton, Hall, E. A. White, Kent, E. Ford, Diggle, Summers, and the Chairman.

div.head: LATCHFORD GOOD TEMPLAR&
div.p: LATCHFORD GOOD TEMPLAR&

The usual weekly session of the Latchford Good Templars was held in the Temperance Hall,on Mon- day evening. The lodge business being over, the following programme of songs, readings, &c., was given, for which the sisters were responsible. The song" Oh, weep for the fallen," as a chorus ; a part song, entitled "If I was a voice." by Mr. D. Ellison, a reading by Bro. L. Ellison, on "The temptation to drink," urging the younger memoers to abstain from alcohol; a song by Sister Jones, entitled "Precious name ;" a reading by Bro. Cooper, on " Happy Homes;" another by Bro. Cook, entitled "Drink, or no drink ;" and a short address by Bro. Adams, bearing upon the advisability of sending representatives to Parliament who were in favour of the local veto. A vote of thanks was then ac- corded to the sisters for their trouble in arranging the programme. THE CHESHIRE AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.

A meeting of the local committee formed in con- nection with the propcsed holding, in 1892, ot the Cheshire Agricultural Society's Show in Warrington was held, on Thursday afternoon, in the Town Hall, the Mayor (Aid. Greenall) presiding. Subscriptions amounting to .£354 were announced, and this sum the Committee considered highly satisfactory, and affording every hope that the amount required, .£5OO, would be realised. A sub-committee consist- ing of the Mayor, Messrs. Gilbert Greenall, Colin Mclver, James Tinsley and H. Milling, were appointed to wait upon the Council of the Agricul- tural Society, at Crewe on the 25th inst., to present a memorial asking the society to hold their show of 1892 at Warrington. It was also decided to con- tinue the subscription list until furthur notice. The Mayor was appointed Chairman of the local Committee. There is every reason to believe that the show will be held in Warriagton next year, and the site will be that adjoining the football field in Wilderspool Causeway. The local Committee will, we understand, ask the society to give prizes for exhibits of local industries. HEALTH AND WEATHER OF WARRINGTON.

For week ending Saturday, 7th Nov., 1891, which was the 45th of the cuirent year, the following births and deaths were registered :—Births : War- rington, 43; Latchford, 6; total 49. Deaths: IVar- rington, 25; Latchford, 5; total 30. The excess of births ovt.r deaths was 19. The death-ratd from all causes was equal to 29.4 per 1,000 against, 25, the average of the previous four weeks, and against 16.64 the corresponding week of last year. The death rate from the seven chief zymotic diseases was equal to 5•9 per 1,000, against 6.34, the average rats or the four incvioue WeCk3, and egainet 1.01 th• corresponding week of 1890. The ages of mortality were- 0 to 1, 8 ; 1 to 5, 12; 5 to 15, 2 ; 15 to 25, 1; 25 to 60, 3; 60 upwards, 4; total 30. The deaths included-2 from measles, 2 from diarrhoea, 1 from phthisis, 3 from brain disease, 9 from lung disease, 2 from tubercular disease, 2 from whooping cough, 3 from diseases of organs of digestion, 1 from results of a fall, 1 from injuries from being run over by a wagon. The following cases of infectious disease have been reported during the week :—Scarlatina ease, typhoid fever lease. Meteor eloyy—The mean temperature was 44.1 Fah., and therefore about the same as the preceding week. The maximum tern- Deraturs 54 F., was reported on the 3rd inst., and the minimum temperature 26 F., on the Is t inst. The rainfall measured nil. The general direc- tion of Ole wind was easterly, the reading of the Anemometer denoting 680 miles.—Joux 11. GOI111.• ILL, Medical Officer of Health.
